long_notes.Induced EMF and Faraday's law:
Induced EMF (Electromotive Force) – The voltage generated in a closed circuit when the magnetic flux through the circuit changes with time.

Faraday’s Law

  • For a single turn: $\mathcal{E}= -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$
  • For $N$ turns: $\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$

where $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ is the magnetic flux ($B$ – magnetic field in tesla, $A$ – area in $m^2$, $\theta$ – angle between $B$ and normal to the loop).

Lenz’s Law – The direction of the induced emf is such that the induced current creates a magnetic field opposing the change in original flux.

QuantitySymbolFormulaSI Unit
Induced emf$\mathcal{E}$$-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$V
Magnetic flux$\Phi$$BA\cos\theta$Wb
Motional emf$Blv$V

Derivation (motional emf): A straight conductor of length $l$ moves with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. The magnetic force on charge $q$ is $F = qvB$. Since $F = q\mathcal{E}$, $\mathcal{E}=vBl$.

Example:

A rectangular loop of width $0.1\,$m and height $0.2\,$m is pulled out of a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\,$T at a constant speed $v=0.3\,$m/s. Find the induced emf while the loop is leaving the field.

Only the side of length $0.2\,$m cuts the flux. Using $\mathcal{E}=Blv$, $\mathcal{E}=0.5\times0.2\times0.3=0.03\,$V. The polarity is such that the induced current opposes the decrease of flux (Lenz’s law).
long_notes.Lenz's law and its applications:
Definition (Lenz’s Law): The induced emf in a closed circuit always opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.

Mathematical Form:

  • Induced emf $\\mathcal{E}= -\\dfrac{d\\Phi}{dt}$
  • Direction given by right‑hand rule for the induced current.

Key Derivation:

StepExpression
Magnetic flux$\\Phi = \\int \\mathbf{B}\\cdot d\\mathbf{A}$
Faraday’s law$\\mathcal{E}= -\\dfrac{d\\Phi}{dt}$
Using $\\mathcal{E}= -N\\dfrac{d\\phi}{dt}$ for $N$ turns$\\mathcal{E}= -N\\dfrac{d}{dt}(BA\\cos\\theta)$

SI Units: emf – volt (V), magnetic flux – weber (Wb), magnetic field – tesla (T), area – $\\text{m}^2$.

Applications:

  • Eddy current brakes
  • Induction cookers
  • Metal detectors
  • Generators and transformers

Example (Solved): A rectangular loop $0.10\\,\\text{m}\\times0.20\\,\\text{m}$ moves with speed $v=2\\,\\text{m s}^{-1}$ into a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\\,\\text{T}$ perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Find the magnitude of the induced emf when the loop is partially inside the field.

Solution: Flux $\\Phi = B\\,l\\,x$, where $x$ is the length inside the field. $\\dfrac{dx}{dt}=v$, so $\\mathcal{E}= -\\dfrac{d\\Phi}{dt}= -B\\,l\\,\\dfrac{dx}{dt}= -B\\,l\\,v$. Substituting $B=0.5\\,\\text{T}$, $l=0.20\\,\\text{m}$, $v=2\\,\\text{m s}^{-1}$ gives $\\mathcal{E}= -(0.5)(0.20)(2)= -0.20\\,\\text{V}$. Magnitude $=0.20\\,\\text{V}$.
long_notes.Self induction and mutual induction:
Self Induction – When a time‑varying current $i(t)$ flows through a coil, the changing magnetic flux linked with the coil itself induces an emf $\\mathcal{E}$ that opposes the change (Lenz’s law).

  • Flux linkage $\\lambda = N\\Phi$.
  • Induced emf $\\mathcal{E} = -\\dfrac{d\\lambda}{dt}= -L\\dfrac{di}{dt}$.
  • Self‑inductance $L = \\dfrac{N\\Phi}{i}$, SI unit henry (H) = $\\dfrac{Wb}{A}$.

Mutual Induction – A varying current in one coil (primary) produces a changing flux that links a second coil (secondary), inducing an emf in the latter.

  • Mutual inductance $M = \\dfrac{N_2\\Phi_{12}}{i_1}=\\dfrac{N_1\\Phi_{21}}{i_2}$.
  • Induced emf in secondary $\\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\\dfrac{di_1}{dt}$.
  • SI unit also henry.

Key Relations

QuantityExpression
Self‑inductance $L$$L = \\dfrac{\\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$ (solenoid)
Mutual inductance $M$$M = k\\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, $0\\le k\\le1$
Energy stored$U = \\dfrac{1}{2}Li^2 = \\dfrac{1}{2}Mi_1i_2$

Example

A solenoid has $N=500$ turns, length $l=0.20\\,\\text{m}$, cross‑section $A=2\\times10^{-4}\\,\\text{m}^2$. The current changes at $\\dfrac{di}{dt}=3\\,\\text{A s}^{-1}$. Find the induced emf.

Solution:

  1. Compute $L = \\dfrac{\\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}=\\dfrac{4\\pi\\times10^{-7}\\times 500^2\\times2\\times10^{-4}}{0.20}=\\,\\text{... H}$ → $L\\approx 1.57\\times10^{-3}\\,\\text{H}$.
  2. Induced emf $|\\mathcal{E}| = L\\dfrac{di}{dt}=1.57\\times10^{-3}\\times3\\approx4.7\\times10^{-3}\\,\\text{V}$.

Thus $\\mathcal{E}\\approx4.7\\,\\text{mV}$, opposing the increase of current.
long_notes.Eddy currents and their effects:
Definition: Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in a bulk conductor when it is subjected to a time‑varying magnetic flux. They flow in closed loops perpendicular to the magnetic field and oppose the change in flux (Lenz's law).

Cause & Effect:

  • Relative motion between a conductor and magnetic field or a varying field induces emf $e=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$.
  • Resulting currents produce magnetic fields that oppose motion – used in magnetic braking, induction heating, and levitation.
  • Energy dissipated as heat: $P=I^{2}R$.

Key Formulas

QuantitySymbolFormulaSI Unit
Induced emf$e$$e=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$volt (V)
Current density (thin plate)$J$$J=\sigma B v$ampere per square metre (A/m$^2$)
Power loss (laminated plate)$P$$P=\frac{B^{2} t^{2} v^{2}}{6\rho}\,A$watt (W)

Mitigation: Use laminated cores, high‑resistivity alloys, or slotted conductors to break the current paths.

Example

A copper plate of thickness $t=2\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}$, width $w=0.10\,\text{m}$ and length $l=0.20\,\text{m}$ moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5\,\text{T}$ with speed $v=5\,\text{m/s}$. Copper resistivity $\rho=1.68\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$. Find the eddy‑current power loss.

Solution:

  1. Area $A = w\times l = 0.10\times0.20 = 0.020\,\text{m}^2$.
  2. Use $P=\frac{B^{2} t^{2} v^{2}}{6\rho}\,A$.
  3. Substitute: $P = \frac{(0.5)^{2}(2\times10^{-3})^{2}(5)^{2}}{6\times1.68\times10^{-8}}\times0.020$.
  4. Calculate numerator: $(0.5)^{2}=0.25$, $(2\times10^{-3})^{2}=4\times10^{-6}$, $(5)^{2}=25$ → $0.25\times4\times10^{-6}\times25 = 2.5\times10^{-5}$.
  5. Denominator: $6\times1.68\times10^{-8}=1.008\times10^{-7}$.
  6. $P = \frac{2.5\times10^{-5}}{1.008\times10^{-7}}\times0.020 \approx 248\,\text{W}$.

Thus the moving plate dissipates approximately $2.5\times10^{2}\,\text{W}$ as heat due to eddy currents.
long_notes.Alternating current (AC) generator and d:
AC Generator (Alternator) – A device that converts mechanical rotation into alternating emf by the principle of electromagnetic induction. When a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates in a uniform magnetic field $B$, the magnetic flux through the coil is $\Phi = N B A \cos \theta$, where $\theta = \omega t$.

Differentiating, the induced emf is
$$\mathcal{E}= -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}= N B A \omega \sin \omega t$$

  • Peak emf $E_{0}=N B A \omega$ (unit: V)
  • RMS emf $E_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{E_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
  • Angular speed $\omega =2\pi f$ (rad/s), $f$ \in Hz

Dynamos (DC Generators) – An AC generator equipped with a split‑ring commutator that reverses the connection of the coil every half‑turn, delivering unidirectional (DC) output. The generated emf is

$$E = \frac{P \Phi Z N}{60 A}$$

  • $P$ – number of poles
  • $\Phi$ – flux per pole (Wb)
  • $Z$ – total conductors
  • $N$ – speed \in r.p.m.
  • $A$ – number of parallel paths

Key Units

QuantitySI Unit
Magnetic field $B$tesla (T)
Area $A$square metre (m$^2$)
Angular speed $\omega$radian per second (rad/s)
Emf $\mathcal{E}$volt (V)

Solved Example

Find the peak emf of a coil having $N=200$ turns, area $A=0.01\,\text{m}^2$, placed \in a magnetic field $B=0.5\,\text{T}$ and rotating at $50$ revolutions per second.

Angular speed $\omega =2\pi\times 50 =100\pi\,\text{rad/s}$.
Peak emf $E_{0}=N B A \omega =200\times0.5\times0.01\times100\pi =100\pi\,\text{V}\approx 314\,\text{V}$.

Thus the generator produces a sinusoidal emf of amplitude $\approx 314\,$V and rms value $\approx 222\,$V.
long_notes.Induction in solenoids, toroids and coil:
Induction in Solenoids, Toroids and Coils

When the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf $e$ is induced (Faraday’s law): $e=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$, where $N$ is the number of turns and $\Phi$ is the flux through one turn. The negative sign denotes Lenz’s law.

Key formulas

QuantityExpressionSI Unit
Flux through a solenoid$\Phi=BA=\mu_0 n I A$weber (Wb)
Induced emf (solenoid)$e=-\mu_0 n A\frac{dI}{dt}$volt (V)
Self‑inductance (solenoid)$L=\mu_0 n^2 A l$henry (H)
Magnetic field (toroid)$B=\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$tesla (T)
Flux per turn (toroid)$\Phi=\frac{\mu_0 N I A}{2\pi r}$Wb
Induced emf (toroid)$e=-\frac{\mu_0 N A}{2\pi r}\frac{dI}{dt}$V
Self‑inductance (toroid)$L=\frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{2\pi r}$H

SI Units

  • Inductance – henry (H) = V·s·A⁻¹
  • Magnetic flux – weber (Wb) = V·s

Example

A solenoid of length $l=0.5\,\text{m}$, $N=200$ turns and cross‑sectional area $A=2\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2$ carries a current that rises uniformly from $0$ to $3\,\text{A}$ in $0.02\,\text{s}$. Find the induced emf.

Solution:

  • Turns per unit length $n=\frac{N}{l}=\frac{200}{0.5}=400\,\text{turn/m}$.
  • Self‑inductance $L=\mu_0 n^2 A l=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times400^2\times2\times10^{-4}\times0.5\approx2.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{H}$.
  • Rate of change of current $\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{3-0}{0.02}=150\,\text{A/s}$.
  • Induced emf $e = L\frac{dI}{dt}=2.0\times10^{-5}\times150\approx3.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{V}$ (≈3 mV).

This result follows directly from $e = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$, confirming Lenz’s law (the emf opposes the increase of current).
long_notes.Energy stored in magnetic fields and ind:
Energy stored in magnetic field

When a current $I$ flows through an inductor of inductance $L$, a magnetic field is set up. The work done in establishing this field is stored as magnetic potential energy $U$.

  • Definition: $U$ is the energy required to build the magnetic field from zero to its final value.
  • Derivation: $dU = V_L\,dQ = L I\,dI$ (since $V_L = L\,dI/dt$ and $dQ = I\,dt$). Integrating, $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$.
  • SI unit: joule (J). $L$ in henry (H), $I$ in ampere (A).
  • Energy density in a uniform magnetic field: $u = \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_0}$ (J/m$^{3}$).

Energy in terms of flux linkage

For a coil with $N$ turns, flux linkage $\lambda = N\Phi$. Energy can also be written as $U = \frac{1}{2\lambda}\,\lambda^{2}= \frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$ where $L = \lambda/I$.

QuantitySymbolFormulaUnit
Inductance$L$$L = \frac{N\Phi}{I}$henry (H)
Magnetic energy$U$$U = \frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$joule (J)

Example

Find the energy stored in a $5\,$H inductor carrying $2\,$A.

Solution: $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\times5\times(2)^{2}= \frac{1}{2}\times5\times4 = 10\,$J.
long_notes.Practical applications of electromagneti:
Definition: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an emf ($e$) in a closed circuit when the magnetic flux linking the circuit changes with time.

Fundamental formula

QuantityExpressionSI unit
Induced emf$e = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$V

Practical applications

  • AC generator (alternator): Rotating coil in uniform $B$ gives $E_{max}=2\pi f N B A$. $f$ in Hz, $A$ in m$^2$.
  • Transformer: $\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{N_s}{N_p}$, ideal $P_{\in}=P_{out}$. Used for voltage step‑up/down.
  • Induction motor: Rotating magnetic field induces emf in rotor; torque $\tau = \frac{P}{\omega}$.
  • Eddy‑current brake: Relative motion of a conductor in $B$ produces opposing emf; braking force $F \propto B^2 v$.
  • Induction heating: Eddy currents $I$ in a metal produce heat $P = I^2 R \propto B^2 f^2 l^2$.

Solved example

A single‑layer coil of $N=200$ turns, area $A=0.01\,\text{m}^2$, rotates at $f=50\,\text{Hz}$ in a uniform magnetic field $B=0.2\,\text{T}$. Find the peak emf.

Solution:

  1. Angular speed $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi\times50 = 100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
  2. Peak emf $E_{max}= N B A \omega = 200\times0.2\times0.01\times100\pi = 4\pi\,\text{V}\approx 12.6\,\text{V}$.

Thus the generator would produce a sinusoidal emf of amplitude $\approx12.6\,$V.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Magnetic flux ($\\Phi$): total magnetic field lines passing through a surface, $\\Phi = \int \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{A}$.
  • Induced emf ($\\varepsilon$): emf generated in a closed loop when the magnetic flux through it changes, given by Faraday's law $\\varepsilon = -\\frac{d\\Phi}{dt}$.
  • Lenz's law: the direction of the induced emf (and hence induced current) is such that it opposes the change in flux that produced it.
  • Self‑inductance ($L$): property of a coil that relates the flux linkage to the current producing it, $L = \\frac{N\\Phi}{I}$.
  • Mutual inductance ($M$): measures how a change of current in one coil induces emf in another, $M = \frac{N_2\\Phi_{21}}{I_1}=\frac{N_1\\Phi_{12}}{I_2}$.
  • Eddy currents: circulating currents induced in bulk conductors exposed to a time‑varying magnetic field; they cause heating and are undesirable in transformers.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Quick recap:

  • Always write the minus sign in Faraday's law; it embodies Lenz's law.
  • Distinguish between flux $\\Phi$ (Webers) and flux linkage $N\\Phi$ (Webers‑turns).
  • For motional emf, use $\\varepsilon = B l v \sin\\theta$ only when the conductor moves perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$; otherwise include the sine factor.
  • Energy stored in an inductor is $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$; never confuse with $U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$ (capacitor).

Common mistakes to avoid:

  • Omitting the negative sign in Faraday's law, leading to wrong direction of induced current.
  • Using area $A$ instead of flux $\\Phi$ when the magnetic field is non‑uniform.
  • Confusing self‑inductance $L$ with mutual inductance $M$; remember $M \leq \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.
  • Neglecting the effect of core material (relative permeability $\mu_r$) on $L$.
  • Assuming eddy currents are always negligible; they become significant at high $f$ and large $B$.

numericals.question: A straight conducting rod of length $0.5\,\text{m}$ moves with a speed of $10\,\text{m/s}$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.2\,\text{T}$. Find the magnitude of the induced emf across its ends.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $l = 0.5\,\text{m}$, $v = 10\,\text{m/s}$, $B = 0.2\,\text{T}$.

Formula: $\varepsilon = B l v$.

Calculation: $\varepsilon = (0.2)(0.5)(10) = 1.0\,\text{V}$.

Answer: $\varepsilon = 1.0\,\text{V}$.

numericals.question: A solenoid of length $0.20\,\text{m}$, cross‑sectional area $1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2$ and $500$ turns is placed in vacuum. Calculate its self‑inductance.

In a pair of coupled coils, coil 1 carries a current $i_1$. The magnetic flux linking coil 2 due to $i_1$ is $\phi_{21}=2.5\times10^{-4}\,i_1\,\text{Wb}$. If coil 2 has $300$ turns, find the mutual inductance $M$ between the coils.
An inductor of inductance $0.20\,\text{H}$ carries a steady current of $5\,\text{A}$. Determine the magnetic energy stored in the inductor.

pyq.question: State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction.
pyq.answer_html: Induced emf $\mathcal{E}$ in a closed circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit: $\mathcal{E}= -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$.

pyq.question: Write the expression for the self‑inductance $L$ of a solenoid of $N$ turns, length $l$ and cross‑sectional area $A$ carrying current $I$.
A rectangular coil of area $20\,\text{cm}^{2}$ rotates with angular speed $\omega=50\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$ in a uniform magnetic field $B=0.2\,\text{T}$. Find the maximum emf induced in the coil.
pyq.answer_html:
Maximum emf $\mathcal{E}_{\max}=NBA\omega$.
Convert area: $A=20\times10^{-4}=2\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{2}$.
Thus $\mathcal{E}_{\max}= (1)(0.2)(2\times10^{-3})(50)=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{V}=20\,\text{mV}$.

pyq.question: Explain qualitatively why the direction of the induced current always opposes the change producing it (Lenz’s law).
pyq.answer_html:
• Changing magnetic flux creates an emf.
  • According to Lenz’s law the induced emf produces a current whose magnetic field opposes the original change in flux.
  • This opposition conserves energy and is a manifestation of the conservation of magnetic flux.

pyq.question: Derive the expression for the emf induced in a straight conductor of length $l$ moving with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Consider a conductor moving in a magnetic field. The magnetic force on a charge $q$ is $\mathbf{F}=q\,\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$.
  2. When $\mathbf{v}\perp\mathbf{B}$, the magnitude of the force is $F=qvB$ and it drives charges from one end to the other, creating a potential difference.
  3. Work done per unit charge $=\frac{F\,l}{q}=vBl$; this is the induced emf $\mathcal{E}$.
  4. Hence $\boxed{\mathcal{E}=Blv}$ (direction given by right‑hand rule).

pyq.question: A coil of $N=200$ turns and area $A=5\,\text{cm}^{2}$ has resistance $R=10\,\Omega$. It is placed in a magnetic field that varies with time as $B=0.1t$ (T, $t$ in s). Find (a) the induced current at $t=2\,\text{s}$, and (b) the energy dissipated as heat in the coil during the first $2\,\text{s}$.
pyq.answer_html:
(a) Flux $\Phi=BA=0.1t\times5\times10^{-4}=5\times10^{-5}t\,\text{Wb}$.
Induced emf $\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}= -N\times5\times10^{-5}= -200\times5\times10^{-5}= -0.01\,\text{V}$.
Current $I=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}=\frac{0.01}{10}=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{A}$ (direction given by Lenz’s law).

(b) Power $P=I^{2}R=(10^{-3})^{2}\times10=10^{-5}\,\text{W}$.
Energy $W=\int_{0}^{2}P\,dt= P\times2=2\times10^{-5}\,\text{J}$.

mcq.q: According to Faraday's law, the magnitude of the induced emf in a coil of $N$ turns is given by
mcq.explain: Faraday's law states $\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$; the negative sign indicates Lenz's law.

mcq.q: If a rectangular loop of area $A$ moves with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$, the induced emf is
mcq.explain: Change of flux $\Delta\Phi = B\,\Delta A = BvA\,\Delta t$, so $\mathcal{E}=\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=BvA$.

mcq.q: The self‑inductance $L$ of a solenoid depends on
options: Number of turns per unit length and cross‑sectional area
mcq.explain: For a solenoid $L=\mu_0 n^2 A l$, where $n$ is turns per unit length and $A$ is cross‑sectional area.

mcq.q: A coil of inductance $L$ carries a current $I$ and is suddenly opened. The induced emf across the terminals is
mcq.explain: From $\mathcal{E}= -L\frac{dI}{dt}$; magnitude $L\frac{dI}{dt}$.

mcq.q:
Assertion (A): Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy.
Reason (R): The induced current always opposes the change producing it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Lenz's law ensures that the induced emf does work opposite to the cause, preventing a perpetual motion machine, thus conserving energy. Hence R correctly explains A.

mcq.q: The mutual inductance $M$ between two coils is maximum when
options: The coils are coaxial and their planes are parallel
The coils are placed side by side with axes perpendicular
The coils have different numbers of turns
mcq.explain: Maximum flux linkage occurs when the magnetic field lines of one coil cut through the other most effectively, i.e., coaxial and parallel.

mcq.q: A circular loop of radius $r$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ whose direction is perpendicular to the axis of rotation. The peak emf induced in the loop is
mcq.explain: Flux $\Phi = B\,\pi r^{2}\cos\omega t$, so $\mathcal{E}= -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=B\,\pi r^{2}\,\omega\sin\omega t$, peak value $B\pi r^{2}\omega$.

mcq.q: When a conducting rod of length $l$ slides on parallel rails in a magnetic field $B$, the induced current is $I=\frac{Blv}{R}$. This expression assumes
options: Uniform magnetic field and negligible self‑inductance
That the rails have zero resistance
That the magnetic field is time‑varying
mcq.explain: Derivation uses $\mathcal{E}=Blv$ and Ohm's law $I=\mathcal{E}/R$, ignoring inductive effects.

mcq.q: If the magnetic flux through a coil changes at a constant rate $k$, the induced emf is
mcq.explain: For $N$ turns, $\mathcal{E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}= -N k$.

mcq.q: A solenoid of length $l$, $N$ turns and cross‑sectional area $A$ carries a current $I$. The magnetic field inside the solenoid is
mcq.explain: For an ideal solenoid $B=\mu_{0} n I$ where $n=N/l$; thus $B=\mu_{0}\frac{N}{l}I$.

long_notes.Introduction to alternating current and:
Alternating Current (AC) – Introduction

AC is a time‑varying electric current that periodically reverses its direction. The standard sinusoidal form is

QuantityExpressionSI Unit
Instantaneous current$i = I_m \sin \omega t$A
Instantaneous voltage$v = V_m \sin \omega t$V
RMS current$I_{rms}=\frac{I_m}{\sqrt{2}}$A
RMS voltage$V_{rms}=\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}$V
Average power$P_{avg}=\frac{1}{2} V_m I_m \cos \phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos \phi$W

Generation of AC

When a rectangular coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$, the magnetic flux is $\Phi = N B A \cos \omega t$. By Faraday’s law, the induced emf is

$e = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}= N B A \omega \sin \omega t$

Thus the generated emf is sinusoidal with peak $E_m = N B A \omega$.

Key Formulas

  • Peak value $X_m$ and RMS value $X_{rms}=\frac{X_m}{\sqrt{2}}$.
  • Phase difference $\phi$ between voltage and current.
  • Power factor $\cos \phi$.

Example

Find the rms voltage of an AC source whose peak voltage is $100\,\text{V}$.

Solution: $V_{rms}=\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{2}}\approx 70.7\,\text{V}$.
long_notes.Sinusoidal alternating current: mathemat:
Definition: A sinusoidal alternating current (AC) is described by a time‑varying quantity of the form $i(t)=I_{m}\sin(\omega t+\phi)$, where $I_{m}$ is the peak (maximum) value, $\omega=2\pi f$ is the angular frequency (rad·s$^{-1}$), $f$ is the frequency (Hz) and $\phi$ is the phase angle (rad).

Phasor representation converts the sinusoid into a rotating vector in the complex plane: $\tilde I=I_{m}\angle\phi$, and the time function is recovered as $i(t)=\Re\{\tilde I e^{j\omega t}\}$. The same applies to voltage $v(t)=V_{m}\sin(\omega t+\theta)$ with phasor $\tilde V=V_{m}\angle\theta$.

Key formulas

  • RMS value: $I_{\text{rms}}=\frac{I_{m}}{\sqrt{2}}$, $V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{m}}{\sqrt{2}}$.
  • Impedance of series $R$–$L$–$C$: $Z=R+jX$, where $X=\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C}$ (ohm).
  • Ohm’s law for phasors: $\tilde I=\frac{\tilde V}{Z}$.
  • Average (real) power: $P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi=\frac{V_{m}I_{m}}{2}\cos\phi$.

SI units

SymbolQuantitySI unit
$I$CurrentA
$V$VoltageV
$\omega$Angular frequencyrad·s$^{-1}$
$Z$Impedance\Omega

Solved example

Given a sinusoidal source $v(t)=100\sin(2\pi\,50\,t)$ V applied across a resistor $R=10\,\Omega$, find the rms voltage, rms current and average power.

  1. Peak voltage $V_{m}=100\,$V.
  2. RMS voltage $V_{\text{rms}}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{2}}=70.71\,$V.
  3. RMS current $I_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{R}=\frac{70.71}{10}=7.07\,$A.
  4. Average power $P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}=70.71\times7.07\approx5.0\times10^{2}\,$W.

Thus $V_{\text{rms}}=70.71\,$V, $I_{\text{rms}}=7.07\,$A and $P=500\,$W.
long_notes.RMS and average values of alternating qu:
Definition: The root‑mean‑square (RMS) value of a periodic quantity $x(t)$ is the square root of its mean square value over one complete cycle.

Mathematically, $$\text{RMS}= \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}x^{2}(t)\,dt}$$ where $T$ is the period. The average (mean) value is $$\overline{x}= \frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}x(t)\,dt$$.

For a sinusoid $x(t)=X_{0}\sin\omega t$ (or $X_{0}\cos\omega t$):

  • Mean square $=\frac{X_{0}^{2}}{2}$, hence $$\text{RMS}= \frac{X_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$$.
  • Average over a full cycle is zero; over a half‑cycle (absolute value) $$\overline{|x|}= \frac{2X_{0}}{\pi}$$.

Key formulas

QuantityRMS valueAverage value (full cycle)
Voltage $v(t)$$V_{\text{rms}}= \dfrac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$$0$
Current $i(t)$$I_{\text{rms}}= \dfrac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$$0$

SI Units: Voltage – volt (V), Current – ampere (A), Power – watt (W). RMS values are expressed \in the same units as the instantaneous quantity.

Example: A resistor of $10\ \Omega$ is connected \to an AC source $v(t)=100\sin(2\pi 50t)\,$V. Find the RMS current and the average power dissipated.

Solution:

  • Peak voltage $V_{0}=100\,$V. $V_{\text{rms}}=100/\sqrt{2}=70.71\,$V.
  • RMS current $I_{\text{rms}}=V_{\text{rms}}/R=70.71/10=7.07\,$A.
  • Average power $P_{\text{avg}}=I_{\text{rms}}^{2}R= (7.07)^{2}\times10\approx 500\,$W.

Thus RMS quantities simplify AC analysis by allowing direct use of DC formulas.
long_notes.Power in AC circuits: instantaneous, ave:
Instantaneous Power: $p(t)=v(t)i(t)$ (unit: W). For sinusoidal sources $v=V_{m}\sin\omega t$, $i=I_{m}\sin(\omega t+\phi)$.

Average (Real) Power: $P_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}p(t)dt=\frac{1}{2}V_{m}I_{m}\cos\phi=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$ (unit: W). $\cos\phi$ is the power factor.

Apparent Power: $S=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}$ (unit: VA).

Reactive Power: $Q=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\sin\phi$ (unit: var). Relationship: $S^{2}=P^{2}+Q^{2}$.

QuantitySymbolFormulaUnit
Instantaneous Power$p$$p=v i$W
Average (Real) Power$P$$P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$W
Apparent Power$S$$S=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}$VA
Reactive Power$Q$$Q=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\sin\phi$var

Example:

  • Given $V_{\text{rms}}=230\,\text{V}$, $I_{\text{rms}}=5\,\text{A}$, power factor $\cos\phi=0.8$ (lagging).
  • Apparent power $S=230\times5=1150\,\text{VA}$.
  • Real power $P=S\cos\phi=1150\times0.8=920\,\text{W}$.
  • $\phi=\cos^{-1}(0.8)\approx36.87^{\circ}$, so $\sin\phi\approx0.6$.
  • Reactive power $Q=S\sin\phi=1150\times0.6=690\,\text{var}$.

Thus $S=1150\,\text{VA}$, $P=920\,\text{W}$, $Q=690\,\text{var}$ and power factor $=0.8$.
long_notes.Phase relationships between voltage and:
Phase relationship between voltage and current

  • Resistive (R) circuit: $v(t)=V_0\sin\omega t$, $i(t)=I_0\sin\omega t$. Voltage and current are in phase ($\phi=0^\circ$). Power factor $=1$.
  • Inductive (L) circuit: $v(t)=L\frac{di}{dt}=V_0\sin\omega t$, $i(t)=I_0\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ with $\phi=+90^\circ$ (current lags voltage). $\tan\phi=\frac{\omega L}{R}$ for RL series.
  • Capacitive (C) circuit: $i(t)=C\frac{dv}{dt}=I_0\sin\omega t$, $v(t)=V_0\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ with $\phi=-90^\circ$ (current leads voltage). $\tan\phi=-\frac{1}{\omega C R}$ for RC series.

Key formulas

QuantityExpressionSI unit
Impedance $Z$$\sqrt{R^{2}+(\omega L)^{2}}$ (pure $L$) or $\sqrt{R^{2}+(\frac{1}{\omega C})^{2}}$ (pure $C$)$\Omega$
Phase angle $\phi$$\tan\phi=\frac{\omega L}{R}$ (RL) , $\tan\phi=-\frac{1}{\omega C R}$ (RC)radian or degree
Power factor$\cos\phi$—

Example

In a series RL circuit $R=50\ \Omega$, $L=0.2\ \text{H}$ and the supply frequency $f=50\ \text{Hz}$. Find $\phi$ and the power factor.

Solution: $\omega=2\pi f=2\pi\times50=100\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. $\tan\phi=\frac{\omega L}{R}= \frac{100\pi\times0.2}{50}= \frac{20\pi}{50}=0.4\pi\approx1.257$. $\phi=\arctan(1.257)\approx51.3^\circ$. Power factor $=\cos\phi\approx0.63$ (lagging).
long_notes.Series LCR circuit: impedance, resonance:
Series LCR Circuit – Impedance, Resonance and Quality Factor

In a series LCR circuit the resistor $R$, inductor $L$ and capacitor $C$ are connected end‑to‑end and the same current $i(t)$ flows through each element. The total opposition to the alternating current is called the impedance $Z$.

  • Impedance: $Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{C})^{2}}$ where $X_{L}=\omega L$ (inductive reactance) and $X_{C}=\frac{1}{\omega C}$ (capacitive reactance). Unit: $\Omega$.
  • Phase angle: $\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_{L}-X_{C}}{R}$; current lags voltage if $\phi>0$.

Resonance

Resonance occurs when $X_{L}=X_{C}$, i.e. $\omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance:

  • $Z_{\text{res}} = R$ (minimum impedance).
  • Current amplitude $I_{\max}=\frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{R}$.
  • Voltage across $L$ or $C$ can be $Q$ times the source voltage.

Quality Factor (Q)

$Q = \frac{\omega_{0} L}{R}=\frac{1}{\omega_{0} C R}=\frac{X_{L}}{R}=\frac{X_{C}}{R}$.

It measures the sharpness of resonance; higher $Q$ \u2192 narrower bandwidth $\Delta \omega = \frac{\omega_{0}}{Q}$.

QuantityExpressionSI Unit
Inductive reactance $X_{L}$$\omega L$$\Omega$
Capacitive reactance $X_{C}$$\frac{1}{\omega C}$$\Omega$
Resonant frequency $f_{0}$$\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$Hz
Quality factor $Q$$\frac{\omega_{0} L}{R}$dimensionless

Example

Given $R=10\,\Omega$, $L=0.2\,\text{H}$, $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$ and $V_{\text{rms}}=100\,\text{V}$, find the resonant frequency, current at resonance and $Q$.

Resonant angular frequency $\omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.2\times 50\times10^{-6}}}=1000\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$, so $f_{0}=\frac{\omega_{0}}{2\pi}\approx159\,\text{Hz}$. At resonance $Z=R$, thus $I_{\max}=\frac{100}{10}=10\,\text{A}$. $Q=\frac{\omega_{0}L}{R}=\frac{1000\times0.2}{10}=20$.
long_notes.Power factor, its correction and applica:
Power Factor (PF) – the ratio of real power $P$ to apparent power $S$ in an AC circuit, $\text{PF}=\frac{P}{S}=\cos\phi$, where $\phi$ is the phase angle between voltage and current. SI unit: dimensionless (range $-1$ to $+1$). A lagging PF (<0) indicates inductive load, leading PF (>0) indicates capacitive load.

Key Relations

  • Apparent power $S = VI$ (VA)
  • Real power $P = VI\cos\phi$ (W)
  • Reactive power $Q = VI\sin\phi = P\tan\phi$ (VAR)
  • Power triangle: $S^{2}=P^{2}+Q^{2}$

PF Correction

To improve a lagging PF, a capacitor supplies leading reactive power $Q_{c}$, reducing net $Q$:

QuantityFormula
Initial reactive power $Q_{1}$$Q_{1}=P\tan\phi_{1}$
Desired reactive power $Q_{2}$$Q_{2}=P\tan\phi_{2}$
Capacitor reactive power $Q_{c}$$Q_{c}=Q_{1}-Q_{2}$
Capacitance $C$ (single‑phase)$C=\frac{Q_{c}}{2\pi f V^{2}}$

Example

A 3 kW motor operates at 230 V, 50 Hz with lagging PF $0.6$. Find the capacitance needed to raise PF to $0.9$.

Solution:

  1. Calculate $\phi_{1}=\cos^{-1}(0.6)$, $\tan\phi_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{1-0.6^{2}}}{0.6}=1.333$.
  2. $Q_{1}=P\tan\phi_{1}=3000\times1.333=4000\,\text{VAR}$.
  3. For PF $0.9$, $\tan\phi_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{1-0.9^{2}}}{0.9}=0.484$.
  4. $Q_{2}=3000\times0.484=1452\,\text{VAR}$.
  5. $Q_{c}=Q_{1}-Q_{2}=4000-1452=2548\,\text{VAR}$.
  6. $C=\frac{2548}{2\pi\times50\times230^{2}}\approx9.6\times10^{-6}\,\text{F}=9.6\,\mu\text{F}$.

Thus a $9.6\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor connected across the motor will correct the PF to $0.9$.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Alternating Current (AC): Current that reverses direction periodically, typically sinusoidal.
  • Peak Value ($V_{0}$, $I_{0}$): Maximum instantaneous value of voltage or current.
  • RMS Value: Equivalent DC value delivering same power; $V_{rms}=V_{0}/\\sqrt{2}$, $I_{rms}=I_{0}/\\sqrt{2}$.
  • Impedance ($Z$): Total opposition to AC, $Z=\\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_{L}-X_{C})^{2}}$.
  • Reactance: $X_{L}=\\omega L$ (inductive), $X_{C}=1/(\\omega C)$ (capacitive).
  • Resonance: Condition $X_{L}=X_{C}$; circuit behaves purely resistive, $f_{0}=1/(2\\pi\\sqrt{LC})$.
  • Power Factor: $\\cos\\phi$, the phase angle between voltage and current; $\\cos\\phi=1$ at resonance.
  • Ohm’s Law for AC: $V=IZ$, where $V$ and $I$ are phasors.
  • KVL for AC: Sum of phasor voltages around a closed loop is zero.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
AC analysis hinges on phasor representation and RMS values. Remember: RMS is not the arithmetic mean; it is the square‑root of the mean of the square. At resonance, impedance reduces to $R$ only; never forget the $X_{L}=X_{C}$ condition.

  • Mixing peak and RMS values in power calculations leads to a factor of 2 error.
  • Using $V_{pp}$ instead of $V_{0}$ in formulas for reactance.
  • Ignoring the sign of $X_{L}-X_{C}$ when computing $Z$; always square the difference.
  • Assuming power factor is always $\cos\phi$ without checking the sign of $\phi$ (lagging vs leading).
  • For series resonance, forgetting that $Q=\\frac{\\omega_{0}L}{R}$, not $\\frac{R}{\\omega_{0}L}$.

numericals.question: A sinusoidal voltage $v(t)=200\sin(2\pi 50 t)$ V is applied across a resistor of $R=50\,\Omega$. Find the average power dissipated in the resistor.
A series LCR circuit has $R=20\,\Omega$, $L=0.1\,$H, $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$ and is connected to an AC source $e(t)=100\sin(2\pi 60 t)$ V. Find the rms current flowing through the circuit.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $R=20\,\Omega$, $L=0.1\,$H, $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$, $V_{peak}=100\,$ V, $f=60\,$Hz.
Formula: $\omega=2\pi f$, $X_L=\omega L$, $X_C=\frac{1}{\omega C}$, $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, $V_{rms}=\frac{V_{peak}}{\sqrt{2}}$, $I_{rms}=\frac{V_{rms}}{Z}$.
Step‑by‑Step:
1. $\omega=2\pi\times60=377\,$rad/s.
2. $X_L=377\times0.1=37.7\,\Omega$, $X_C=\frac{1}{377\times50\times10^{-6}}=53.1\,\Omega$.
3. Net reactance $X=X_L-X_C=-15.4\,\Omega$.
4. $Z=\sqrt{20^2+(-15.4)^2}=\sqrt{637}=25.24\,\Omega$.
5. $V_{rms}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{2}}=70.71\,$ V.
6. $I_{rms}=\frac{70.71}{25.24}=2.80\,$ A.
Answer: $I_{rms}=2.80\,$ A.

pyq.question: Define the rms (root‑mean‑square) value of an alternating current and write its relation with the peak value.
pyq.answer_html: RMS value $I_{rms}=\\frac{I_{max}}{\\sqrt{2}}$ (or $V_{rms}=\\frac{V_{max}}{\\sqrt{2}}$). It is the equivalent dc value that produces the same heating effect.

pyq.question: State the expression for average power dissipated in a purely resistive AC circuit.
pyq.answer_html: Average power $P_{avg}=I_{rms}^2 R = \\frac{V_{max}^2}{2R}$.

pyq.question: Derive the expression for inductive reactance $X_L$ in an AC circuit of frequency $f$.
pyq.answer_html:
For a sinusoidal current $i=I_{max}\\sin\\omega t$, the induced emf $e = L\\frac{di}{dt}=L\\omega I_{max}\\cos\\omega t = I_{max}X_L\\sin(\\omega t+\\frac{\\pi}{2})$.

Hence $X_L = \\omega L = 2\\pi f L$.

pyq.question: Explain why the current leads the voltage by $90^\circ$ in a purely inductive AC circuit.
pyq.answer_html:
• Induced emf $e = L\\frac{di}{dt}$ is proportional to the rate of change of current.
  • If $i=I_{max}\\sin\\omega t$, then $e = L\\omega I_{max}\\cos\\omega t = I_{max}X_L\\sin(\\omega t+\\frac{\\pi}{2})$.
  • Thus the voltage (emf) reaches its maximum $\frac{\pi}{2}$ rad (90°) before the current, i.e., current lags voltage by $90^\circ$.

pyq.question: A series RLC circuit has $R=10\,\Omega$, $L=0.2\,\text{H}$, $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$ and is connected to a source of frequency $50\,\text{Hz}$. Calculate (a) the resonant frequency $f_0$, (b) the inductive reactance $X_L$, (c) the capacitive reactance $X_C$, (d) the net impedance $Z$, and (e) the power factor.
pyq.answer_html:
(a) $f_0=\\frac{1}{2\\pi\\sqrt{LC}}=\\frac{1}{2\\pi\\sqrt{0.2\times50\times10^{-6}}}=\\frac{1}{2\\pi\\times0.003162}=50.3\,\text{Hz}$ (approximately).

(b) $X_L=2\\pi f L = 2\\pi\times50\times0.2 = 62.8\,\Omega$.

(c) $X_C=\\frac{1}{2\\pi f C}=\\frac{1}{2\\pi\times50\times50\times10^{-6}}=63.7\,\Omega$.

(d) Net reactance $X = X_L - X_C = -0.9\,\Omega$ (almost purely resistive). $Z=\\sqrt{R^2+X^2}=\\sqrt{10^2+(-0.9)^2}=10.04\,\Omega$.

(e) Power factor $\cos\phi =\\frac{R}{Z}=\\frac{10}{10.04}=0.996\approx 1$ (circuit is nearly in‑phase).

mcq.q: The peak value $V_{0}$ of an alternating voltage is related to its rms value $V_{rms}$ by which of the following?
mcq.explain: For a sinusoidal voltage, $V_{rms}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$, hence $V_{0}=\sqrt{2}\,V_{rms}$.

mcq.q: The average power dissipated in a purely resistive AC circuit is $P=\frac{V_{rms}I_{rms}}{\cos\phi}$. What is the value of the power factor $\cos\phi$ for a pure resistor?
mcq.explain: In a pure resistor, voltage and current are in phase, so the phase angle $\phi=0^{\circ}$ and $\cos\phi=1$.

mcq.q: If the frequency of an AC source is doubled, the inductive reactance $X_{L}$ of an inductor changes how?
mcq.explain: Inductive reactance $X_{L}=2\pi fL$, so doubling $f$ doubles $X_{L}$.

mcq.q: A series RLC circuit has $R=10\,\Omega$, $L=0.2\,\text{H}$ and $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$. At what angular frequency $\omega_{0}$ does resonance occur?
mcq.explain: Resonance in a series RLC occurs at $\omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. Substituting $L$ and $C$ gives $\omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.2\times 50\times10^{-6}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-5}}}=10^{2.5}=316\,\text{rad/s}$.

mcq.q: The quality factor $Q$ of a series RLC circuit is given by $Q=\frac{\omega_{0}L}{R}$. For the circuit in the previous question, what is $Q$?
In a transformer, if the primary has $N_{1}=200$ turns and the secondary has $N_{2}=50$ turns, what is the ratio of secondary rms voltage $V_{2}$ to primary rms voltage $V_{1}$?
mcq.explain: For an ideal transformer, $\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}=\frac{50}{200}=\frac{1}{4}$, so $V_{2}=\frac{1}{4}V_{1}$.

mcq.q: The instantaneous power in a purely inductive AC circuit is $p(t)=V_{0}I_{0}\sin\omega t\cos\omega t$. What is the average power over a full cycle?
mcq.explain: For a pure inductor, voltage and current are $90^{\circ}$ out of phase, making the average of $\sin\omega t\cos\omega t$ over a cycle zero; thus average power is $0$.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): In a series RLC circuit at resonance, the current is maximum. Reason (R): At resonance the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance, making the net reactance zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: At resonance $X_{L}=X_{C}$, net reactance $X=0$, so the circuit behaves like a pure resistor and current $I=V/R$ is maximum. Hence both statements are true and R explains A.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): The phase angle between voltage and current in a series RLC circuit is $\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{X_{L}-X_{C}}{R}\right)$. Reason (R): When $X_{L}=X_{C}$, the circuit is at resonance and $\phi=0^{\circ}$.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: The given formula for $\phi$ is correct. At resonance $X_{L}=X_{C}$, the numerator becomes zero, giving $\phi=0^{\circ}$. Thus both statements are true and R explains A.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): In a half-wave rectifier, the average output voltage is $V_{avg}=\frac{V_{m}}{\pi}$. Reason (R): The output waveform contains only the positive half cycles of the input sinusoid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: For a half-wave rectifier, the average (dc) value of the output is $V_{avg}=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}V_{m}\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac{V_{m}}{\pi}$. This occurs because only the positive half cycles appear at the output, making both statements true and R explains A.

long_notes.Introduction to electromagnetic waves:
Definition: An electromagnetic (EM) wave is a transverse wave consisting of mutually perpendicular electric ($\vec{E}$) and magnetic ($\vec{B}$) fields that propagate through space at the speed of light without requiring a material medium.

Key Relations and Formulas

  • Speed of EM wave in vacuum: $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} \;\text{(m/s)}$
  • Relation between field amplitudes: $E = c\,B$
  • Wave equation (for $\vec{E}$ or $\vec{B}$): $\nabla^{2}\vec{E}=\mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial^{2}\vec{E}}{\partial t^{2}}$
  • Frequency‑wavelength relation: $c = \lambda f$
  • Energy density: $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu_0 B^{2}$ (J/m$^3$)
  • Poynting vector: $\vec{S}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$, magnitude $S = u\,c$ (W/m$^2$)

SI Units

QuantitySymbolUnit
Electric field$E$V·m$^{-1}$
Magnetic field$B$T (tesla)
Permittivity of free space$\epsilon_0$F·m$^{-1}$
Permeability of free space$\mu_0$H·m$^{-1}$
Speed of light$c$m·s$^{-1}$

Solved Example

Find the wavelength of an EM wave whose frequency is $f = 5\times10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

  1. Use $c = \lambda f$.
  2. Rearrange: $\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$.
  3. Substitute $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\text{m·s}^{-1}$ and $f = 5\times10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$:
  4. $\lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{5\times10^{14}} = 6\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}$.

Thus the wave lies in the visible spectrum (yellow light).
long_notes.Electromagnetic spectrum and its regions:
Electromagnetic Spectrum – a continuous range of electromagnetic waves ordered by wavelength ($\lambda$) or frequency ($ u$). The fundamental relation $c = \lambda u$ (with $c = 3 imes10^8\, ext{m s}^{-1}$) connects them.

Major Regions and Typical Ranges

RegionWavelength $\lambda$ (m)Frequency $ u$ (Hz)Energy $E$ (J)
Radio$>10^{-1}$$<10^{9}$$<10^{-24}$
Microwave$10^{-3}$ – $10^{-1}$$10^{9}$ – $10^{11}$$10^{-24}$ – $10^{-22}$
Infrared$7 imes10^{-7}$ – $10^{-3}$$3 imes10^{11}$ – $4 imes10^{14}$$10^{-22}$ – $10^{-20}$
Visible$4 imes10^{-7}$ – $7 imes10^{-7}$$4.3 imes10^{14}$ – $7.5 imes10^{14}$$2.5 imes10^{-19}$ – $3.1 imes10^{-19}$
Ultraviolet$10^{-8}$ – $4 imes10^{-7}$$7.5 imes10^{14}$ – $3 imes10^{16}$$3.1 imes10^{-19}$ – $1.2 imes10^{-17}$
X‑ray$10^{-11}$ – $10^{-8}$$3 imes10^{16}$ – $3 imes10^{19}$$1.2 imes10^{-17}$ – $1.2 imes10^{-14}$
Gamma$<10^{-11}$$>3 imes10^{19}$$>1.2 imes10^{-14}$

Key Formulas

  • Wave speed: $c = \lambda u$
  • Photon energy: $E = h u = \dfrac{h c}{\lambda}$, where $h = 6.626 imes10^{-34}\, ext{J s}$.

SI Units

  • $\lambda$: metre (m)
  • $ u$: hertz (Hz)
  • $E$: joule (J)

Example: Find the frequency of an X‑ray having wavelength $\lambda = 0.1\, ext{nm}$.

Solution:

  1. Convert wavelength: $0.1\, ext{nm}=0.1 imes10^{-9}\, ext{m}=1 imes10^{-10}\, ext{m}$.
  2. Use $ u = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}$:
  3. $ u = \dfrac{3 imes10^{8}}{1 imes10^{-10}} = 3 imes10^{18}\, ext{Hz}$.
  4. Energy can be obtained if required: $E = h u = 6.626 imes10^{-34} imes3 imes10^{18}=1.99 imes10^{-15}\, ext{J}$.

Thus the X‑ray lies in the $10^{18}$–$10^{19}\, ext{Hz}$ band, characteristic of the X‑ray region.
long_notes.Derivation of the electromagnetic wave e:
Definition: An electromagnetic (EM) wave is a self‑sustaining transverse disturbance of electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ that propagates through free space with speed $c$.

Maxwell’s equations in free space (no charges, no currents)

  • $ abla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0$
  • $ abla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$
  • $ abla imes\mathbf{E}=- rac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$
  • $ abla imes\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}$

Derivation of the wave equation

Take the curl of Faraday’s law:

$$\nabla imes(\nabla imes\mathbf{E})=-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\nabla imes\mathbf{B})$$

Using the vector identity $\nabla imes(\nabla imes\mathbf{E})=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E})-\nabla^2\mathbf{E}$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0$, we get

$$-\nabla^2\mathbf{E}=-\mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}$$

or

$$\nabla^2\mathbf{E}=\mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}$$

Similarly,

$$\nabla^2\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf{B}}{\partial t^2}$$

Both $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ satisfy the same wave equation with wave speed

$$c= rac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}$$

SI Units

QuantitySymbolSI Unit
Permeability of free space$\mu_0$$4\pi imes10^{-7}\, ext{N A}^{-2}$
Permittivity of free space$\epsilon_0$$8.854 imes10^{-12}\, ext{F m}^{-1}$
Speed of light$c$$3 imes10^{8}\, ext{m s}^{-1}$

Solved Example

Given a plane wave travelling \in $+x$ direction: $\mathbf{E}=E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\,\hat{y}$. Find $\mathbf{B}$ and verify the wave equation.

  1. From $\nabla imes\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t$, compute $\nabla imes\mathbf{E}= -kE_0\sin(kx-\omega t)\,\hat{z}$.
  2. Integrate w.r.t. $t$: $\mathbf{B}= rac{kE_0}{\omega}\cos(kx-\omega t)\,\hat{z}= rac{E_0}{c}\cos(kx-\omega t)\,\hat{z}$ (since $\omega/k=c$).
  3. Substitute $\mathbf{B}$ into $\nabla^2\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial^2\mathbf{B}/\partial t^2$; both sides give $-k^2\mathbf{B}$, confirming the wave equation.

Thus the derived equations correctly describe propagation of EM waves in vacuum.
long_notes.Propagation of electromagnetic waves in:
Definition: An electromagnetic (EM) wave is a self‑sustaining transverse disturbance of electric field $\\vec{E}$ and magnetic field $\\vec{B}$ that propagates through vacuum at the speed of light.

Derivation from Maxwell’s equations (vacuum):

  • Faraday’s law: $\\nabla\\times\\vec{E} = -\\frac{\\partial \\vec{B}}{\\partial t}$
  • Maxwell‑Ampère law: $\\nabla\\times\\vec{B} = \\mu_0\\epsilon_0\\frac{\\partial \\vec{E}}{\\partial t}$

Taking the curl of Faraday’s law and substituting the second equation gives the wave equation

$$\\nabla^{2}\\vec{E}=\\mu_0\\epsilon_0\\frac{\\partial^{2}\\vec{E}}{\\partial t^{2}}$$

Similarly, $\\nabla^{2}\\vec{B}=\\mu_0\\epsilon_0\\frac{\\partial^{2}\\vec{B}}{\\partial t^{2}}$.

The propagation speed is

$$c=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\mu_0\\epsilon_0}}\\approx 3\\times10^{8}\\,\\text{m s}^{-1}$$

and the fields are related by

$$\\vec{E}=c\\,\\vec{B}\\quad\\text{(for a plane wave)}$$

QuantitySymbolSI Unit
Electric field$\\vec{E}$V m$^{-1}$
Magnetic field$\\vec{B}$T (tesla)
Permittivity of free space$\\epsilon_0$F m$^{-1}$
Permeability of free space$\\mu_0$H m$^{-1}$
Speed of light$c$m s$^{-1}$

Example: A plane wave travelling \in +x direction is described by $\\vec{E}=E_0\\cos(kx-\\omega t)\\hat{y}$. Using Maxwell‑Ampère law, $\\vec{B}=\\frac{E_0}{c}\\cos(kx-\\omega t)\\hat{z}$. Verify $E_0 = cB_0$ and $\\omega = ck$, confirming propagation at speed $c$.
long_notes.Energy, momentum and radiation pressure:
Energy density of an EM wave is $\frac{\epsilon_0 E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$ (J·m$^{-3}$). For a plane wave $E=cB$, giving $u=\epsilon_0 E^2=\frac{B^2}{\mu_0}$.

Poynting vector $\vec{S}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$ (W·m$^{-2}$). Its time‑average $\langle S\rangle = u c$.

Momentum density $\vec{g}=\frac{\vec{S}}{c^2}$ (kg·m$^{-2}$·s$^{-1}$). For a plane wave $g=\frac{u}{c}$.

Radiation pressure $p=\frac{\langle S\rangle}{c}=\frac{I}{c}$ for total absorption, $p=\frac{2I}{c}$ for perfect reflection (Pa).

QuantityFormulaSI unit
Energy density $u$$u=\frac{\epsilon_0 E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$J·m$^{-3}$
Poynting vector $S$$S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}EB$ (average $=u c$)W·m$^{-2}$
Momentum density $g$$g=\frac{S}{c^2}$kg·m$^{-2}$·s$^{-1}$
Radiation pressure $p$$p=\frac{I}{c}$ (absorption) $\; p=\frac{2I}{c}$ (reflection)Pa

Example: A laser of power $P=5\,\text{W}$ produces a circular beam of diameter $1\,\text{mm}$ (area $A=2\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2$). Find the pressure on a perfectly absorbing plate.

Intensity $I=\frac{P}{A}=\frac{5}{2\times10^{-6}}=2.5\times10^{6}\,\text{W·m}^{-2}$.

Pressure $p=\frac{I}{c}=\frac{2.5\times10^{6}}{3\times10^{8}}=8.33\times10^{-3}\,\text{Pa}$.

If the plate were perfectly reflecting, $p$ would be twice this value.
long_notes.Poynting vector and intensity of electro:
Definition: The Poynting vector $\mathbf{S}$ represents the rate of energy flow per unit area carried by an electromagnetic wave.

Mathematically, $$\mathbf{S}=\\frac{1}{\\mu_0}\\mathbf{E}\\times\\mathbf{B}$$ where $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are the electric and magnetic fields and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space ($4\\pi\\times10^{-7}\,\text{H m}^{-1}$).

Direction: $\mathbf{S}$ is perpendicular \to both $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and points \in the direction of wave propagation.

Intensity (average): For a sinusoidal plane wave, the time‑averaged magnitude is $$I=\\langle S\\rangle=\\frac{1}{2}\\,c\\,\\varepsilon_0\\,E_0^{2}=\\frac{1}{2}\\,\\frac{c}{\\mu_0}\\,B_0^{2}$$ where $E_0$, $B_0$ are amplitudes, $c=1/\\sqrt{\\mu_0\\varepsilon_0}$.

SI units: $\mathbf{S}$ – watt per square metre (W m$^{-2}$); $I$ – same.

QuantitySymbolFormulaUnit
Poynting vector$\\mathbf{S}$$\\frac{1}{\\mu_0}\\mathbf{E}\\times\\mathbf{B}$W m$^{-2}$
Intensity$I$$\\frac{1}{2}c\\varepsilon_0E_0^{2}$W m$^{-2}$

Example: A plane wave \in vacuum has $E_0=300\,\text{V m}^{-1}$. Find its intensity.

Solution: $I=\\frac{1}{2}c\\varepsilon_0E_0^{2}=\\frac{1}{2}(3\\times10^{8})(8.85\\times10^{-12})(300)^{2}\\approx1.2\,\text{W m}^{-2}$.
long_notes.Polarization of electromagnetic waves:
Definition: Polarization of an electromagnetic (EM) wave refers to the orientation of the electric field vector $\mathbf{E}$ (and consequently the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$) in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. For a monochromatic plane wave, $\mathbf{E}$ oscillates in a fixed direction (linear), rotates uniformly (circular), or traces an ellipse (elliptical).

Types of Polarization

  • Linear: $\mathbf{E}$ oscillates along a single line; $\mathbf{B}$ stays perpendicular to $\mathbf{E}$.
  • Circular: $\mathbf{E}$ rotates with constant magnitude; right‑handed if rotation follows right‑hand rule.
  • Elliptical: General case; combination of linear and circular components.

Key Formulas

PhenomenonFormulaSI Unit
Malus’ Law (intensity after a polarizer)$I=I_0\cos^{2}\theta$W/m$^2$
Intensity of unpolarized light after one ideal polarizer$I=\dfrac{I_0}{2}$W/m$^2$
Brewster’ angle (no reflection for p‑polarized light)$\tan\theta_B=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$radians (or degrees)

SI Units

  • Electric field $\mathbf{E}$: volt per metre (V/m)
  • Magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$: tesla (T)
  • Intensity $I$: watt per square metre (W/m$^2$)

Example: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0=100\,\text{W/m}^2$ passes through two ideal linear polarizers whose transmission axes make an angle $\theta=30^{\circ}$. Find the emergent intensity.

  1. After the first polarizer, $I_1=\dfrac{I_0}{2}=50\,\text{W/m}^2$.
  2. Applying Malus’ law for the second polarizer, $I_2=I_1\cos^{2}\theta=50\cos^{2}30^{\circ}=50\times\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2}=50\times\dfrac{3}{4}=37.5\,\text{W/m}^2$.

Thus the final intensity is $37.5\,\text{W/m}^2$.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Electromagnetic Wave: A transverse wave consisting of mutually perpendicular electric ($\vec{E}$) and magnetic ($\vec{B}$) fields that propagate together at the speed of light.
  • Transverse Nature: Both $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ are perpendicular to the direction of propagation and to each other.
  • Maxwell’s Equations (in free space):
    • $ abla\cdot\vec{E}=0$
    • $ abla\cdot\vec{B}=0$
    • $ abla imes\vec{E}= - rac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t}$
    • $ abla imes\vec{B}= \mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial \vec{E}}{\partial t}$
  • Wave Equation: Both $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ satisfy $ abla^{2}\vec{E}=\mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial^{2}\vec{E}}{\partial t^{2}}$ and similarly for $\vec{B}$.
  • Poynting Theorem: Energy flux per unit area is given by $\vec{S}= rac{1}{\mu_0}\vec{E} imes\vec{B}$; its magnitude equals the intensity $I$ of the wave.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Summary: Electromagnetic waves are self‑sustaining transverse waves that travel at $c=3\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ in vacuum. Their electric and magnetic fields are in phase, related by $E=cB$, and carry energy and momentum described by the Poynting vector.

Common Mistakes to Avoid:

  • Confusing $c$ (speed in vacuum) with $v$ (speed in a medium). Use $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$ for the latter.
  • Omitting the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in intensity and energy density formulas for sinusoidal waves.
  • Treating $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ as independent; they are linked by $E=cB$ and Maxwell’s curl equations.
  • Using $\lambda = c/f$ inside a medium without replacing $c$ by $v$.
  • Neglecting direction of $\vec{S}$; it is given by $\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$, not $\vec{E}\cdot\vec{B}$.

numericals.question: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has a frequency $\nu =5\times10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$. Find its wavelength $\lambda$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $\nu =5\times10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$, $c=3\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$.

Formula: $\lambda =\frac{c}{\nu}$.

Calculation:
$$\lambda =\frac{3\times10^{8}}{5\times10^{14}}\,\text{m}=6\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}$$

Answer: $\lambda =6\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ (or $600\,\text{nm}$).

numericals.question: The refractive index of a certain medium is $n=1.5$. Determine the speed $v$ of an electromagnetic wave in this medium.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $n=1.5$, $c=3\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$.

Formula: $v=\frac{c}{n}$.

Calculation:
$$v=\frac{3\times10^{8}}{1.5}\,\text{m/s}=2\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$$

Answer: $v=2\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$.

numericals.question: Find the energy $E$ of a photon whose wavelength is $\lambda =400\,\text{nm}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $\lambda =400\,\text{nm}=4\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}$, $h=6.626\times10^{-34}\,\text{J·s}$, $c=3\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$.

Formula: $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$.

Calculation:
$$E=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{4\times10^{-7}}\,\text{J}=4.97\times10^{-19}\,\text{J}$$

Answer: $E\approx5.0\times10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ (or $3.1\,\text{eV}$).

numericals.question: Show that for a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum the ratio of the electric‑field amplitude $E_0$ to the magnetic‑field amplitude $B_0$ equals the speed of light $c$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Plane wave in vacuum, fields $\mathbf{E}=E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat{y}$, $\mathbf{B}=B_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\hat{z}$.

Proof:
From Maxwell's equation $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$ we obtain $kE_0=\omega B_0$.
Using the wave relation $\omega =ck$, we get $kE_0=c k B_0$.

Cancel $k$ (non‑zero) to obtain $E_0=cB_0$ or $\frac{E_0}{B_0}=c$.

Conclusion: $\displaystyle\frac{E_0}{B_0}=c$.

numericals.question: A plane electromagnetic wave has an electric‑field amplitude $E_0=200\,\text{V/m}$. Find the corresponding magnetic‑field amplitude $B_0$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $E_0=200\,\text{V/m}$, $c=3\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$.

Formula: $E_0=cB_0\;\Rightarrow\;B_0=\frac{E_0}{c}$.

Calculation:
$$B_0=\frac{200}{3\times10^{8}}\,\text{T}=6.67\times10^{-7}\,\text{T}$$

Answer: $B_0=6.7\times10^{-7}\,\text{T}$ (approximately).

numericals.question: The average intensity (magnitude of the Poynting vector) of an electromagnetic wave is $S=500\,\text{W/m}^2$. Determine the electric‑field amplitude $E_0$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $S=500\,\text{W/m}^2$, $c=3\times10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{H/m}$.

Formula: $S=\frac{E_0^2}{2\mu_0 c}$ \;\Rightarrow\; $E_0=\sqrt{2\mu_0 c S}$.

Calculation:
$$E_0=\sqrt{2\times4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3\times10^{8}\times500}\,\text{V/m}$$
$$E_0=\sqrt{2\times4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1.5\times10^{11}}\,\text{V/m}$$
$$E_0\approx\sqrt{3.77\times10^{5}}\,\text{V/m}=6.14\times10^{2}\,\text{V/m}$$

Answer: $E_0\approx6.1\times10^{2}\,\text{V/m}$.

pyq.question: Define an electromagnetic wave and state its speed in vacuum.
pyq.answer_html:
An electromagnetic wave is a transverse wave consisting of mutually perpendicular electric ($E$) and magnetic ($B$) fields that propagate together.
Speed in vacuum $c = 3\times10^8\,\text{m/s}$.

pyq.question: Write the relation between the electric field amplitude $E_0$ and magnetic field amplitude $B_0$ for an electromagnetic wave in vacuum.
pyq.answer_html: For a plane wave in vacuum, $E_0 = c\,B_0$.

pyq.question: Derive the expression for the intensity $I$ of a plane electromagnetic wave in terms of its electric field amplitude $E_0$.
pyq.answer_html:
Instantaneous Poynting vector $\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$.
For a sinusoidal wave $E=E_0\cos\omega t$, $B=\frac{E_0}{c}\cos\omega t$.
Average intensity $I=\langle S\rangle =\frac{1}{2}\frac{E_0^2}{\mu_0 c}=\frac{1}{2}c\epsilon_0 E_0^2$.

pyq.question: A radio wave of frequency $1\,\text{MHz}$ travels in free space. Calculate its wavelength.
pyq.answer_html: Wavelength $\lambda = \frac{c}{f}=\frac{3\times10^8}{1\times10^6}=3\times10^2\,\text{m}=300\,\text{m}$.

pyq.question: Explain how linear polarization of an electromagnetic wave can be produced using a Polaroid sheet. Include a brief description of a suitable diagram.
pyq.answer_html:
• Unpolarized light contains electric vectors in all directions perpendicular to propagation.
• A Polaroid sheet has a preferred transmission axis.
• Only the component of the electric field parallel to this axis passes; the perpendicular component is absorbed.
• The emerging wave has its electric field oscillating only along the transmission axis – it is linearly polarized.
• Diagram description: Draw an incident wave with random $E$-vectors, a Polaroid sheet with a vertical transmission axis, and the transmitted wave showing $E$ only vertical.

pyq.question: A plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum has an average Poynting vector magnitude $S = 5\,\text{W/m}^2$. Find the amplitudes $E_0$ and $B_0$ of the wave.
pyq.answer_html:
Average intensity $S = \frac{1}{2}c\epsilon_0 E_0^2$.
Thus $E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2S}{c\epsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times5}{(3\times10^8)(8.85\times10^{-12})}} \approx 1.09\times10^2\,\text{V/m}.$
Magnetic amplitude $B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} \approx \frac{1.09\times10^2}{3\times10^8} \approx 3.6\times10^{-7}\,\text{T}.$

mcq.q: The speed of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is $c = 3\times10^{8}$ m/s. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: It depends on the medium's permittivity only
It is equal to the speed of light in glass
mcq.explain: In vacuum, electromagnetic waves travel at $c$, which is a constant independent of frequency, wavelength or any material property.

mcq.q: For a plane monochromatic wave travelling in the $+x$ direction, the electric and magnetic fields are given by $\vec{E}=E_{0}\hat{y}\cos(kx-\omega t)$ and $\vec{B}=B_{0}\hat{z}\cos(kx-\omega t)$. What is the relationship between $E_{0}$ and $B_{0}$?
mcq.explain: For electromagnetic waves in vacuum, $E_{0}=cB_{0}$ because $\vec{E}=c\,\vec{B}\times\hat{k}$.

mcq.q: The intensity $I$ of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to which of the following?
mcq.explain: Intensity $I=\frac{1}{2}c\epsilon_{0}E_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{c}{\mu_{0}}B_{0}^{2}=c\epsilon_{0}E_{0}B_{0}$, so all three are proportional.

mcq.q: A radio wave of frequency $1\,\text{MHz}$ is incident on a perfectly conducting surface. The reflected wave will have:
mcq.explain: Reflection from a perfect conductor does not change frequency or wavelength; only the phase may change.

mcq.q: The Poynting vector for a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum is $\vec{S}=\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$. Its magnitude is $S=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{\mu_{0}c}$. What is the average value $\langle S\rangle$ over a complete cycle?
mcq.explain: The time average of $\cos^{2}(\omega t)$ over a cycle is $1/2$, giving $\langle S\rangle=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2\mu_{0}c}$.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): In a waveguide, the cutoff frequency for the $TE_{mn}$ mode is given by $f_{c}=\frac{c}{2}\sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^{2}}$.\nReason (R): The cutoff occurs when the propagation constant along the guide becomes zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: The formula for $f_{c}$ is derived by setting the longitudinal propagation constant $\beta=0$, which is exactly the reason stated.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): The energy density of an electromagnetic wave is equally shared between electric and magnetic fields.\nReason (R): In vacuum $\epsilon_{0}E^{2}=\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}B^{2}$ for a plane wave.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: For a plane wave in vacuum $u_{E}=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{0}E^{2}$ and $u_{B}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{B^{2}}{\mu_{0}}$, and using $E=cB$ gives $u_{E}=u_{B}$; the reason shows the equality.

mcq.q: If the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave is halved, what happens to its photon energy?
mcq.explain: Photon energy $E=h\nu=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$; halving $\lambda$ doubles $\nu$, thus $E$ doubles.

mcq.q: A linearly polarized wave traveling in the $+z$ direction has electric field $\vec{E}=E_{0}\hat{x}\cos(kz-\omega t)$. What is the direction of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$?
mcq.explain: Using $\vec{B}=\frac{1}{c}\hat{k}\times\vec{E}$, with $\hat{k}=\hat{z}$ and $\vec{E}$ along $\hat{x}$ gives $\vec{B}$ along $\hat{y}$.

mcq.q: The radiation pressure exerted by a perfectly absorbing surface on an incident electromagnetic wave of intensity $I$ is:
mcq.explain: For a perfectly absorbing surface, radiation pressure $P=I/c$; for a perfectly reflecting surface it would be $2I/c$.
