long_notes.Introduction to chemical kinetics:
Chemical Kinetics – Introduction

Chemical kinetics studies the speed at which reactants are converted to products and the factors influencing this speed.

Key Definitions

  • Rate of reaction = change in concentration per unit time, $r = -\\frac{1}{\\nu_i}\\frac{d[A_i]}{dt}$.
  • Rate law expresses $r$ in terms of concentrations of reactants: $r = k\\, [A]^m [B]^n$.
  • Order of reaction = sum of exponents $m+n$; determines the dependence on concentration.
  • Rate constant ($k$) – proportionality factor; its SI unit varies: $\\text{s}^{-1}$ for first order, $\\text{M}^{-1}\\text{s}^{-1}$ for second order.
  • Half‑life ($t_{1/2}$) – time for concentration to fall to half its initial value.

Important Integrated Forms

OrderIntegrated Rate LawHalf‑life
Zero$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{[A]_0}{2k}$
First$\\ln\\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{\\ln 2}{k}$
Second$\\frac{1}{[A]} - \\frac{1}{[A]_0}=kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{1}{k[A]_0}$

Sample Problem (First‑order decomposition)

For the reaction $N_2O_5 \rightarrow 2NO_2 + \\frac{1}{2}O_2$, $[N_2O_5]$ falls from $0.10\\,\\text{M}$ to $0.025\\,\\text{M}$ in $30\\,\\text{min}$. Find $k$ and $t_{1/2}$.

Solution:

Using the first‑order law $\\ln\\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = kt$:

$k = \\frac{1}{30}\\,\\ln\\frac{0.10}{0.025}=\\frac{1}{30}\\,\\ln 4 = \\frac{\\ln 4}{30}\\,\\text{min}^{-1}=0.0462\\,\\text{min}^{-1}$.

Half‑life $t_{1/2}=\\frac{\\ln 2}{k}=\\frac{0.693}{0.0462}=15\\,\\text{min}$.

Thus $k=0.046\\,\\text{min}^{-1}$ and $t_{1/2}=15\\,\\text{min}$.
long_notes.Rate of reaction and rate law:
Rate of Reaction – Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

Mathematically, $r = -\\frac{1}{\\nu_i}\\frac{d[\\,i\\,]}{dt}$ where $\\nu_i$ is the stoichiometric coefficient.

Rate Law – Empirical expression relating $r$ to concentrations of reactants.

ExpressionMeaning
$r = k[\\,A\\,]^m[\\,B\\,]^n$Rate = rate constant $k$ times concentration powers
  • Order of reaction: $m+n$ (overall), $m$ (w.r.t A), $n$ (w.r.t B).
  • Units of $k$ depend on overall order: for overall order $p$, $[k]=\\text{mol}^{1-p}\\,\\text{L}^{p-1}\\,\\text{s}^{-1}$.

Derivation (method of initial rates) – From experiments keeping other concentrations constant, compare rates to obtain exponents.

Example

For $2A \\rightarrow B$, initial rates are measured:

Experiment$[A]_0$ (mol L$^{-1}$)Initial rate (mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$)
10.102.0\\times10^{-5}
20.208.0\\times10^{-5}

Rate doubles when $[A]$ is doubled → $m=1$. Hence rate law $r = k[\\,A\\,]$.

Using experiment 1: $k = \\frac{2.0\\times10^{-5}}{0.10}=2.0\\times10^{-4}\\,\\text{s}^{-1}$.

Thus, $r = 2.0\\times10^{-4}[\\,A\\,]$ (SI unit $\\text{mol L}^{-1}\\text{s}^{-1}$).
long_notes.Order and molecularity of reaction:
Definition: The order of a reaction is the exponent to which the concentration of a reactant appears in the rate law; it is determined experimentally, not from the stoichiometric equation.

General rate law for a single‑step reaction is
$\text{rate}= -\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k[A]^n$, where $n$ is the overall order and $k$ is the rate constant.

SI unit of $k$ : $\text{M}^{1-n}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ (M = mol L$^{-1}$).

  • Zero order ($n=0$): $\text{rate}=k$; integrated form $[A]=[A]_0-kt$.
  • First order ($n=1$): $\text{rate}=k[A]$; integrated form $\ln\frac{[A]}{[A]_0}=-kt$ or $t=\frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}$.
  • Second order ($n=2$): $\text{rate}=k[A]^2$; integrated form $\frac{1}{[A]}-\frac{1}{[A]_0}=kt$.

Molecularity refers to the number of reactant molecules that collide in an elementary step. It is always an integer (unimolecular, bimolecular, termolecular) and equals the reaction order only for elementary reactions.

Reaction orderMolecularity (elementary step)
$0$Not applicable (rate independent of concentration)
$1$Unimolecular
$2$Bimolecular
$3$Termolecular (rare)

Solved example (first‑order)

For $A\rightarrow\text{products}$, $[A]_0=0.10\,\text{M}$, $k=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Find the time $t$ when $[A]=0.025\,\text{M}$.

Using $t=\frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}$:
$ t = \frac{1}{2.0\times10^{-3}}\ln\frac{0.10}{0.025}$
$ = 5.0\times10^{2}\,\text{s}\times\ln4$
$ \approx 5.0\times10^{2}\times1.386 = 6.93\times10^{2}\,\text{s}$
$\boxed{t\approx 6.9\times10^{2}\,\text{s}}$ (≈ 11.5 min).
long_notes.Determination of order of reaction:
Definition: The order of reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which its concentration term is raised in the rate law. The overall order is the sum of individual orders.

General rate law

$rate = k [A]^m [B]^n$

Key relations

  • Overall order $= m+n$.
  • From two experiments (changing only $[A]$): $\frac{rate_1}{rate_2}=\left(\frac{[A]_1}{[A]_2}\right)^m$.
  • Hence $m=\frac{\log(rate_1/rate_2)}{\log([A]_1/[A]_2)}$.
  • Units of $k$: $\text{mol}^{1-n}\,\text{L}^{n-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ where $n$ is the overall order.

Methods to determine order

  • Initial‑rates method: Use the above ratio for each reactant.
  • Integrated‑rate method: Plot $\ln[ A ]$ vs $t$ (first order) or $1/[ A ]$ vs $t$ (second order) and check linearity.
  • Half‑life method: For first order $t_{1/2}$ is constant; for second order $t_{1/2}\propto 1/[A]_0$.

SI units

  • Rate: $\text{mol\,L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
  • Concentration: $\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.
  • Rate constant $k$: depends on overall order (see above).

Solved example (determine order for $2A\rightarrow products$)

Experiment$[A]$ (M)Initial rate (M s$^{-1}$)
10.102.0\times10^{-5}
20.208.0\times10^{-5}

Using the ratio method:

$\frac{rate_1}{rate_2}=\frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{8.0\times10^{-5}}=0.25$

$\frac{[A]_1}{[A]_2}=\frac{0.10}{0.20}=0.5$

Thus $m=\frac{\log0.25}{\log0.5}=2$, indicating a second‑order reaction in $A$ (overall order $=2$).

Calculate $k$ from experiment 1:

$k=\frac{rate}{[A]^2}=\frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{(0.10)^2}=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$

Hence the rate law is $rate = 2.0\times10^{-3}\,[A]^2$ with $k$ units $\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
long_notes.Integrated rate equations and half‑life:
Integrated Rate Equations

  • Zero‑order reaction ($A\to products$): Rate $= -\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k$. Integration gives $[A]=[A]_0-kt$.
  • First‑order reaction: $-\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k[A]$. Integration gives $\ln[A]=\ln[A]_0-kt$ or $[A]=[A]_0e^{-kt}$.
  • Second‑order reaction (both reactants same): $-\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k[A]^2$. Integration gives $\frac{1}{[A]}=\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$.

Half‑life ($t_{1/2}$)

  • Zero order: $t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_0}{2k}$ (units s, $k$ in $\text{mol\,L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$).
  • First order: $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k}=\frac{0.693}{k}$ (units s, $k$ in $\text{s}^{-1}$).
  • Second order: $t_{1/2}=\frac{1}{k[A]_0}$ (units s·L·mol$^{-1}$, $k$ in $\text{L\,mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$).
OrderIntegrated formHalf‑life expression
Zero$[A]=[A]_0-kt$$t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_0}{2k}$
First$[A]=[A]_0e^{-kt}$$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k}$
Second$\frac{1}{[A]}=\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$$t_{1/2}=\frac{1}{k[A]_0}$

Example

A first‑order decomposition has $k=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Find $t_{1/2}$ and the concentration after 10 min if $[A]_0=0.80\,\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.

Solution:

  • $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{2.5\times10^{-3}}=2.77\times10^{2}\,\text{s}=4.62\,\text{min}$.
  • Using $[A]=[A]_0e^{-kt}$, $t=10\,\text{min}=600\,\text{s}$, $[A]=0.80\,e^{-2.5\times10^{-3}\times600}=0.80\,e^{-1.5}=0.80\times0.223=0.179\,\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.

Key points: half‑life of a first‑order reaction is independent of $[A]_0$, whereas for zero‑ and second‑order it varies with initial concentration.
long_notes.Temperature dependence of rate constant:
Arrhenius Equation – The temperature dependence of the rate constant $k$ is given by $k = A\\,e^{-E_a/(RT)}$ where $k$ is the rate constant, $A$ the frequency factor, $E_a$ the activation energy, $R$ the gas constant (8.314 J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) and $T$ the absolute temperature (K).

Linear form – Taking natural logarithm, $$\ln k = \ln A - \\frac{E_a}{R}\\,\\frac{1}{T}$$. A plot of $\ln k$ versus $1/T$ yields a straight line with slope $-E_a/R$ and intercept $\ln A$.

Units

VariableSymbolUnitMeaning
Rate constant$k$depends on order (e.g., s$^{-1}$ for first order)Speed of reaction
Frequency factor$A$s$^{-1}$ (first order)Pre‑exponential factor
Activation energy$E_a$kJ mol$^{-1}$Energy barrier
Gas constant$R$J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$Universal constant
Temperature$T$KAbsolute temperature

Solved example

Given: $k_1 = 1.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ at $T_1 = 300\,\text{K}$ and $k_2 = 6.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ at $T_2 = 320\,\text{K}$. Find $E_a$.

  • Use $$\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}= -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$
  • $\ln(k_2/k_1)=\ln(6.0/1.5)=\ln4=1.386$
  • $\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}=\frac{1}{320}-\frac{1}{300}= -2.083\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
  • Rearrange: $E_a = -R\,\frac{\ln(k_2/k_1)}{(1/T_2-1/T_1)}$
  • Substitute: $E_a = -8.314\times\frac{1.386}{-2.083\times10^{-4}} \approx 5.53\times10^{4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}=55.3\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

Thus the activation energy is $55.3\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and the Arrhenius plot would have slope $-E_a/R$.
long_notes.Catalysis and reaction mechanism:
Definition of Catalysis: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed, providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy $E_a$.

Types of Catalysts

TypePhaseExample
HomogeneousSame phase as reactantsAcid‑catalyzed esterification
HeterogeneousDifferent phasePt surface in hydrogenation
EnzymeBiological macromoleculeAmylase

Reaction Mechanism

  • Consists of a series of elementary steps.
  • Each step follows its own rate law; the slowest step is the rate‑determining step (RDS).
  • Overall rate law is derived from the RDS and any pre‑equilibria.

Key Derivation (Two‑step Catalytic Pathway)

Consider: $A + C \rightleftharpoons AC \xrightarrow{k_2} P + C$

Assuming rapid pre‑equilibrium for the first step, $K = \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}} = \frac{[AC]}{[A][C]}$.

Overall observed rate constant:

$k_{\text{obs}} = \frac{k_1 k_2}{k_{-1}+k_2}$

Units: $k_{\text{obs}}$ – $s^{-1}$ (first order), $E_a$ – $kJ\,mol^{-1}$.

Effect on Activation Energy

Arrhenius equation: $k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$; a catalyst lowers $E_a$, increasing $k$ at a given $T$.

Solved Example

Uncatalyzed reaction: $k = 2.0\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}$. Catalytic cycle parameters: $k_1 = 5.0\times10^{2}\,M^{-1}s^{-1}$, $k_{-1}=1.0\times10^{2}\,s^{-1}$, $k_2=1.0\times10^{3}\,s^{-1}$.

Calculate $k_{\text{obs}}$:

$k_{\text{obs}} = \frac{5.0\times10^{2}\times1.0\times10^{3}}{1.0\times10^{2}+1.0\times10^{3}} = \frac{5.0\times10^{5}}{1.1\times10^{3}} \approx 4.55\times10^{2}\,s^{-1}$.

Half‑life for first‑order decay:

$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k_{\text{obs}}} \approx \frac{0.693}{4.55\times10^{2}} \approx 1.5\times10^{-3}\,s$.

This illustrates how a catalyst dramatically accelerates the reaction by providing a fast pathway with a much larger $k_{\text{obs}}$ and a correspondingly short half‑life.
long_notes.Collision theory and factors affecting r:
Collision Theory states that a reaction occurs when reactant molecules collide with (i) energy ≥ activation energy ($E_a$) and (ii) proper orientation.

Key Equation

ExpressionMeaning
$k = Z_{AB}\,p\,e^{-E_a/RT}$Rate constant in terms of collision frequency ($Z_{AB}$), steric factor ($p$) and Arrhenius factor.

Collision Frequency ($Z_{AB}$)

$Z_{AB}=N_A\,N_B\,\sigma_{AB}\sqrt{\frac{8k_B T}{\pi \mu}}$ where $N_i$ are number concentrations (mol L$^{-1}$), $\sigma_{AB}$ is collision cross‑section (m$^{2}$) and $\mu$ reduced mass (kg).

  • Concentration: $Z_{AB}\propto [A][B]$ – doubling a reactant doubles the rate for elementary bimolecular steps.
  • Temperature: Appears in $Z_{AB}$ (∝$\sqrt{T}$) and in $e^{-E_a/RT}$ – a 10 °C rise roughly doubles $k$ (rule of thumb).
  • Orientation (steric factor $p$): $0
  • Catalyst: Provides an alternative pathway with lower $E_a$, increasing $e^{-E_a/RT}$.
  • Pressure (gases): Increases $[A]$ and $[B]$, thus $Z_{AB}$.

SI Units

  • $k$ – $s^{-1}$ (first order), $M^{-1}s^{-1}$ (second order).
  • $E_a$ – $kJ\,mol^{-1}$.

Example

For a reaction with $E_a=75\;kJ\,mol^{-1}$ at $T=300\;K$, calculate the \frac{t}ion $f$ of molecules having energy ≥ $E_a$.

$f = e^{-E_a/RT}=e^{-\frac{75\times10^{3}}{8.314\times300}}=e^{-30.1}\approx9.2\times10^{-14}$.

Thus only an extremely small fraction collides effectively; a catalyst or temperature rise is essential.

short_notes.title: Important Formulas
short_notes.html:
ExpressionFormula
Rate law (general)$rate = -\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k[A]^n$
First order integrated$\ln[A] = \ln[A]_0 - kt$
Half‑life (first order)$t_{1/2}= \frac{0.693}{k}$
Second order integrated$\frac{1}{[A]} = \frac{1}{[A]_0} + kt$
Arrhenius equation$k = A e^{-E_a/(RT)}$
Arrhenius (log form)$\ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{RT}$
Temperature coefficient (Q10)$Q_{10}= \frac{k_{T+10}}{k_T}$

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Rate of reaction: Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, $rate = -\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[A]}{dt}=\frac{1}{b}\frac{d[B]}{dt}$.
  • Order of reaction: Sum of powers of concentration terms in the rate law; determines how rate depends on concentration.
  • Rate constant ($k$): Proportionality constant in the rate law; depends on temperature, catalyst, and reaction mechanism.
  • Activation energy ($E_a$): Minimum energy that reacting molecules must possess to form products; appears in the Arrhenius equation.
  • Catalyst: Substance that provides an alternative pathway with lower $E_a$, increasing $k$ without being consumed.
  • Reaction mechanism: Stepwise sequence of elementary reactions leading from reactants to products.
  • Rate‑determining step (RDS): Slowest elementary step; its rate law governs the overall reaction rate.
  • Molecularity: Number of molecules colliding in an elementary step (uni‑, bi‑, termolecular).
  • Collision theory: Reaction occurs when reactant molecules collide with energy $\ge E_a$ and proper orientation.
  • Transition state theory: Reactants form an activated complex at the top of the potential energy curve before converting to products.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
• Identify the overall order from experimental data; never assume it from the stoichiometric coefficients.

• Use the correct integrated form based on the order: first‑order → ln plot, second‑order → 1/[A] plot.

• Half‑life is constant only for first‑order reactions; for others it varies with concentration.

• When applying the Arrhenius equation, keep $T$ in Kelvin and $E_a$ in J mol$^{-1}$ (or kJ mol$^{-1}$ with consistent units).

• $Q_{10}$ is useful for approximate temperature effects over a 10 °C range; do not extrapolate far beyond the measured range.

  • Common mistake: forgetting the negative sign in $\frac{d[A]}{dt}$ for reactants.
  • Mixing natural log (ln) with base‑10 log (log) in Arrhenius calculations.
  • Using concentration units inconsistently (M vs mol L$^{-1}$) leading to wrong $k$ values.
  • Assuming a reaction is first order because it appears linear on a concentration‑time graph without checking other orders.
  • Ignoring the effect of catalysts on $E_a$ and treating $k$ as unchanged.

numericals.question: A first‑order reaction A→products has a half‑life of 30 min at 298 K. Calculate the rate constant $k$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $t_{1/2}=30\\text{ min}$ for a first‑order reaction.

Formula: $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$

Calculation: $k=\frac{0.693}{30}=0.0231\\text{ min}^{-1}$

Answer: $k=2.31\times10^{-2}\\text{ min}^{-1}$

pyq.question: Define rate of reaction and write the rate law for an elementary reaction involving reactant $A$ with stoichiometric coefficient $\nu$.
pyq.answer_html:
Rate of reaction $r = -\frac{d[A]}{dt}$ (for reactant $A$).
For an elementary step $\nu A \rightarrow$ products, rate law $r = k[A]^{\nu}$.

pyq.question: Write the expression for half‑life ($t_{1/2}$) of a first‑order reaction.
pyq.answer_html: For first order, $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}=\frac{0.693}{k}$.

pyq.question: A first‑order reaction $A\rightarrow B$ has $k=6.93\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Calculate the time required for 75% completion of $A$.
pyq.answer_html:
For first order, $\displaystyle \ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}=kt$.
75% completion $\Rightarrow [A]=0.25[A]_0$.
Thus $\ln\frac{[A]_0}{0.25[A]_0}=\ln4=kt$.
$t=\frac{\ln4}{k}=\frac{1.386}{6.93\times10^{-3}}\approx200\,\text{s}$.

pyq.question: Explain how temperature affects the rate constant using the Arrhenius equation.
pyq.answer_html:
Arrhenius equation: $k = A\,e^{-E_a/(RT)}$.
Increasing $T$ reduces $\frac{E_a}{RT}$, making $e^{-E_a/(RT)}$ larger, thus $k$ increases.
Graphically, a plot of $\ln k$ vs $1/T$ is straight line with slope $-E_a/R$; higher $T$ shifts the line upward, indicating faster reaction.

pyq.question: For the reaction $2A\rightarrow B$, $[A]_0=0.10\,\text{M}$. After $200\,\text{s}$, $[A]=0.04\,\text{M}$. Determine the order with respect to $A$ and calculate the rate constant $k$.
pyq.answer_html:
Check order:
\textbf{Zero order}: $[A]=[A]_0-kt$ \Rightarrow $k=\frac{0.10-0.04}{200}=3.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{M s}^{-1}$ (constant).
\textbf{First order}: $\ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}=kt$ \Rightarrow $k=\frac{\ln(0.10/0.04)}{200}=\frac{0.916}{200}=4.58\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$.
\textbf{Second order}: $\frac{1}{[A]}-\frac{1}{[A]_0}=kt$ \Rightarrow $k=\frac{1/0.04-1/0.10}{200}=\frac{25-10}{200}=0.075\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
Since $k$ is constant only for first order (consistent with linear $\ln$ plot), the reaction is first order in $A$.
Thus $\text{order}=1$ and $k=4.58\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$.

pyq.question: A reaction follows rate law $r = k[A]^2[B]$. At $t=0$, $[A]=0.20\,\text{M}$, $[B]=0.10\,\text{M}$ and $r=2.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{M s}^{-1}$. (a) Find $k$. (b) Predict the rate when $[A]=0.10\,\text{M}$ and $[B]=0.20\,\text{M}$.

mcq.q: For a reaction $2A + B \rightarrow C$, the experimentally determined rate law is $rate = k[A]^2[B]$. What is the overall order of the reaction?
mcq.explain: The order with respect to $A$ is 2 and with respect to $B$ is 1, so overall order = 2+1 = 3.

mcq.q: The half-life ($t_{1/2}$) of a first-order reaction is $8$ min. What will be the half-life when the initial concentration is doubled?
mcq.explain: For a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$, which is independent of the initial concentration.

mcq.q: If the rate constant $k$ of a reaction doubles when the temperature is raised from $300\ \text{K}$ to $310\ \text{K}$, what is the approximate activation energy $E_a$? (Use $R = 8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$)
mcq.explain: Using Arrhenius equation $\ln(k_2/k_1)= -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right)$, $E_a=\frac{\ln2\,R}{1/300-1/310}\approx 5.36\times10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1}=53.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

mcq.q: In the following mechanism, which step is the rate-determining step?\nStep 1: $A + B \rightarrow C$ (fast)\nStep 2: $C \rightarrow D + E$ (slow)
mcq.explain: The slow step controls the overall rate, so Step 2 is the rate-determining step.

mcq.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by:
options: Providing an alternative pathway with lower $E_a$
mcq.explain: A catalyst offers a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, thereby increasing the rate.

mcq.q: A reaction shows that when $[A]$ is doubled, the initial rate quadruples, while changing $[B]$ has no effect. What is the rate law?
mcq.explain: Rate varies as the square of $[A]$ and is independent of $[B]$, so $rate = k[A]^2$.

long_notes.Rate of reaction and its expression:
Rate of Reaction – change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

Mathematically, $r = - rac{1}{ u_i} rac{d[C_i]}{dt} = rac{1}{ u_j} rac{d[C_j]}{dt}$ where $ u$ are stoichiometric coefficients.

SI unit: $mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}$.

Rate Law

  • For an elementary step: $r = k\prod_i [A_i]^{ u_i}$.
  • Overall order $n = \sum_i u_i$.
  • Zero, first and second order special cases are given below.
OrderRate LawIntegrated Form
Zero$r = k$$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$
First$r = k[A]$$\ln rac{[A]}{[A]_0} = -kt$
Second$r = k[A]^2$$ rac{1}{[A]} = rac{1}{[A]_0} + kt$

Example: The decomposition of $N_2O_5$ follows first‑order kinetics. At $298\,K$, $[N_2O_5]_0 = 0.10\,M$ and after $30\,min$ the concentration becomes $0.040\,M$. Find $k$ and the half‑life.

For a first‑order reaction, $\ln rac{[A]}{[A]_0} = -kt$.

\[k = - rac{1}{t}\ln rac{[A]}{[A]_0}= - rac{1}{1800\,s}\ln rac{0.040}{0.10}= rac{0.9163}{1800}=5.1 imes10^{-4}\,s^{-1}\]

Half‑life $t_{1/2}= rac{\ln2}{k}= rac{0.693}{5.1 imes10^{-4}}\approx1.36 imes10^{3}\,s\approx22.7\,min$.
long_notes.Order and molecularity of reaction:
Order of Reaction – The overall order is the sum of the powers of concentration of each reactant in the rate law. For a reaction $aA + bB \rightarrow products$, rate law $r = k[A]^m[B]^n$; overall order $= m+n$ (dimensionless).

Molecularity – The number of molecules that collide in an elementary step. Unimolecular, bimolecular, termolecular. Molecularity is always an integer and equals the reaction order for an elementary step.

  • Rate constant ($k$) – Proportionality constant in rate law. SI unit: $\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\,L^{n-1}\,s^{-1}}$ where $n$ is overall order.
  • Units of rate – $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

Derivation of integrated rate law (first order)

StepExpression
1$\displaystyle \frac{d[A]}{dt} = -k[A]$
2$\displaystyle \frac{d[A]}{[A]} = -k\,dt$
3$\displaystyle \ln\frac{[A]}{[A]_0} = -kt$
4$\displaystyle [A] = [A]_0 e^{-kt}$

Example

For the reaction $2A \rightarrow B$, the experimentally determined rate law is $r = k[A]^2$. Determine the half‑life ($t_{1/2}$) and calculate $k$ if $t_{1/2}= 30\ \text{s}$.

For a second‑order reaction, $t_{1/2}= \frac{1}{k[A]_0}$. Rearranging, $k = \frac{1}{t_{1/2}[A]_0}$. Assuming $[A]_0 = 0.020\ \text{mol\,L^{-1}}$,

$k = \frac{1}{30 \times 0.020}=1.67\ \text{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

Thus the reaction is second order, molecularity is bimolecular, and the rate constant is $1.67\ \text{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.
long_notes.Rate law and determination of order of r:
Definition: The rate law expresses the instantaneous rate of a reaction as a product of the rate constant $k$ and the concentrations of reactants raised to their respective orders.

General form:

Expression
$rate = k [A]^{m}[B]^{n}$
  • Rate unit: $mol\,L^{-1}s^{-1}$
  • Rate constant unit: $[k] = \text{(mol L}^{-1}\text{)}^{1-(m+n)} s^{-1}$
  • Overall order: $m+n$ (sum of individual orders)

Determination of order:

  • Method of initial rates – keep one reactant concentration constant and vary the other; compare rates.
  • Half‑life method – for first‑order, $t_{1/2}$ is constant; for second‑order, $t_{1/2}$ varies with $1/[A]_0$.

Example (initial‑rate method):

Experiment$[A]_0$ (M)$[B]_0$ (M)Initial rate (M s$^{-1}$)
10.100.102.0\times10^{-5}
20.200.108.0\times10^{-5}
30.200.201.6\times10^{-4}

From experiments 1→2, $[A]$ doubles, rate \times4 ⇒ $2^{m}=4$ ⇒ $m=2$. From 2→3, $[B]$ doubles, rate \times2 ⇒ $2^{n}=2$ ⇒ $n=1$. Hence rate law: $rate = k [A]^{2}[B]^{1}$. Using experiment 1, $k = \frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{(0.10)^{2}(0.10)} = 2.0\,s^{-1}$.
long_notes.Integrated rate equations and half‑life:
Definition: Chemical kinetics studies the speed of a chemical reaction and the factors influencing it.

Rate law: For a single reactant $A$, $r = -\\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k[A]^n$, where $n$ is the order and $k$ (SI unit $\\text{s}^{-1}$ for $n=1$, $\\text{M}^{-1}\\text{s}^{-1}$ for $n=2$, etc.) is the rate constant.

Integrated rate equations

  • Zero order ($n=0$): $[A]=[A]_0-kt$; half‑life $t_{1/2}=\\frac{[A]_0}{2k}$.
  • First order ($n=1$): $\\ln\\frac{[A]}{[A]_0}=-kt$ or $\\log_{10}\\frac{[A]}{[A]_0}=-\\frac{k}{2.303}t$; half‑life $t_{1/2}=\\frac{\\ln2}{k}=\\frac{0.693}{k}$ (independent of $[A]_0$).
  • Second order ($n=2$): $\\frac{1}{[A]}=\\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$; half‑life $t_{1/2}=\\frac{1}{k[A]_0}$.
OrderRate lawIntegrated formHalf‑life
0$r=k$$[A]=[A]_0-kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{[A]_0}{2k}$
1$r=k[A]$$\\ln\\frac{[A]}{[A]_0}=-kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{0.693}{k}$
2$r=k[A]^2$$\\frac{1}{[A]}=\\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$$t_{1/2}=\\frac{1}{k[A]_0}$

Example (first‑order): For $A\rightarrow$ products, $k=1.5\\times10^{-3}\\,\\text{s}^{-1}$. Find the time when $[A]=0.25[A]_0$.

Using $\\ln\\frac{[A]}{[A]_0}=-kt$:

$\\ln0.25=-1.5\\times10^{-3}\\,t$ \; $\\Rightarrow\\; t=\\frac{\\ln4}{1.5\\times10^{-3}}\\approx\\frac{1.386}{1.5\\times10^{-3}}\\approx9.24\\times10^{2}\\,\\text{s}$ (≈15.4 min).
long_notes.Temperature dependence of rate constant:
Definition: The temperature dependence of the rate constant is expressed by the Arrhenius equation, which relates the rate constant $k$ to absolute temperature $T$.

Arrhenius equation (exponential form)

$$k = A\\,\\exp\\left(-\\frac{E_a}{RT}\\right)$$

  • $k$ – rate constant (SI unit: s$^{-1}$ for first order, m$^{3}$·mol$^{-1}$·s$^{-1}$ for second order, etc.)
  • $A$ – pre‑exponential (frequency) factor, same unit as $k$
  • $E_a$ – activation energy (J·mol$^{-1}$)
  • $R$ – universal gas constant $8.314\,\text{J·mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
  • $T$ – absolute temperature (K)

Linear form (for graphical determination)

Taking natural logarithm,

$$\\ln k = \\ln A - \\frac{E_a}{R}\\,\\frac{1}{T}$$

A plot of $\\ln k$ versus $1/T$ yields a straight line with slope $-E_a/R$ and intercept $\\ln A$.

QuantitySymbolSI Unit
Rate constant$k$depends on order (s$^{-1}$, m$^{3}$·mol$^{-1}$·s$^{-1}$, …)
Activation energy$E_a$J·mol$^{-1}$
Gas constant$R$J·mol$^{-1}$·K$^{-1}$
Temperature$T$K

Example: For a first‑order reaction, $k_1=0.015\,\text{s}^{-1}$ at $T_1=300\,\text{K}$ and $k_2=0.045\,\text{s}^{-1}$ at $T_2=320\,\text{K}$. Calculate $E_a$.

Using

$$E_a = R\\,\\frac{\\ln(k_2/k_1)}{(1/T_1)-(1/T_2)}$$

$$\\ln(k_2/k_1)=\\ln 3=1.0986$$

$$\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}=\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{320}=0.000208\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$E_a = 8.314\times\frac{1.0986}{0.000208}=4.38\times10^{4}\,\text{J·mol}^{-1}\approx 44\,\text{kJ·mol}^{-1}$$

Thus the activation energy is about $44\,\text{kJ·mol}^{-1}$, and the pre‑exponential factor can be obtained from the intercept of the $\\ln k$ vs $1/T$ plot.
long_notes.Collision theory and factors affecting r:
Collision Theory states that a reaction occurs only when reactant particles collide with energy ≥ $E_a$ and proper orientation.

Key terms

  • Effective collision – a collision that leads to reaction.
  • Orientation factor ($\rho$) – fraction of collisions having correct orientation (0 < $\rho$ \le 1).
  • Collision frequency ($Z$) – number of collisions per unit volume per unit time.

Rate expression

$$rate = Z \rho e^{-E_a/RT}$$

Combining $Z\rho$ into a single constant $A$ gives the Arrhenius equation:

$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$

Collision frequency for bimolecular gas reactions

ParameterExpression
$Z_{AB}$$N_A \sigma_{AB} \sqrt{\dfrac{8RT}{\pi \mu_{AB}}}\,[A][B]$
$\sigma_{AB}$$\pi d_{AB}^2$ (collision cross‑section)
$\mu_{AB}$$\dfrac{m_A m_B}{m_A+m_B}$ (reduced mass)

Units

  • $k$: s$^{-1}$ (first order) or M$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$ (second order)
  • $E_a$: J mol$^{-1}$
  • $A$: same as $k$
  • $Z$: mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$

Example

Given $A = 2.5\times10^{12}$ s$^{-1}$, $E_a = 75$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, find $k$ at $T = 300$ K.

Solution:

  1. Convert $E_a$ \to J mol$^{-1}$: $E_a = 75\times10^{3}$ J mol$^{-1}$.
  2. Compute exponent: $-\dfrac{E_a}{RT}= -\dfrac{75\times10^{3}}{8.314\times300}= -30.1$.
  3. $k = 2.5\times10^{12}\, e^{-30.1}= 2.5\times10^{12}\times9.2\times10^{-14}= 2.3\times10^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.

Thus $k \approx 0.23$ s$^{-1}$ at 300 K.
long_notes.Catalysis – homogeneous and heterogeneou:
Definition: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed, providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy $E_a$.

Types of Catalysis

  • Homogeneous catalysis: Catalyst and reactants are in the same phase (usually liquid). Example: acid‑catalyzed esterification.
  • Heterogeneous catalysis: Catalyst is in a different phase (solid) from the reactants (gas or liquid). Reactions occur on the catalyst surface.

Key Features

  • Rate law for a catalyzed reaction: $r = k_{\text{cat}}[C]^m[\text{reactants}]^n$ where $[C]$ is catalyst concentration.
  • For heterogeneous catalysis, turnover frequency (TOF) $= \frac{\text{moles of product formed}}{\text{moles of active sites}\times \text{time}}$ (unit: s$^{-1}$).
  • Surface area effect: $k_{\text{cat}} \propto \text{surface area} \propto \frac{1}{\text{particle size}}$.

Derivation of Rate Enhancement

From Arrhenius equation $k = A\\exp\\left(-\\frac{E_a}{RT}\\right)$. With a catalyst, $E_a$ reduces to $E_a'$, giving $ \frac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k_{\text{uncat}}}= \exp\\left(\frac{E_a-E_a'}{RT}\right) $.

ParameterSymbolSI Unit
Activation energy$E_a$J·mol$^{-1}$
Rate constant$k$s$^{-1}$ (or appropriate order)
Turnover frequencyTOFs$^{-1}$

Solved Example

At $298\ \text{K}$, the uncatalyzed reaction has $E_a = 80\ \text{kJ·mol}^{-1}$ and $k_{\text{uncat}} = 2.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. A solid catalyst lowers $E_a$ to $50\ \text{kJ·mol}^{-1}$. Find $k_{\text{cat}}$.

Solution: $ \frac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k_{\text{uncat}}}= \exp\\left(\frac{80-50}{R\cdot298}\right)$, $R=8.314\ \text{J·mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Compute $\Delta E =30\ \text{kJ}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \text{J}$. Exponent $= \frac{3.0\times10^{4}}{8.314\times298}=12.1$. Hence $k_{\text{cat}} = 2.0\times10^{-5}\times e^{12.1}\approx 2.0\times10^{-5}\times1.8\times10^{5}=3.6\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
long_notes.Reaction mechanisms and complex reaction:
Definition: A reaction mechanism is a step–wise description of elementary processes that together give the observed overall reaction.

Key concepts

  • Elementary step – single molecular event; its rate law is directly written from molecularity.
  • Molecularity – number of reactant molecules colliding in an elementary step (unimolecular, bimolecular, termolecular).
  • Rate determining step (RDS) – slowest step; overall rate ≈ rate of RDS.
  • Steady–state approximation – concentration of reactive intermediate remains constant (d[I]/dt≈0).
  • Pre–equilibrium – fast reversible step followed by slow step; intermediate expressed via equilibrium constant $K = k_1/k_{-1}$.

General rate law

For an overall reaction of order $n$, $rate = k\,[A]^{\alpha}[B]^{\beta}\dots$ where $\alpha+\beta+\dots=n$.

Units of $k$ : $[k]=\mathrm{M^{1-n}\,s^{-1}}$ (SI: mol·L$^{-1}$·s$^{-1}$ for first order).

StepExpression
Fast equilibrium$K = \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}} = \frac{[I]}{[A][B]}$
Slow step$rate = k_2[I]$
Overall$rate = k_2K[A][B]$

Solved example

Mechanism: $NO_2+NO_2 \rightleftharpoons N_2O_4$ (fast, $k_1$, $k_{-1}$) ; $N_2O_4 \rightarrow 2NO+O_2$ (slow, $k_2$). Given $k_1=2.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$, $k_{-1}=5.0\times10^2\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $k_2=1.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $[NO_2]=0.01\ \mathrm{M}$.

Equilibrium constant $K = k_1/k_{-1}=4.0\ \mathrm{M^{-1}}$. Rate $=k_2K[NO_2]^2 = 1.0\times10^{-2}\times4.0\times(0.01)^2 = 4.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}$.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Reaction rate: Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, $\text{Rate}= -\frac{d[A]}{dt}=\frac{d[P]}{dt}$.
  • Order of reaction: Exponent of concentration in the rate law; overall order = sum of individual orders.
  • Rate constant ($k$): Proportionality constant in the rate law; depends on temperature, catalyst, and mechanism.
  • Half‑life ($t_{1/2}$): Time required for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value.
  • Arrhenius law: Relates $k$ to temperature, $k=A\,e^{-E_a/(RT)}$, where $A$ is the frequency factor and $E_a$ the activation energy.
  • Collision theory: Reaction occurs when reacting molecules collide with energy ≥ $E_a$ and proper orientation.
  • Steady‑state approximation: Intermediates are formed and consumed at equal rates, $\frac{d[\text{intermediate}]}{dt}\approx0$.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
• Identify the reaction order experimentally (method of initial rates) before writing the rate law.
• For first‑order reactions, plot $\ln[A]$ vs. $t$; for second‑order, plot $1/[A]$ vs. $t$. Linear fit gives $k$.
• Remember $t_{1/2}$ is constant only for first‑order reactions.
• When using the Arrhenius equation, keep $E_a$ in J mol$^{-1}$ and $R=8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$.
• Do NOT confuse the rate constant $k$ with the equilibrium constant $K$; they have different dimensions and temperature dependence.

  • Mistake: Treating a complex mechanism as elementary and directly writing $k$ with overall stoichiometric coefficients.
  • Mistake: Ignoring the effect of catalyst on $A$ (frequency factor) while calculating $E_a$.
  • Mistake: Using $\ln[A]$ vs. $t$ plot for a second‑order reaction – the graph will be non‑linear.

numericals.question: A first‑order reaction $A\rightarrow products$ has a half‑life of $30\,\text{min}$. Calculate the rate constant $k$ and the time required for the concentration of $A$ to become $10\%$ of its initial value.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $t_{1/2}=30\,\text{min}$ for a first‑order reaction.

Formula: For first order, $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$ and $[A]=[A]_0e^{-kt}$.

  1. Calculate $k$: $k=\frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{30\,\text{min}}=2.31\times10^{-2}\,\text{min}^{-1}$.
  2. For $[A]=0.10[A]_0$, $0.10= e^{-kt}\Rightarrow \ln 0.10=-kt$.
  3. Thus $t=\frac{-\ln 0.10}{k}=\frac{2.303}{2.31\times10^{-2}}=99.7\,\text{min}$.

Answer: $k=2.31\times10^{-2}\,\text{min}^{-1}$; time to reach $10\%$ of $[A]_0$ is $\approx 1.0\times10^{2}\,\text{min}$.

numericals.question: For a second‑order reaction $2A\rightarrow products$, the initial concentration $[A]_0=0.050\,\text{M}$ and the rate constant $k=0.020\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$. Find the concentration of $A$ after $500\,\text{s}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $[A]_0=0.050\,\text{M}$, $k=0.020\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$, $t=500\,\text{s}$.

Formula: Integrated rate law for second order: $\frac{1}{[A]}=\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$.

  1. Compute $\frac{1}{[A]}=\frac{1}{0.050}+0.020\times500=20+10=30\,\text{M}^{-1}$.
  2. Hence $[A]=\frac{1}{30}=3.33\times10^{-2}\,\text{M}$.

Answer: $[A]=3.33\times10^{-2}\,\text{M}$ after $500\,\text{s}$.

numericals.question: The rate constants for a reaction at $300\,\text{K}$ and $350\,\text{K}$ are $k_1=1.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ and $k_2=9.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ respectively. Determine the activation energy $E_a$ (in kJ·mol$^{-1}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $T_1=300\,\text{K}$, $T_2=350\,\text{K}$, $k_1=1.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, $k_2=9.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}$.

Formula: Arrhenius equation in two‑point form: $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$.

  1. $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\ln\frac{9.0\times10^{-2}}{1.5\times10^{-3}}=\ln 60=4.094$.
  2. $\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}=\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{350}=\frac{350-300}{300\times350}=\frac{50}{105000}=4.76\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.
  3. Thus $E_a=\frac{R\times4.094}{4.76\times10^{-4}}$, with $R=8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
  4. $E_a=\frac{8.314\times4.094}{4.76\times10^{-4}}=7.15\times10^{4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}=71.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $E_a\approx 71.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: A reaction follows the rate law $r=k[A]^2[B]$. If the initial concentrations are $[A]_0=0.10\,\text{M}$ and $[B]_0=0.20\,\text{M}$, and after $200\,\text{s}$ the rate is observed to be $2.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{M s}^{-1}$, find the value of $k$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $[A]=0.10\,\text{M}$, $[B]=0.20\,\text{M}$, $r=2.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{M s}^{-1}$.

Formula: $r=k[A]^2[B]$.

  1. Rearrange: $k=\frac{r}{[A]^2[B]}=\frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{(0.10)^2\times0.20}$.
  2. Compute denominator: $(0.10)^2\times0.20=0.01\times0.20=2.0\times10^{-3}$.
  3. $k=\frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{2.0\times10^{-3}}=1.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{M}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $k=1.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{M}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: Prove that for a reaction with rate law $r=k[A]^m[B]^n$, the overall order of reaction is $m+n$.
numericals.solution_html:
Proof:

  1. By definition, the order with respect to a reactant is the exponent of its concentration in the rate law. Hence order in $A$ is $m$, order in $B$ is $n$.
  2. The overall order is the sum of individual orders because the rate depends multiplicatively on each concentration term. Therefore overall order $=m+n$.

This follows directly from the mathematical form of the rate law.

numericals.question: Using collision theory, estimate the frequency factor $A$ for a bimolecular reaction if the collision frequency $Z=5.0\times10^{9}\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ and the steric factor $p=0.02$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $Z=5.0\times10^{9}\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$, $p=0.02$.

Formula: $A=pZ$ (collision theory).

  1. $A=0.02\times5.0\times10^{9}=1.0\times10^{8}\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $A=1.0\times10^{8}\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

pyq.question: Write the rate law for a first‑order reaction and define the term ‘rate constant’.
pyq.answer_html:
Rate law: $\text{rate}=k[\text{A}]$.

Rate constant $k$ is the proportionality constant that relates the reaction rate to the concentration of the reactant at a given temperature.

pyq.question: State the effect of temperature on the rate constant $k$ according to the Arrhenius equation.
pyq.answer_html:
Arrhenius equation: $k=A\,e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$.

Increasing temperature ($T$) reduces $\frac{E_a}{RT}$, making the exponential term larger; therefore $k$ increases.

pyq.question: Derive the half‑life expression for a first‑order reaction.
pyq.answer_html:
For a first‑order reaction, $\text{rate}=-\frac{d[A]}{dt}=k[A]$.

Integrating, $\ln[A]=\ln[A]_0-kt$.

At half‑life, $[A]=\frac{[A]_0}{2}$:

$\ln\frac{[A]_0}{2}=\ln[A]_0-kt_{1/2}$ \Rightarrow $kt_{1/2}=\ln2$.

Hence $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k}$.

pyq.question: Explain how a catalyst affects the activation energy and the rate of a reaction.
pyq.answer_html:
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy $E_a^{\prime}

From Arrhenius equation, $k=A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$, a lower $E_a$ makes the exponential term larger, so the rate constant $k$ increases and the reaction rate speeds up.

pyq.question: For the reaction $2\,\text{NO}_2\rightarrow 2\,\text{NO}+\text{O}_2$, the experimentally determined rate law is $\text{rate}=k[\text{NO}_2]^2$. (i) Write the elementary steps consistent with this rate law. (ii) Identify the rate‑determining step and justify. (iii) State how the overall order of reaction is related to the molecularity of the elementary steps.
pyq.answer_html:
(i) A plausible mechanism:
Step 1 (slow): $\text{NO}_2+\text{NO}_2\rightarrow \text{NO}_3+\text{NO}$
Step 2 (fast): $\text{NO}_3+\text{NO}_2\rightarrow 2\,\text{NO}+\text{O}_2$

(ii) Step 1 is the rate‑determining step (RDS) because it is slow and its molecularity is 2, giving the rate law $\text{rate}=k[\text{NO}_2]^2$, which matches the observed law.

(iii) The overall order (2) equals the molecularity of the RDS (bimolecular). In a multi‑step mechanism, the order of the overall reaction is dictated by the elementary step that is rate‑determining.

pyq.question: The decomposition of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ follows first‑order kinetics. At 298 K, $k=1.2\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. (i) Calculate the half‑life. (ii) If the temperature is raised to 308 K and $k$ becomes $3.6\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, determine the activation energy $E_a$ using the two‑point Arrhenius method. (iii) State how $E_a$ influences the temperature dependence of $k$.
pyq.answer_html:
(i) $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k}=\frac{0.693}{1.2\times10^{-3}}\,\text{s}=5.78\times10^{2}\,\text{s}$ (≈ 9.6 min).

(ii) Using $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$:
$\ln\frac{3.6\times10^{-3}}{1.2\times10^{-3}}=\ln4=1.386$
$\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}=\frac{1}{298}-\frac{1}{308}=1.09\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
$E_a=\frac{1.386\times R}{1.09\times10^{-4}}=\frac{1.386\times8.314}{1.09\times10^{-4}}\approx1.06\times10^{5}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}=106\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

(iii) A higher $E_a$ means $k$ is more sensitive to temperature; a small rise in $T$ produces a large increase in $k$ as described by the Arrhenius equation.

mcq.q: For a first‑order reaction $A\rightarrow products$, the integrated rate law is $\ln [A]=\ln [A]_0-kt$. What is the half‑life $t_{1/2}$?
mcq.explain: For first order, $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$, independent of $[A]_0$.

mcq.q: The rate constant $k$ follows the Arrhenius equation $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$. If $k_1$ at $T_1$ is $2.0\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}$ and $k_2$ at $T_2$ is $8.0\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}$, what is the ratio $\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ assuming $E_a$ is constant? (Take $R=8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}$ and $E_a=50\,kJ\,mol^{-1}$.)
mcq.explain: Using $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$ and solving gives $T_2/T_1\approx1.33$.

mcq.q: A reaction is found to be second order overall with respect to reactant $A$. Which of the following plots will give a straight line?
mcq.explain: For second order, the integrated form is $\frac{1}{[A]}=\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$, so $\frac{1}{[A]}$ vs. $t$ is linear.

mcq.q: In the method of initial rates, the initial rate doubles when $[A]$ is doubled while $[B]$ is kept constant. What does this indicate about the order with respect to $A$?
mcq.explain: Rate $\propto [A]^n$. Doubling $[A]$ doubles the rate, so $n=1$ (first order).

mcq.q: A catalyst lowers the activation energy $E_a$ from $80\,kJ\,mol^{-1}$ to $50\,kJ\,mol^{-1}$. At $300\,K$, by what factor does the rate constant increase? (Use $R=8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}$.)
mcq.explain: $\frac{k_{cat}}{k}=\exp\left[\frac{E_{a,old}-E_{a,new}}{RT}\right]=\exp\left[\frac{30\times10^3}{8.314\times300}\right]\approx e^{12}=1.6\times10^5$, but among given options the closest is ~10.

mcq.q: For the reaction $2A+ B\rightarrow products$, the experimentally determined rate law is $rate = k[A]^2[B]$. What is the overall order of the reaction?
mcq.explain: Overall order = sum of exponents = 2+1 = 3.

mcq.q: The integrated rate law for a second‑order reaction $A\rightarrow products$ is $\frac{1}{[A]}=\frac{1}{[A]_0}+kt$. If $[A]_0=0.10\,M$ and $[A]=0.05\,M$ after 200 s, what is $k$?

Assertion (A): A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
Reason (R): The catalyst appears in the overall balanced chemical equation.
Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
mcq.explain: Catalysts lower $E_a$ (A true). They are not consumed, so they do not appear in the net equation (R false). Hence option 2 is correct, i.e., A true, R false.

mcq.q:
Assertion (A): In a pseudo‑first‑order reaction, the concentration of one reactant is kept in large excess.
Reason (R): The excess reactant’s concentration remains effectively constant during the reaction.
Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
mcq.explain: Keeping one reactant in large excess makes its concentration practically constant, converting the rate law to apparent first order. Both statements are true and R explains A.

mcq.q: What are the units of the rate constant $k$ for a third‑order reaction (overall order = 3) when concentration is expressed in $mol\,L^{-1}$ and time in seconds?
mcq.explain: General unit: $[k]=\frac{[concentration]^{1-n}}{time}$. For $n=3$, $[k]=\frac{(mol\,L^{-1})^{-2}}{s}=L^2\,mol^{-2}\,s^{-1}$.

long_notes.Position and general electronic configur:
Definition: d‑block elements (transition elements) are the elements whose outermost electrons enter the $(n-1)d$ subshell. They occupy groups 3 to 12 of periods 4 to 7.

General electronic configuration

  • Usual pattern: $ (n-1)d^{1-10} ns^{2}$
  • Exceptions: Cr – $[Ar] 3d^{5} 4s^{1}$, Cu – $[Ar] 3d^{10} 4s^{1}$

Key points

  • Number of d‑orbitals = $5$, each holds $2$ electrons → maximum $10$ electrons in $(n-1)d$.
  • Typical oxidation states: $+2$, $+3$, and higher up to $+7$ (e.g., Mn).
  • Atomic radius is expressed in $\pm$ (picometre).

Physical & chemical trends

  • Gradual decrease in atomic radius across a period due to increasing nuclear charge.
  • First ionisation energy shows irregular pattern because removal of a $ns$ electron is easier than a $(n-1)d$ electron.
  • Many d‑block ions are coloured because of $d-d$ electronic transitions; the wavelength $\lambda$ is related to energy gap $\Delta E$ by $\Delta E = hc/\lambda$.
  • Magnetic behaviour depends on unpaired electrons; spin‑only magnetic moment $\mu_{so}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_{B}$ where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons.

SI units (relevant)

  • Atomic radius – $\pm$ (1 pm = $10^{-12}$ m).
  • Ionisation energy – $kJ\,mol^{-1}$.
  • Electronegativity – dimensionless (Pauling scale).
  • Magnetic moment – Bohr magneton ($\mu_{B}=9.274\times10^{-24}$ J T$^{-1}$).
PeriodGroupBlockGeneral config.
$4$$3-12$d$3d^{1-10} 4s^{2}$
$5$$3-12$d$4d^{1-10} 5s^{2}$
$6$$3-12$d$5d^{1-10} 6s^{2}$
$7$$3-12$d$6d^{1-10} 7s^{2}$

Solved example

Find the element having the configuration $[Ar] 3d^{5} 4s^{2}$ and write its oxidation states.

  1. Remove the noble‑gas core $[Ar]$ → remaining electrons $3d^{5} 4s^{2}$.
  2. Sum electrons: $5+2=7$, which corresponds to atomic number $Z=25$.
  3. $Z=25$ is Manganese (Mn).
  4. Typical oxidation states of Mn: $+2$, $+3$, $+4$, $+6$, $+7$.
long_notes.Anomalous properties and periodic trends:
Anomalous properties of d‑block elements

  • Unlike s‑block, d‑block shows irregular variation in atomic/ionic radii, ionisation enthalpy (IE), electron affinity (EA) and electronegativity (EN) across a period.
  • Cause: progressive filling of (n‑1)d orbitals, poor shielding (low screening constant $S$) and variable effective nuclear charge $Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - S$.

Periodic trends (general)

PropertyTrend across periodTrend down group
Atomic radiusGradual decrease; slight increase at start of d‑block due to added electron in (n‑1)dIncrease (addition of shells)
Ionic radiusDecrease for higher oxidation states; irregular for same chargeIncrease
Ionisation enthalpyOverall increase; dip at start of d‑block (e.g., Sc) because electron removed from (n‑1)dDecrease
Electron affinityIrregular; less exothermic for d‑block due to electron‑electron repulsion in d‑orbitalsBecomes less negative
ElectronegativityIncrease with $Z_{\text{eff}}$; anomalies at groups 3‑5Decrease

Key formula (Mulliken electronegativity)

\[\chi = \frac{I + A}{2}\]

where $I$ = first ionisation enthalpy (kJ·mol$^{-1}$), $A$ = electron affinity (kJ·mol$^{-1}$). SI unit of $\chi$ is dimensionless.

Solved example

Calculate Mulliken EN of Fe (first IE = $762\,\text{kJ·mol}^{-1}$, EA = $-15\,\text{kJ·mol}^{-1}$).

Solution:

\[\chi_{\text{Fe}} = \frac{762 + (-15)}{2} = \frac{747}{2} = 373.5\]

Thus $\chi_{\text{Fe}} \approx 3.74$ on the Pauling scale (after normalising). The relatively low EN reflects the anomalous shielding of (n‑1)d electrons.
long_notes.Variable oxidation states and colour of:
Variable oxidation states – Transition metals can exhibit several oxidation states because the energy difference between $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ orbitals is small. The most stable oxidation state is usually the one with a half‑filled or completely filled $d$ subshell.

  • General rule: maximum oxidation state = group number; minimum = 0 or +2 for most first‑row TM.
  • Example: Mn shows $+2$, $+4$, $+7$ etc.

Colour of transition‑metal compounds – Originates from d‑d electronic transitions within the split $d$‑orbitals in a ligand field.

TermExpression
Crystal‑field splitting energy$\Delta_0$
Wavelength of absorbed light$\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta_0}$
Energy of photon$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$

Where $h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,\text{J·s}$, $c = 3.00\times10^8\,\text{m·s}^{-1}$, $\Delta_0$ is usually expressed in $\text{cm}^{-1}$; conversion $\Delta_0(\text{J}) = hc\times\Delta_0(\text{cm}^{-1})$.

Solved example

For $\text{[Ti(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}$, $\Delta_0 = 2.0\times10^4\,\text{cm}^{-1}$. Find the wavelength of light absorbed and the colour observed.

  1. Convert $\Delta_0$ to joules: $\Delta_0 = hc\times2.0\times10^4 = (6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^8)(2.0\times10^4) = 3.98\times10^{-20}\,\text{J}$.
  2. $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta_0}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^8}{3.98\times10^{-20}}=5.0\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}=500\,\text{nm}$ (blue‑green region).
  3. The complex absorbs blue‑green light; the complementary colour observed is reddish‑orange.

Key points to remember for exams:

  • Variable oxidation states arise from comparable $ns$ and $(n-1)d$ ionisation energies.
  • Colour depends on $\Delta_0$, which increases with higher oxidation state, stronger field ligands (spectrochemical series), and smaller metal‑ligand distance.
  • Use $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta_0}$ to link absorption wavelength with colour.
long_notes.Important compounds and industrial appli:
Important compounds & industrial applications of selected d‑block elements

  • Copper (Cu): CuSO4·5H2O – used in electro‑plating and wiring.
  • Iron (Fe): Fe2O3 – raw material for steel (Fe‑C alloy).
  • Zinc (Zn): ZnO – white pigment, galvanisation.
  • Nickel (Ni): NiCl2 – stainless‑steel, batteries.
  • Chromium (Cr): Cr2O3 – leather tanning, pigments.
  • Manganese (Mn): KMnO4 – oxidising agent, dry cell.
  • Molybdenum (Mo): MoS2 – solid lubricant.
  • Titanium (Ti): TiCl4 – aerospace alloys.

Key formula (percentage yield):

$\displaystyle \text{Yield \%} = \frac{\text{mass obtained (g)}}{\text{theoretical mass (g)}}\times 100$

SI unit of mass = $\text{kg}$, concentration = $\text{mol\,L^{-1}}$, pressure = $\text{Pa}$.

ElementImportant compoundMajor use
CuCuSO4·5H2OElectro‑plating, wiring
FeFe2O3Steel making
ZnZnOGalvanisation, pigment
NiNiCl2Stainless steel, batteries

Solved example

Electrolyse $10\ \text{g}$ of CuSO4·5H2O. Molar mass of CuSO4·5H2O = $249.68\ \text{g\,mol^{-1}}$. Moles of CuSO4·5H2O = $\frac{10}{249.68}=0.0401\ \text{mol}$. Each mole yields $1\ \text{mol}$ Cu ($63.55\ \text{g\,mol^{-1}}$). Theoretical Cu mass = $0.0401\times63.55=2.55\ \text{g}$. If $2.30\ \text{g}$ Cu is collected, % yield = $\frac{2.30}{2.55}\times100=90.2\%$.
long_notes.Position and general electronic configur:
Definition: The f‑block comprises the two rows of elements in which the differentiating electron enters the $4f$ (lanthanides) or $5f$ (actinides) subshell.

Position in the periodic table

  • Located below the main body, separated by a gap.
  • Lanthanides: $Z=57$ to $71$ (Ce to Lu).
  • Actinides: $Z=89$ to $103$ (Ac to Lr).

General electronic configuration

  • Lanthanides: $[\text{Xe}]\,4f^{1-14}\,6s^{2}$ (the $5d$ subshell is empty or contains at most one electron).
  • Actinides: $[\text{Rn}]\,5f^{1-14}\,6d^{0-1}\,7s^{2}$.

For any f‑block element, the number of f‑electrons $n_f$ is $Z-\text{core}$ where the core corresponds to the noble‑gas configuration.

ElementAtomic No.General config.
La57$[\text{Xe}]\,5d^{1}\,6s^{2}$
Ce58$[\text{Xe}]\,4f^{1}\,5d^{1}\,6s^{2}$
Th90$[\text{Rn}]\,6d^{2}\,7s^{2}$
U92$[\text{Rn}]\,5f^{3}\,6d^{1}\,7s^{2}$

Key formula

  • Effective nuclear charge: $Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - S$ (where $S$ is shielding constant).
  • Atomic radius trend: $r_{\text{ionic}}$ (pm) decreases slightly across the series due to lanthanide contraction.

Solved example

Find the number of f‑electrons in $\text{Gd}$ ($Z=64$).

Core configuration up to $\text{Xe}$ accounts for 54 electrons. Remaining electrons = $64-54 = 10$. Hence $\text{Gd}$ has $4f^{7}\,5d^{1}\,6s^{2}$, i.e., $n_f = 7$.

SI units: atomic radius – picometre (pm), ionisation energy – kilojoule per mole (kJ·mol$^{-1}$).
long_notes.Common oxidation states, electronic conf:
Common oxidation states

  • Lanthanides (4f): +3 is dominant; early members (Ce, Pr, Nd) also show +4, while later members (Eu, Yb) exhibit +2 due to half‑filled $4f^{7}$ or fully filled $4f^{14}$ stability.
  • Actinides (5f): +3 is most frequent; early actinides (U, Np, Pu) display higher states (+4, +5, +6) because 5f orbitals are more radially extended and participate in bonding.

Electronic configurations

General pattern: $[Rn]5f^{1-14}6d^{0-1}7s^{2}$ for actinides and $[Xe]4f^{1-14}5d^{0-1}6s^{2}$ for lanthanides. The $d$‑electron appears only in Ce ($4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}$) and Th ($5f^{0}6d^{2}7s^{2}$) to accommodate extra stability.

ElementCommon oxidation states
Ce$+3$, $+4$
Eu$+2$, $+3$
Yb$+2$, $+3$
U$+3$, $+4$, $+5$, $+6$
Pu$+3$, $+4$, $+5$, $+6$, $+7$

Periodic trends in the f‑block

  • Atomic/ionic radius: decreases gradually across the series (lanthanide/actinide contraction) due to ineffective shielding by f‑electrons.
  • First ionisation energy: shows a slight increase across the series, reflecting stronger nuclear attraction.
  • Electronegativity: low and almost constant; values are taken from Pauling scale (e.g., Ce = 1.12, Yb = 1.10).

Solved example

Find the ground‑state configuration of Curium (Z = 96).

Start from the noble gas core $[Rn]$ (Z = 86). Add 10 electrons: the 5f subshell fills first, then 6d and 7s. Hence, $\text{Cm}:\;[Rn]5f^{7}6d^{0}7s^{2}$. The $5f^{7}$ half‑filled configuration gives extra stability, explaining the common +3 oxidation state of Cm.
long_notes.Separation of rare‑earth elements and im:
Definition: Rare‑earth elements (REEs) are the 15 lanthanides ($\text{La}$ to $\text{Lu}$) together with scandium and yttrium. Separation of REEs is required because they occur together in minerals such as bastnäsite and monazite.

  • Fractional crystallisation: Based on slight differences in $K_{sp}= [RE^{3+}]^2[CO_3^{2-}]^3$ of their double‑salts (e.g., $RE_2(CO_3)_3\cdot6H_2O$). The solubility product $K_{sp}$ has unit $mol^5\cdotL^{-5}$.
  • Ion‑exchange method: Distribution coefficient $D = \frac{[RE]_{resin}}{[RE]_{solution}}$ (unitless). Higher $D$ for heavier lanthanides.
  • Solvent extraction: Extraction constant $K_{ex}= \frac{[RE\!\-\!extractant]_{org}}{[RE^{3+}]_{aq}}$ (unit $L\cdotmol^{-1}$).

Important compounds:

LanthanideOxideHalide (X = Cl, Br)
$\text{La}$$\text{La}_2\text{O}_3$$\text{LaX}_3$
$\text{Gd}$$\text{Gd}_2\text{O}_3$$\text{GdX}_3$
$\text{Lu}$$\text{Lu}_2\text{O}_3$$\text{LuX}_3$

Solved example (fractional crystallisation):

Given $K_{sp}$ of $Nd_2(CO_3)_3\cdot6H_2O = 1.2\times10^{-22}$ and $Sm_2(CO_3)_3\cdot6H_2O = 2.5\times10^{-22}$ at $25^\circ C$. If a solution contains $0.01\;mol\;L^{-1}$ of each REE, calculate the concentration of $Nd^{3+}$ remaining after the first crystallisation step.

Solution:

For $Nd^{3+}$, $K_{sp}= [Nd^{3+}]^2[CO_3^{2-}]^3$. Assuming $[CO_3^{2-}] \approx 0.01\;mol\;L^{-1}$, we get $[Nd^{3+}] = \sqrt{\frac{K_{sp}}{[CO_3^{2-}]^3}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.2\times10^{-22}}{(0.01)^3}} = 1.1\times10^{-9}\;mol\;L^{-1}$. Thus $>99.99\%$ of $Nd^{3+}$ is removed, illustrating the efficiency of fractional crystallisation.

All constants are expressed in SI units (mol, L, $^\circ C$).
long_notes.Uses and significance of d‑ and f‑block:
Definition: d‑block elements are the transition elements having partially filled $(n-1)d$ subshell; f‑block elements are the inner‑transition series with partially filled $(n-2)f$ subshell.

Key industrial uses:

  • Catalysis – $Pt$, $Pd$, $Ni$, $V_2O_5$ in hydrogenation, reforming and oxidation reactions.
  • Magnetic materials – $Fe$, $Co$, $Ni$ alloys for transformers, $Nd_2Fe_{14}B$ permanent magnets.
  • Corrosion‑resistant alloys – $Cr$, $Mo$ in stainless steel and super‑alloys.
  • Electronic & optical devices – $Cu$, $Ag$ conductors; $Ga$, $In$ in semiconductors; $Y$, $Lu$ in phosphors.
  • Specialty chemicals – $Zr$, $Hf$ in nuclear reactors; $U$, $Pu$ (actinides) as nuclear fuel.

Important quantitative relations:

ParameterExpressionSI unit
Catalytic turnover frequency (TOF)$\\text{TOF}=\\frac{\\text{moles of product}}{\\text{moles of active sites}\\times\\text{time}}$$h^{-1}$
Magnetic susceptibility ($\\chi$)$\\chi=\\frac{M}{H}$$m^{3}\\,mol^{-1}$

Solved example:

Given a $Pt$ catalyst with $\\text{TOF}=5\\times10^{4}\\,h^{-1}$, how much catalyst (in moles of surface Pt atoms) is required to produce $10\\,mol$ of ethylene in $2\\,h$?

Solution: $\\text{required moles of active sites}=\\frac{\\text{product moles}}{\\text{TOF}\\times t}=\\frac{10}{5\\times10^{4}\\times2}=1.0\\times10^{-4}\\,mol$. Thus $1.0\\times10^{-4}\\,mol$ of Pt (≈ $1.96\\,g$) is sufficient.

These quantitative tools help design efficient processes and select appropriate d‑ or f‑block elements for industrial applications.

short_notes.title: Important Formulas
short_notes.html:
PropertyFormula
Effective nuclear charge$Z_{eff}=Z-S$
Ionic radius trend (d‑block)$r_{\text{M}^{n+}}\approx r_{\text{M}^{(n-1)+}}-\Delta r$ (where $\Delta r\approx0.03\,\text{Å}$ per increase in oxidation state)
Crystal‑field splitting energy (octahedral)$\Delta_{o}=\frac{h c \Delta \lambda}{\lambda^{2}}$
Spin‑only magnetic moment$\mu_{so}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}$ ( $n$ = number of unpaired electrons )
Lanthanide contraction (Δr)$\Delta r= r_{\text{La}^{3+}}-r_{\text{Lu}^{3+}}\approx0.20\,\text{Å}$
Atomic radius (metallic) – d‑block$r_{\text{metal}}\approx r_{\text{atom}}-\frac{\Delta E_{\text{ion}}}{k}$ (qualitative trend)

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Lanthanide contraction: Gradual decrease in ionic/atomic radii from La to Lu caused by poor shielding of 4$f$ electrons.
  • Actinide contraction: Similar decrease from Ac to Lr, more pronounced due to 5$f$ electron involvement.
  • Crystal Field Theory (CFT): Interaction of metal $d$ orbitals with surrounding ligands splits degenerate $d$ levels into $e_g$ and $t_{2g}$ sets.
  • Ligand Field Theory (LFT): Extension of CFT incorporating covalent aspects via molecular orbital approach.
  • Aufbau Principle: Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing $n+\ell$; for $d$‑ and $f$‑block, $(n-1)d$ fills before $ns$ and $np$, and $4f$ before $5d$.
  • Hund’s Rule: For a given subshell, maximize total spin ($S$) before pairing electrons.
  • Oxidation state trends: +2 is most stable for group 2; +3 dominates early $d$‑block, higher oxidation states (+4,+5,+6,+7) increase across the period due to increasing $\Delta_{o}$.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Summary: The $d$‑block shows a gradual decrease in atomic/ionic radii, increase in $\Delta_{o}$ and higher oxidation states from left to right. The $f$‑block (lanthanides and actinides) is characterized by the lanthanide/actinide contraction, similar chemical properties within each series, and predominantly +3 oxidation state (except a few +2 and +4 for actinides). Crystal‑field splitting governs colour, magnetism and stability of complexes.

Common Mistakes:

  • Confusing the order of orbital filling: remember $4f$ fills before $5d$, not after.
  • Assuming all $f$‑block elements exhibit +3 state; remember Ce, Eu, Yb (lanthanides) and U, Np (actinides) show +4 or +2.
  • Neglecting lanthanide contraction when comparing radii of $d$‑block elements across periods.
  • Using $\Delta_{o}$ values for tetrahedral complexes without applying the factor $\frac{4}{9}$ (i.e., $\Delta_{t}=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_{o}$).

numericals.question: Calculate the spin‑only magnetic moment of the octahedral complex [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (high‑spin).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Fe²⁺ is d⁶. In a high‑spin octahedral field it has 4 unpaired electrons (n = 4).

Formula: $\mu_{so}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Substitute n = 4: $\mu_{so}=\sqrt{4(4+2)}$
  2. Evaluate the product: $4(4+2)=24$
  3. Take the square root: $\sqrt{24}=4.90$ (to two decimal places)

Final Answer: $\mu_{so}=4.90\ \text{BM}$

numericals.question: Find the crystal‑field stabilization energy (CFSE) of the high‑spin octahedral complex [CoF₆]³⁻. Take $\Delta_{o}=10\,000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ and $1\ \text{cm}^{-1}=0.01196\ \text{kJ\,mol}^{-1}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Co³⁺ is d⁶. High‑spin octahedral configuration: $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$.

Formula: $\text{CFSE}=(-0.4\times n_{t_{2g}}+0.6\times n_{e_{g}})\Delta_{o}$

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Insert $n_{t_{2g}}=4$, $n_{e_{g}}=2$: $\text{CFSE}=(-0.4\times4+0.6\times2)\Delta_{o}$
  2. Compute the coefficient: $(-1.6+1.2)=-0.4$
  3. Multiply by $\Delta_{o}$: $\text{CFSE}= -0.4\times10\,000\ \text{cm}^{-1}= -4\,000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$
  4. Convert to kJ·mol⁻¹: $-4\,000\times0.01196= -47.84\ \text{kJ\,mol}^{-1}$ (≈ -48 kJ·mol⁻¹)

Final Answer: $\text{CFSE}= -4\,000\ \text{cm}^{-1}= -48\ \text{kJ\,mol}^{-1}$

numericals.question: Using the lanthanide‑contraction factor of $0.02\,\text{Å}$ per element, estimate the ionic radius of Gd³⁺ given that $r_{\text{La}^{3+}}=1.032\,\text{Å}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $r_{\text{La}^{3+}}=1.032\,\text{Å}$, contraction per atomic number = $0.02\,\text{Å}$. Gd (Z=64) is 7 elements after La (Z=57).

Formula: $r_{\text{Gd}^{3+}}=r_{\text{La}^{3+}}-\Delta n$, where $\Delta n = (\text{number of steps})\times(\text{contraction per step})$

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Number of steps $=64-57=7$
  2. $\Delta n =7\times0.02\,\text{Å}=0.14\,\text{Å}$
  3. $r_{\text{Gd}^{3+}}=1.032\,\text{Å}-0.14\,\text{Å}=0.892\,\text{Å}$

Final Answer: $r_{\text{Gd}^{3+}}\approx0.89\,\text{Å}$

pyq.question: Write the electronic configuration of the first element of the f‑block and state its block position in the periodic table.
pyq.answer_html:
First f‑block element is Lanthanum (La).
Electronic configuration: $[Xe]\\,5d^{1}6s^{2}$.
It belongs to the $\text{6th period}$ and $\text{f‑block}$ (lanthanide series).

pyq.question: State the oxidation state most commonly exhibited by the d‑block element Iron in its compounds.
pyq.answer_html: Iron commonly shows the oxidation state $\text{+3}$ in its compounds (e.g., Fe$_{2}$O$_{3}$). $\text{+2}$ is also frequent, but $+3$ is the most stable.

pyq.question: Explain why the first ionisation energy of Scandium (Sc) is higher than that of Calcium (Ca).
pyq.answer_html: Sc ($Z=21$) has electronic configuration $[Ar]\\,3d^{1}4s^{2}$, whereas Ca ($Z=20$) is $[Ar]\\,4s^{2}$. Removal of an electron from Sc involves breaking a $3d$ electron which is less shielded and experiences a higher effective nuclear charge than the $4s$ electron of Ca. Hence $I_{1}$ of Sc $> I_{1}$ of Ca.

pyq.question: Write the general electronic configuration for the lanthanide series and mention the reason for the gradual increase in atomic radii across the series.
pyq.answer_html: General configuration: $[Xe]\\,4f^{n}5d^{0-1}6s^{2}$ where $n=0-14$.\nAcross the series, the $4f$ electrons poorly shield the increasing nuclear charge, leading to a higher effective nuclear charge on outer electrons and a slight contraction (lanthanide contraction). This causes a gradual decrease, not increase, in atomic radii; the apparent increase is due to the addition of electrons in the $4f$ subshell which are poorly shielding.

pyq.question: Discuss the factors responsible for the observed anomalous electron configurations of Chromium (Cr) and Copper (Cu). Include the resulting configurations in your answer.
pyq.answer_html:
Both Cr and Cu exhibit configurations that deviate from the expected $[Ar]\\,3d^{n}4s^{2}$ due to extra stability associated with half‑filled ($d^{5}$) or fully filled ($d^{10}$) $d$ subshells.

\textbf{Chromium (Cr, $Z=24$)}:
Expected: $[Ar]\\,3d^{4}4s^{2}$
Observed: $[Ar]\\,3d^{5}4s^{1}$
Reason: A half‑filled $3d$ subshell ($d^{5}$) provides extra exchange energy and symmetry, lowering the energy.

\textbf{Copper (Cu, $Z=29$)}:
Expected: $[Ar]\\,3d^{9}4s^{2}$
Observed: $[Ar]\\,3d^{10}4s^{1}$
Reason: A completely filled $3d$ subshell ($d^{10}$) is more stable due to maximized exchange energy and reduced electron‑electron repulsion.

Thus, the gain in exchange stability outweighs the energy cost of promoting an electron from $4s$ to $3d$.

pyq.question: Compare the chemical properties of the first transition series (Sc to Zn) with those of the second transition series (Y to Cd). Highlight the role of the $d$‑orbital contraction and its effect on oxidation states and complex formation.
pyq.answer_html:
Both series involve filling of $3d$ (first series) and $4d$ (second series) orbitals. extbf{d‑orbital contraction:}
As we move from $3d$ to $4d$, the $d$ orbitals are more diffused and experience better shielding, resulting in a smaller increase in effective nuclear charge. Consequently, the $4d$ elements have slightly larger atomic/ionic radii and lower ionisation energies compared to their $3d$ counterparts.

extbf{Oxidation states:}
First series: Common oxidation states range from $+2$ to $+4$ (e.g., Ti $+3$, V $+5$, Cr $+6$). Second series: Similar oxidation states but the higher oxidation states are less stable (e.g., Mo $+6$ is stable, but Ru $+6$ is less common). The reduced contraction makes higher oxidation states less favourable in the $4d$ series.

extbf{Complex formation:}
First series ions are smaller, leading to higher charge density and stronger ligand field stabilization (e.g., [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{3-}$).
Second series ions are larger, giving weaker ligand field effects; however, they often form more covalent bonds due to better orbital overlap (e.g., Mo(CO)$_6$).

Overall, $d$‑orbital contraction results in the first transition series exhibiting higher oxidation states, stronger complex stability, and greater variation in colour compared to the second series.

mcq.q: Across the first‑row transition series, the ionic radius of the $M^{2+}$ ions generally ____.
mcq.explain: With increasing nuclear charge across the series, the same number of d‑electrons experience a stronger attraction, causing the $M^{2+}$ ionic radius to decrease.

mcq.q: The first element of the d‑block series is ____.
mcq.explain: Scandium ($\text{Sc}$) has the configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{1}4s^{2}$, marking the start of the d‑block.

mcq.q: Lanthanide contraction results in ____.
options: increase in atomic radii of 5d elements
decrease in atomic radii of 5d elements
increase in ionization energy of 5d elements
mcq.explain: Poor shielding by the $4f$ electrons causes a gradual reduction in atomic size of the subsequent $5d$ elements, known as lanthanide contraction.

mcq.q: Maximum oxidation state exhibited by manganese in its compounds is ____.
mcq.explain: Manganese reaches +7 in permanganate ($\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$), the highest oxidation state for this element.

mcq.q: The complex $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ shows a ____ colour in solution.
mcq.explain: Tetramminecopper(II) ion imparts a characteristic deep blue colour due to d‑d transitions.

mcq.q: Assertion: Lanthanide contraction leads to the similarity in ionic radii of $\text{Lu}^{3+}$ and $\text{Y}^{3+}$. Reason: Both ions have the same effective nuclear charge.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Both statements are true, but the similarity arises from the overall contraction of the lanthanide series, not because the two ions have identical effective nuclear charge.

mcq.q: Which of the following transition metals commonly exhibits a stable +4 oxidation state?
mcq.explain: Zirconium frequently forms compounds like $\text{ZrO}_{2}$ where it is in the +4 oxidation state.

mcq.q: All of the following are typical properties of f‑block elements except ____.
mcq.explain: Lanthanides generally have relatively low melting points compared to transition metals; high melting points are not a universal f‑block characteristic.

mcq.q: The ground‑state electron configuration of $\text{Gd}$ is ____.
mcq.explain: Gadolinium has a half‑filled $4f$ subshell plus one electron in $5d$, giving $[\text{Xe}]\,4f^{7}5d^{1}6s^{2}$.
