long_notes.Nomenclature and classification of haloa:
Definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are organic compounds containing a carbon‑halogen bond of the type $R\!\! -\!X$ where $R$ is an alkyl group and $X$ = $F,\,Cl,\,Br,\,I$. Haloarenes (aryl halides) have the halogen directly attached to an aromatic ring ($Ar\!\! -\!X$).

Classification:

  • Based on the hybridisation of the carbon bearing $X$: $sp^3$ (saturated), $sp^2$ (allylic/vinylic), $sp$ (acetylenic).
  • According to the number of halogen atoms: monohalo, dihalo, polyhalo.
  • According to the nature of $X$: primary, secondary, tertiary (for haloalkanes).

Key Nomenclature Rules (IUPAC):

  1. Identify the longest carbon chain containing the carbon attached to $X$; this becomes the parent hydrocarbon.
  2. Number the chain to give the carbon bearing $X$ the lowest possible locant.
  3. Replace the terminal “‑e” of the parent name with “‑halo” (e.g., $\text{propane} \rightarrow \text{chloropropane}$).
  4. If more than one halogen is present, list them alphabetically with their locants (e.g., $1\!\! -\!bromo\!\! -\!2\!\! -\!chloro\!\! -\!propane$).
  5. For haloarenes, the aromatic ring is the parent; the halogen is indicated as a prefix (e.g., $\text{bromobenzene}$).

Physical Data (Typical):

TypeGeneral FormulaExampleBoiling Point ($^\circ$C)
Alkyl halide$R\!\! -\!X$CH$_3$CH$_2$Cl12.3
Aryl halide$Ar\!\! -\!X$C$_6$H$_5$Br156

Solved Example:

Find the IUPAC name of $\text{CH}_3\!\! -\!\text{CH}_2\!\! -\!\text{CH}_2\!\! -\!\text{Cl}$.

  1. Longest chain = 3 carbon atoms → parent = $\text{propane}$.
  2. Number from the end nearest the halogen → chlorine on carbon‑1.
  3. Replace “‑e” with “‑chloro” and add locant: $1\!\! -\!\text{chloropropane}$.
long_notes.Methods of preparation of haloalkanes:
Definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are organic compounds in which one hydrogen atom of an alkane is replaced by a halogen ($\\mathrm{X = F, Cl, Br, I}$).

Methods of preparation

MethodReagents / Conditions
Addition to alkenesAlkene + $\\mathrm{HX}$ (room temp) → haloalkane; $\\mathrm{X_2}$ (UV) → vicinal dihalide; $\\mathrm{X_2/H_2O}$ → halohydrin then $\\mathrm{NaOH}$ → haloalkane
From alcohols$\\mathrm{R-OH + HX}$ (conc., $\\ge 60^{\circ}C$) or $\\mathrm{SOCl_2}$, $\\mathrm{PCl_5}$, $\\mathrm{PCl_3}$ (0–25°C) → $\\mathrm{R-X}$ + $\\mathrm{HCl}$
From alkyl sulfonates$\\mathrm{R-OSO_2R'} + NaX$ (dry $\\mathrm{Acetone}$, reflux) → $\\mathrm{R-X}$ + $\\mathrm{NaOSO_2R'}$ (Finkelstein reaction)
From carboxylic acids$\\mathrm{R-COOH}$ + $\\mathrm{PBr_3}$ → $\\mathrm{R-Br}$ + $\\mathrm{CO_2}$ (decarboxylative bromination)

Key points

  • Primary alkyl halides are best obtained via $\\mathrm{S_N2}$ pathways (e.g., $\\mathrm{SOCl_2}$).
  • Secondary/tertiary halides often arise from $\\mathrm{S_N1}$ conditions (e.g., $\\mathrm{PCl_5}$).
  • Reaction rate for $\\mathrm{S_N2}$: $\\mathrm{Rate = k[RX][Y^-]}$ (second order).
  • Temperature is expressed in $\\mathrm{^{\circ}C}$; pressure in $\\mathrm{atm}$.

Solved example

Prepare $\\mathrm{1\text{-}chloropropane}$ from $\\mathrm{1\text{-}propanol}$ using thionyl chloride.

  1. Write the reaction:
    $\\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH + SOCl_2 \xrightarrow{0-25^{\circ}C} CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl + SO_2 \uparrow + HCl \uparrow}$
  2. Mechanism: $\\mathrm{S_N2}$ – $\\mathrm{Cl^-}$ attacks the carbon bearing the –OH while $\\mathrm{SOCl_2}$ converts –OH to a good leaving group ($\\mathrm{OSOCl}$).
  3. Conditions: Add $\\mathrm{SOCl_2}$ dropwise to chilled $\\mathrm{1\text{-}propanol}$, stir 30 min, then distill the product (bp $\\approx 46^{\circ}C$).
  4. Yield calculation (if 10 g $\\mathrm{SOCl_2}$ used, excess): theoretical $m_{product}=\frac{10\,g}{119.0\,g\,mol^{-1}}\times 78.5\,g\,mol^{-1}=6.6\,g$; actual 5.5 g → % yield $=\frac{5.5}{6.6}\times100=83\%$.
long_notes.Physical properties of haloalkanes and h:
Definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are organic compounds containing a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br, I) covalently bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Haloarenes (aryl halides) have the halogen attached to an aromatic carbon.

Physical properties and trends:

  • Boiling point ($T_b$) and melting point ($T_m$) increase with molecular weight and with the size of the halogen (F<Cl<Br<I).
  • Polarity of C–X bond ($\mu$) follows $\\text{C–F}>\\text{C–Cl}>\\text{C–Br}>\\text{C–I}$, influencing dipole moment (unit: Debye, D) and intermolecular forces.
  • Density ($\rho$) of haloalkanes is higher than corresponding alkanes; typical units $kg\\,m^{-3}$.
  • Solubility in water decreases from fluorides to iodides; hydrogen bonding possible only for C–F.
  • Refractive index ($n_D$) increases with atomic mass; dimensionless.

Representative boiling points (°C):

Compound$T_b$ (°C)
Methyl fluoride$-78$
Methyl chloride$-24$
Methyl bromide$3.6$
Methyl iodide$42$

Key colligative formula (boiling‑point elevation): $$\\Delta T_b = i\\,K_b\\,m$$ where $i$ = van’t Hoff factor, $K_b$ = ebullioscopic constant (°C·kg·mol$^{-1}$), $m$ = molality (mol·kg$^{-1}$).

Solved example: A $1\\,\\text{m}$ aqueous solution of chloroethane ($\\text{C}_2\\text{H}_5\\text{Cl}$) dissociates into $\\text{C}_2\\text{H}_5^+$ and $\\text{Cl}^-$, so $i=2$. For water $K_b=0.512\\,^{\\circ}\\text{C\\,kg\\,mol}^{-1}$. Calculate $\\Delta T_b$.

Solution: $$\\Delta T_b = i K_b m = 2 \times 0.512 \times 1 = 1.024\\,^{\\circ}\\text{C}$$. Hence the solution boils at $100 + 1.024 = 101.024\\,^{\\circ}\\text{C}$.
long_notes.Nucleophilic substitution reactions (SN1:
Definitions

  • SN1 (Unimolecular) substitution: A two‑step mechanism where the rate‑determining step is the formation of a carbocation; overall rate depends only on the substrate concentration.
  • SN2 (Bimolecular) substitution: A single concerted step where the nucleophile attacks the substrate from the backside, leading to inversion of configuration; rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile.

Rate Laws & Kinetic Order

  • SN1: $\text{Rate}=k[RX]$  (first order, $\text{s}^{-1}$).
  • SN2: $\text{Rate}=k[RX][Nu^-]$  (second order, $\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$).

Key Equations

  • Arrhenius: $k=A e^{-E_a/(RT)}$ where $A$ is the pre‑exponential factor, $E_a$ (kJ·mol$^{-1}$) is activation energy, $R=8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $T$ (K).
  • Half‑life for SN1 (first order): $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k}$.

Mechanistic Features

FeatureSN1SN2
Rate‑determining stepCarbocation formationBack‑side attack
OrderFirstSecond
Solvent effectPolar protic stabilises carbocationPolar aprotic favours nucleophile
StereochemistryRacemisation (planar carbocation)Inversion (Walden inversion)

Factors Influencing Rate

  • Substrate: tertiary > secondary > primary for SN1; primary > secondary > tertiary for SN2 (steric hindrance).
  • Nucleophile strength: strong bases (e.g., $\text{OH}^-$, $\text{CN}^-$) accelerate SN2.
  • Leaving group ability: $\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$.

Solved Example (SN2)

Given $k=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ at 298 K for the reaction $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}+\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{OH}+\text{Br}^-$. If $[\text{CH}_3\text{Br}]=0.010\,\text{M}$ and $[\text{OH}^-]=0.020\,\text{M}$, calculate the rate.

\[\text{Rate}=k[\text{CH}_3\text{Br}][\text{OH}^-]=2.5\times10^{-3}\times0.010\times0.020=5.0\times10^{-7}\,\text{M s}^{-1}\]

The reaction proceeds at $5.0\times10^{-7}\,\text{M s}^{-1}$ under the stated conditions.
long_notes.Elimination reactions (E1 and E2):
Elimination Reactions (E1 & E2)

Elimination removes a leaving group (LG) and a β-hydrogen from adjacent carbon atoms, forming a C=C double bond.

E1 (Unimolecular Elimination)

  • Two-step mechanism: (i) ionisation – $R\text{–}LG \rightarrow R^{+} + LG^{-}$, (ii) deprotonation – $R^{+} + B^{-} \rightarrow Alkene + BH$.
  • Rate law: $rate = k[substrate]$ (first order).
  • Rate constant unit: $s^{-1}$.
  • Favoured by weak bases, polar protic solvents, and tertiary substrates.

E2 (Bimolecular Elimination)

  • Concerted one-step: $R\text{–}CH_{2}\text{–}CH_{2}\text{–}LG + B^{-} \rightarrow Alkene + LG^{-} + BH$.
  • Rate law: $rate = k[substrate][base]$ (second order).
  • Rate constant unit: $M^{-1}s^{-1}$.
  • Requires a strong base, polar aprotic solvent, and anti-periplanar geometry of H and LG.

Key Rules

  • Zaitsev’s rule: the more substituted alkene is preferred unless a bulky base is used.
  • Anti-periplanar arrangement is mandatory for E2; E1 proceeds via planar carbocation.
ReactionRate LawOrder
E1$rate = k[substrate]$1st
E2$rate = k[substrate][base]$2nd

Solved Example

Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with aqueous NaOH (25 °C).

  1. Substrate is tertiary → favours E2 with strong base NaOH.
  2. Anti-periplanar H is on a methyl group; removal gives isobutene:
  3. Overall equation: $$(CH_{3})_{3}C\text{–}Br + NaOH \rightarrow (CH_{3})_{2}C=CH_{2} + NaBr + H_{2}O$$

Rate expression: $rate = k[(CH_{3})_{3}C\text{–}Br][OH^{-}]$.
long_notes.Reactions of haloarenes (electrophilic a:
Reactions of Haloarenes

Haloarenes undergo two characteristic aromatic substitutions:

  • Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS): substitution of a hydrogen atom by an electrophile. The aromatic ring retains its conjugated system.
  • Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution (SNAr): replacement of a halogen by a nucleophile via addition‑elimination (Meisenheimer complex) when the ring is activated by strong –NO₂, –CN, –COOR groups.

Key formulas

  • Arrhenius rate expression: $k = A\,e^{-E_a/(R\,T)}$ ( $k$ in $s^{-1}$ or $M^{-1}s^{-1}$, $E_a$ in $kJ\,mol^{-1}$, $R = 8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}$ ).
  • Hammett equation for EAS: $\log\frac{k_X}{k_H}= \rho\,\sigma$ where $k_X$ is rate constant for substituted haloarene, $\sigma$ is substituent constant, $\rho$ is reaction constant.
  • SNAr rate (second order): $k = k_1[ArX][Nu^-]$ (units $M^{-1}s^{-1}$).
Substituent$\sigma$ (para)Effect on EAS
–NO₂$+0.78$deactivates
–CH₃$-0.17$activates

Typical mechanism (SNAr)

  1. Attack of $Nu^-$ on $C$ bearing $X$, forming a Meisenheimer σ‑complex.
  2. Departure of $X^-$ restoring aromaticity.

Solved Example

Calculate the relative rate of nitration of chlorobenzene compared to benzene using $\rho = -0.5$ and $\sigma_{p\text{-Cl}} = +0.23$.

Using Hammett: $\log\frac{k_{Cl}}{k_H}= \rho\,\sigma = (-0.5)(+0.23)= -0.115$ → $\frac{k_{Cl}}{k_H}=10^{-0.115}=0.77$. Thus chlorobenzene nitrates ~23 % slower than benzene.
long_notes.Mechanistic aspects and factors affectin:
Definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) and haloarenes are organic compounds containing a carbon‑halogen bond. Their reaction rates depend on the mechanism (SN1, SN2, E1, E2) and several kinetic factors.

Rate Laws & Key Equations

MechanismRate LawRate Constant Expression
SN1$rate = k[RX]$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$
SN2$rate = k[RX][Nu^-]$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$
E1$rate = k[RX]$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$
E2$rate = k[RX][Base]$$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$

Factors affecting rate

  • Substrate structure: Primary > secondary > tertiary for SN2; opposite for SN1/E1.
  • Nucleophile/Base strength: Strong, less‑sterically hindered nucleophiles accelerate SN2; strong bases favor E2.
  • Solvent: Polar protic stabilises ions → faster SN1/E1; polar aprotic stabilises nucleophile → faster SN2/E2.
  • Leaving group ability: $I^- > Br^- > Cl^- > F^-$ (higher ability → lower $E_a$).
  • Temperature: $rate \propto e^{-E_a/RT}$; higher $T$ increases both $k$ and the proportion of elimination.

Solved Example

For the SN2 reaction $CH_3CH_2CH_2Br + I^- \rightarrow CH_3CH_2CH_2I + Br^-$ in acetone, $k = 2.5 \\times 10^3\;M^{-1}s^{-1}$ at $298\;K$. If $[RX]=0.010\;M$ and $[I^-]=0.020\;M$, calculate the initial rate.

Solution: $rate = k[RX][I^-] = (2.5 \\times 10^3)(0.010)(0.020) = 5.0 \\times 10^2\;M\,s^{-1}$.

Thus, a strong, unhindered nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent gives a rapid SN2 substitution.
long_notes.Industrial applications and environmenta:
Industrial Applications

  • Production of Vinyl chloride (precursor to PVC): $C_2H_4 + Cl_2 \rightarrow C_2H_3Cl + HCl$.
  • Synthesis of Chloroform and Carbon tetrachloride by chlorination of methane: $CH_4 + 3Cl_2 \rightarrow CCl_4 + 3HCl$.
  • Manufacture of Pharmaceutical intermediates such as chlorobenzene \rightarrow phenylalanine derivatives.
  • Preparation of Solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) via controlled chlorination of methanol.

Key Formula

ProcessBalanced Equation
Vinyl chloride$C_2H_4 + Cl_2 \rightarrow C_2H_3Cl + HCl$
Chloroform$CHCl_3 + H_2O \rightarrow CO_2 + 3HCl$ (hydrolysis)

Environmental Impact

  • Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) – bioaccumulate in food chain.
  • Release of HCl leads to acid rain; SI unit for concentration $[HCl]$ in $mol\,L^{-1}$.
  • Some haloarenes act as ozone‑depleting substances; ozone depletion potential (ODP) expressed relative to $CCl_4$.

Solved Example

Calculate mass of vinyl chloride produced when $5.0\ \text{mol}$ of ethylene reacts completely with excess $Cl_2$.

Given$n_{C_2H_4}=5.0\ \text{mol}$
Reaction stoichiometry$1\ mol\ C_2H_4 \rightarrow 1\ mol\ C_2H_3Cl$
Molar mass $M_{C_2H_3Cl}=62.5\ \text{g\ mol}^{-1}$
Mass $= n \times M$$m = 5.0 \times 62.5 = 312.5\ \text{g}$

Thus $312.5\ \text{g}$ of vinyl chloride is obtained.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Haloalkane (Alkyl halide): Halogen attached to a saturated carbon.
  • Haloarene (Aryl halide): Halogen attached directly to an aromatic ring.
  • SN1 Reaction: Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution; rate $Rate = k[RX]$ (first order). Involves carbocation intermediate.
  • SN2 Reaction: Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution; rate $Rate = k[RX][Nu]$ (second order). Concerted backside attack.
  • Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS): Substitution of a hydrogen on benzene by a halogen (or other electrophile) via sigma complex.
  • Reactivity Order of Halogens (in haloalkanes): $I > Br > Cl > F$ (due to bond strength and leaving ability).
  • Reactivity Order of Substituted Haloalkanes: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$ for SN1; $1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$ for SN2.
  • Reactivity Order of Haloarenes (EAS): $NO_2 > Cl > Br > I$ (strong -I and -R effects of -NO_2 deactivate the ring).
  • Rate Law for Halogenation of Alkanes: $Rate = k[RH][Cl_2]$ (radical chain mechanism).

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Quick Summary

  • Identify the type of substrate: primary, secondary, tertiary or aromatic.
  • SN1 favours tertiary, polar protic solvents; SN2 favours primary, polar aprotic solvents.
  • In haloarenes, halogen is a deactivating, ortho‑/para‑directing group; substitution occurs via EAS, not SN1/SN2.
  • Remember the order of leaving group ability: $I^- > Br^- > Cl^- > F^-$.
  • For quantitative problems, use $Rate = k[RX]$ (SN1) or $Rate = k[RX][Nu]$ (SN2) and Arrhenius equation for temperature dependence.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating haloarenes like haloalkanes – they undergo EAS, not nucleophilic substitution.
  • Confusing the reactivity order of halogens in SN1/SN2 (it is based on leaving ability, not bond strength alone).
  • Ignoring solvent effect – polar protic solvents stabilize carbocations (SN1) while polar aprotic solvents accelerate SN2.
  • Using $Rate = k[RX][Nu]$ for tertiary substrates – steric hindrance makes SN2 impossible.
  • Overlooking the -I and -R effects of substituents on aromatic reactivity.

numericals.question: Calculate the rate of SN2 reaction for 1‑bromobutane with NaOH at 25 °C if the rate constant $k_{\text{SN2}}=1.2\times10^{3}\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ and concentrations are $[\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}]=0.025\,\text{M}$, $[\text{NaOH}]=0.10\,\text{M}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $k_{\text{SN2}}=1.2\times10^{3}\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$, $[\text{RX}]=0.025\,\text{M}$, $[\text{Nu}^{-}]=0.10\,\text{M}$.

Formula (SN2): $\text{Rate}=k_{\text{SN2}}[\text{RX}][\text{Nu}^{-}]$.

Step‑by‑Step:

  1. Substitute the values: $\text{Rate}=1.2\times10^{3}\times0.025\times0.10$.
  2. Calculate: $1.2\times10^{3}\times0.025=30$; $30\times0.10=3$.

Final Answer: $\text{Rate}=3\,\text{M}\,\text{s}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: For the SN1 hydrolysis of tert‑butyl chloride, the rate constant $k_{\text{SN1}}=2.5\times10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. If the initial concentration of $\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}=0.040\,\text{M}$, calculate the half‑life $t_{1/2}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $k_{\text{SN1}}=2.5\times10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ (first order).

Formula (first order): $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$.

Step‑by‑Step:

  1. $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{2.5\times10^{-5}}$.
  2. Divide: $0.693\div2.5\times10^{-5}=2.77\times10^{4}\,\text{s}$.

Final Answer: $t_{1/2}=2.77\times10^{4}\,\text{s}\;(\approx7.7\,\text{h})$.

numericals.question: A 5.00 g sample of 1‑chloropropane is hydrolysed with excess NaOH. Calculate the volume of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (at STP) formed. (Molar masses: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}=78.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}=18.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $m(\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{Cl})=5.00\\,\\text{g}$, $M_{\\text{RX}}=78.5\\,\\text{g mol}^{-1}$, $M_{\\text{H}_2\\text{O}}=18.0\\,\\text{g mol}^{-1}$, reaction: $\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{Cl}+\\text{NaOH}\\rightarrow\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{OH}+\\text{NaCl}$ (1:1).

Formula: $n=\\frac{m}{M}$, $V_{\\text{STP}}=n\\times22.4\\,\\text{L}$.

Step‑by‑Step:

  1. $n_{\\text{RX}}=\\frac{5.00}{78.5}=0.0637\\,\\text{mol}$.
  2. From stoichiometry, $n_{\\text{H}_2\\text{O}}=0.0637\\,\\text{mol}$.
  3. $V=0.0637\\times22.4=1.43\\,\\text{L}$.

Final Answer: $1.43\\,\\text{L}$ of water (as vapour) at STP.

numericals.question: In the preparation of bromobenzene, 0.500 mol of bromine reacts with excess benzene. The isolated product mass is 84.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (Molar mass of bromobenzene = 157 g mol$^{-1}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $n_{\\text{Br}_2}=0.500\\,\\text{mol}$, theoretical $n_{\\text{C}_6\\text{H}_5\\text{Br}}=0.500\\,\\text{mol}$ (1:1), $M_{\\text{C}_6\\text{H}_5\\text{Br}}=157\\,\\text{g mol}^{-1}$, actual mass $=84.0\\,\\text{g}$.

Formula: $\\text{Theoretical mass}=n\\times M$, $\\%\\text{Yield}=\\frac{\\text{Actual}}{\\text{Theoretical}}\\times100$.

Step‑by‑Step:

  1. Theoretical mass $=0.500\\times157=78.5\\,\\text{g}$.
  2. $\\%\\text{Yield}=\\frac{84.0}{78.5}\\times100=107\\%$.

Final Answer: $\\%\\text{Yield}=107\\%$ (indicates experimental error; actual yield cannot exceed 100 %).

pyq.question: Write the general method for preparation of haloalkanes by free radical halogenation of alkanes.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Mix the alkane with a halogen ($\mathrm{Cl_2}$ or $\mathrm{Br_2}$) in the presence of light or a peroxide catalyst.
2. Initiation: $\mathrm{Cl\!\cdot \;\xrightarrow{h\nu}\; Cl\!\cdot}$ (or $\mathrm{Br\!\cdot}$).
3. Propagation: $\mathrm{Cl\!\cdot + RH \rightarrow R\!\cdot + HCl}$ and $\mathrm{R\!\cdot + Cl_2 \rightarrow RCl + Cl\!\cdot}$ (similarly for Br).
4. Termination: combination of radicals.
5. Isolate the haloalkane by distillation or extraction.

pyq.question: State the IUPAC name of the compound $\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-Br}$.
pyq.answer_html: The longest chain contains three carbon atoms; the substituent is bromine at carbon‑1. IUPAC name: 1‑bromopropane.

pyq.question: Explain the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution (SN2) in haloalkanes with an example.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Single step bimolecular process – rate $=k[\text{haloalkane}][\text{nucleophile}]$.
2. Nucleophile attacks the carbon bearing the leaving group from the backside, forming a pentavalent transition state.
3. Simultaneous breaking of the $\mathrm{C\!\!–\!X}$ bond and formation of the $\mathrm{C\!\!–\!Nu}$ bond.
Example: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br + OH^- \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH + Br^-}$ (ethanol formation).
4. Inversion of configuration (Walden inversion) if the carbon is chiral.

pyq.question: Why does chlorobenzene undergo nucleophilic substitution only under harsh conditions? Explain with resonance.
pyq.answer_html: In chlorobenzene the $\mathrm{C\!\!–\!Cl}$ bond participates in resonance with the aromatic ring: $\mathrm{Cl}$ donates its lone pair into the ring, giving partial double‑bond character to $\mathrm{C\!\!–\!Cl}$. This delocalisation stabilises the C–Cl bond and reduces its polarity, making $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ a poor leaving group. Consequently, a strong nucleophile and high temperature (or a catalyst) are required to overcome the activation barrier for the $\mathrm{S_NAr}$ pathway.

pyq.question: Write the complete mechanism for the conversion of 1‑chlorobutane to 1‑butanol using aqueous NaOH. Include all intermediates and indicate the type of reaction.
pyq.answer_html:
Step 1 – Nucleophilic attack (SN2):
$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl + OH^- \xrightarrow{\text{polar aprotic}} \[\text{Transition state}\] \rightarrow CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH + Cl^-}$
• Back‑side attack by $\mathrm{OH^-}$ on the carbon bearing $\mathrm{Cl}$.
• Pentavalent transition state with partial bonds to $\mathrm{Cl}$ and $\mathrm{OH}$.
• Simultaneous bond formation and bond breaking gives inversion of configuration (if chiral).
Overall reaction (substitution): $\mathrm{RCl + NaOH \rightarrow ROH + NaCl}$.
• Type of reaction: nucleophilic substitution ($\mathrm{S_N2}$) because a primary haloalkane is involved.

pyq.question: Compare the reactivity order of haloalkanes (I > Br > Cl > F) in SN2 reactions and explain the factors responsible.
pyq.answer_html:
Reactivity order: $\mathrm{RI > RBr > RCl > RF}$.
Reasons:
1. Bond strength: C–I bond ($\approx 238\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) is weakest, so it breaks easily; C–F bond is strongest ($\approx 485\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).
2. Atomic size & polarizability: Larger halogens (I, Br) are more polarizable, stabilising the transition state.
3. Leaving group ability: Better leaving groups form more stable anions; $\mathrm{I^-}$ is larger and more stable than $\mathrm{F^-}$.
4. Solvation effects: In polar aprotic solvents, the nucleophile is less solvated, highlighting intrinsic leaving‑group ability; still, the intrinsic trend remains.
Thus, weaker C–X bond, larger size, and better leaving‑group stability make I > Br > Cl > F for SN2.

mcq.q: Which of the following haloalkanes undergoes nucleophilic substitution predominantly by the $\text{SN1}$ mechanism?
mcq.explain: Tertiary haloalkanes like $\text{tert-butyl bromide}$ form stable carbocations, favoring the $\text{SN1}$ pathway.

mcq.q: The order of reactivity of haloalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution ($\text{SN2}$) is:
mcq.explain: In $\text{SN2}$ reactions, reactivity decreases with increasing steric hindrance: primary $>$ secondary $>$ tertiary.

mcq.q: Which method is used for the preparation of aryl halides (haloarenes) from phenols?
options: Diazotisation of aniline followed by Sandmeyer reaction
Halogenation of benzene in presence of FeCl$_3$
mcq.explain: Aniline is diazotised to form a diazonium salt, which on treatment with CuX (Sandmeyer) gives the corresponding haloarene.

mcq.q: The boiling point of $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ is lower than that of $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$. This is mainly due to:
mcq.explain: Boiling point correlates with molar mass; $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ (80 g/mol) is heavier than $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ (50 g/mol).

mcq.q: Which of the following statements about the reaction of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ with Na in liquid NH$_3$ is correct?
options: It undergoes nucleophilic aromatic substitution via benzyne intermediate
It gives phenol as the major product
It does not react under these conditions
mcq.explain: Chlorobenzene reacts with Na/NH$_3$ through the benzyne mechanism, a characteristic nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

mcq.q: In the Wurtz–Fittig reaction, a mixture of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$ in presence of Na gives:
mcq.explain: The cross‑coupling of aryl and alkyl halides in Wurtz–Fittig yields the mixed product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ (toluene).

mcq.q: Which of the following haloalkanes is most suitable for preparation of an alkene by dehydrohalogenation using alcoholic KOH?
mcq.explain: A secondary haloalkane like $\text{1-bromo-2-methylpropane}$ undergoes $E2$ elimination readily with alcoholic KOH to give the more substituted alkene.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$ is more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$.\nReason (R): The C–I bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Iodine is a better leaving group due to the weaker C–I bond, making $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$ more reactive.

mcq.q: The rate of $\text{SN1}$ reaction of $\text{tert-butyl chloride}$ in water is increased by:
options: Adding a strong base like NaOH
Adding a polar protic solvent like ethanol
Adding a non‑polar solvent like hexane
mcq.explain: Polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation intermediate, accelerating the $\text{SN1}$ pathway.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements about the physical properties of haloarenes is correct?
options: They are more basic than benzene
They have higher boiling points than corresponding haloalkanes due to π‑π interactions
They undergo rapid $\text{SN2}$ reactions with $\text{NaI}$ in acetone
They are soluble in water because of hydrogen bonding
mcq.explain: Haloarenes exhibit higher boiling points than haloalkanes of similar molar mass owing to stronger intermolecular forces, including π‑π stacking.

long_notes.Nomenclature and classification of haloa:
Definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are organic compounds containing at least one halogen atom (F, Cl, Br, I) covalently bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Haloarenes are aromatic analogues where the halogen is attached to an sp$^2$ carbon of the benzene ring.

  • Classification of haloalkanes (based on carbon bearing the halogen):
    TypeGeneral FormulaExample
    Primary$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-X}$1‑bromoethane
    Secondary$\text{R-CHX- R'}$2‑chloropropane
    Tertiary$\text{R-CX(R')_2}$2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane
  • Classification of haloarenes: Monohaloarenes, di‑haloarenes, poly‑haloarenes; ortho, meta, para positional isomers.

Nomenclature Rules (IUPAC):

  • Identify the longest carbon chain containing the carbon bearing the halogen; number it to give the lowest possible locant to the halogen.
  • Use the prefix “halo‑” (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo) followed by the parent alkane name.
  • If more than one identical halogen is present, use di‑, tri‑, tetra‑ as prefixes and give separate locants (e.g., 1,2‑dichloroethane).
  • For haloarenes, the aromatic ring is the parent; the halogen is indicated by the same prefixes with the locant (e.g., 4‑bromophenol).

Key Formula (Moles of NaOH required for nucleophilic substitution): $n_{\text{NaOH}} = n_{\text{haloalkane}} \times \nu$, where $\nu$ is the stoichiometric coefficient (usually 1 for $\text{SN}2$).

Solved Example:

Calculate the mass of NaOH needed to completely react with $0.50\,\text{mol}$ of 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane in an $\text{SN}1$ reaction.

  1. Reaction: $\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{CBr} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH} + \text{NaBr}$
  2. From the equation, $\nu = 1$, so $n_{\text{NaOH}} = 0.50\,\text{mol}$.
  3. Molar mass of NaOH = $22.99 + 15.999 + 1.008 = 39.997\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Mass $= n \times M = 0.50\,\text{mol} \times 39.997\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 20.0\,\text{g}$.

Thus, $20.0\,\text{g}$ of NaOH will completely convert $0.50\,\text{mol}$ of the haloalkane.
long_notes.Methods of preparation of haloalkanes an:
Definitions

  • Haloalkane: An alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by halogen atoms (Cl, Br, I, F).
  • Haloarene: An aromatic compound containing one or more halogen substituents on the benzene ring.

Key Methods of Preparation

MethodReagents / ConditionsMechanism
From alkenes (addition)$\text{HX}$ (or $\text{X}_2$) in presence of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$Electrophilic addition (Markovnikov)
From alcohols$\text{HX}$ (conc.) or $\text{PCl}_5$, $\text{SOCl}_2$; $\text{ZnCl}_2$ (Lucas reagent)SN1 (tertiary) / SN2 (primary)
From alkyl halides (halogen exchange)Na$\text{X}$ in acetone (Finkelstein); Cu$\text{X}$, NaCN (nucleophilic substitution)SN2
From carboxylic acidsHBr, $\text{PBr}_3$ (decarboxylation)Radical decarboxylation
From Grignard reagentsR$\text{MgX}$ + $\text{RX}$ → R–R' + MgX$_2$Coupling
Haloarenes – electrophilic aromatic substitution$\text{X}_2$ + FeCl$_3$ (Cl), AlCl$_3$ (Br)σ‑complex formation
Haloarenes – Sandmeyer reactionAr–N$_2^+$Cl$^-$ + CuX (X = Cl, Br, CN)Radical substitution via diazonium salt

Rate Laws (SI Units)

  • Halogenation of alkanes: $Rate = k[RH][X_2]$; $k$ in $M^{-1}s^{-1}$.
  • SN1: $Rate = k[RX]$; $k$ in $s^{-1}$.
  • SN2: $Rate = k[RX][Nu^-]$; $k$ in $M^{-2}s^{-1}$.

Solved Example

Prepare 1‑chloropropane from 1‑propanol using Lucas reagent.

  1. Reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + HCl \xrightarrow{\text{ZnCl}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + H_2O$.
  2. Mechanism: Primary alcohol undergoes SN2 attack by $Cl^-$ generated in situ.
  3. Calculation (if 10.0 g 1‑propanol, $M_{\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}}=60.1\,g\,mol^{-1}$):
    $n = \frac{10.0}{60.1}=0.166\,mol$; theoretical $m_{\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}} = 0.166\times 78.5=13.0\,g$.
    If 11.5 g product obtained, % yield $=\frac{11.5}{13.0}\times100=88.5\%$.

This concise table‑driven format aligns with the CBSE Class 12 syllabus and aids quick revision for exams.
long_notes.Physical properties and trends in boilin:
Definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) and haloarenes (aryl halides) are organic compounds containing a carbon‑halogen bond.

Key factors influencing physical properties

  • Intermolecular forces – dipole‑dipole, London dispersion and, for H‑bond donors, hydrogen bonding.
  • Polarity – depends on C–X bond dipole moment $\mu = \delta \times d$.
  • Molecular mass – heavier halogen → stronger dispersion forces.

Boiling‑point trend

SeriesTrend
Haloalkanes (same carbon skeleton)$\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} < \text{CH}_3\text{Br} < \text{CH}_3\text{I}$
Haloarenes (same ring)$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{F} < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$

Explanation: As atomic size and mass increase, London dispersion forces ($F_{\text{L}} \propto \alpha$) increase, raising $T_{\text{b}}$.

Solubility in water

  • Small, highly polar haloalkanes (e.g., CH$_2$Cl$_2$) are moderately soluble.
  • Heavier halides are sparingly soluble because dispersion forces dominate.
  • Haloarenes are essentially insoluble due to aromatic π‑system and lack of H‑bonding.

Polarity order (C–X bond)

$\mu_{\text{C–F}} > \mu_{\text{C–Cl}} > \mu_{\text{C–Br}} > \mu_{\text{C–I}}$ because electronegativity difference $\Delta \chi$ decreases down the group.

Solved Example

Calculate the dipole moment of the C–Cl bond in chloromethane if $\Delta \chi = 0.5$ and bond length $d = 1.78\ \text{Å}$. Using $\mu = 0.208\ \Delta \chi \times d$ (Debye, $d$ in Å), $\mu = 0.208 \times 0.5 \times 1.78 = 0.185\ \text{D}$. Hence chloromethane is polar ($\mu \approx 0.19\ \text{D}$).

These trends help predict boiling points, solubility and reactivity of haloalkanes and haloarenes in the CBSE exam.
long_notes.Mechanism and kinetics of nucleophilic s:
Definitions

  • SN1: unimolecular nucleophilic substitution; rate depends only on substrate.
  • SN2: bimolecular nucleophilic substitution; rate depends on substrate and nucleophile.

Kinetic Expressions

ReactionRate lawOrderUnit of $k$
SN1$rate = k[RX]$First order$s^{-1}$
SN2$rate = k[RX][Nu^-]$Second order$M^{-1}s^{-1}$

Derivation (SN1)

For the slow step $RX \rightarrow R^+ + X^-$, $$\\frac{d[RX]}{dt} = -k[RX]$$ integrating gives $$[RX]_t = [RX]_0 e^{-kt}$$.

Key Factors

  • Stability of carbocation (SN1) – tertiary > secondary > primary.
  • Strength and steric hindrance of nucleophile (SN2) – strong, unhindered nucleophile favours SN2.
  • Solvent polarity – polar protic stabilises ions (SN1); polar aprotic enhances nucleophilicity (SN2).

Solvent Effect on Rate Constant

Arrhenius equation: $$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$ where $A$ (s$^{-1}$ or M$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$) is frequency factor, $E_a$ (kJ·mol$^{-1}$) activation energy.

Solved Example

At 298 K, the SN2 reaction between $CH_3Br$ and $OH^-$ follows $rate = k[CH_3Br][OH^-]$. Initial concentrations: $[CH_3Br]_0 = 0.010\;M$, $[OH^-]_0 = 0.020\;M$. After 500 s, $[CH_3Br] = 0.006\;M$. Find $k$.

For second‑order reaction, $$\\frac{1}{[CH_3Br]_t} - \\frac{1}{[CH_3Br]_0} = k[OH^-]t$$ (since $[OH^-]$ ≈ constant). Plugging values: $$\\frac{1}{0.006} - \\frac{1}{0.010} = k(0.020)(500)$$ $$166.67 - 100 = 5000k$$ $$66.67 = 5000k$$ $$k = 1.33\\times10^{-2}\;M^{-1}s^{-1}$$.

This $k$ value confirms a typical SN2 rate constant in polar aprotic solvent.
long_notes.Mechanism and kinetics of elimination re:
Elimination Reactions (E1 & E2)

Definition: An elimination reaction removes two atoms or groups from adjacent carbon atoms, forming a double bond. E1 proceeds via a unimolecular, two‑step pathway; E2 is a concerted bimolecular process.

  • E1: Rate‑determining step is loss of leaving group → carbocation. Rate law: $rate = k[RX]$ (first order, $s^{-1}$).
  • E2: Simultaneous removal of proton by base and departure of leaving group. Rate law: $rate = k[RX][Base]$ (second order, $M^{-1}s^{-1}$).

Kinetic Expressions

StepRate LawUnits of $k$
E1$rate = k[RX]$$s^{-1}$
E2$rate = k[RX][Base]$$M^{-1}s^{-1}$

Key Formulae

  • Arrhenius: $$k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$$ where $A$ (s$^{-1}$ or M$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$), $E_a$ (kJ·mol$^{-1}$), $R = 8.314$ J·mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, $T$ (K).
  • Degree of elimination: $\alpha = \frac{\text{moles of alkene formed}}{\text{initial moles of substrate}}$.

Solved Example

At $298\,K$, $k_{E2}=2.5\times10^{-3}\,M^{-1}s^{-1}$. For $[CH_3CH_2Br]=0.010\,M$ and $[OH^-]=0.020\,M$, calculate the rate.

Using $rate = k[RX][Base]$:

$rate = 2.5\times10^{-3}\times0.010\times0.020 = 5.0\times10^{-7}\,M\,s^{-1}$.

The reaction follows second‑order kinetics, confirming an E2 mechanism.
long_notes.Reactions of haloarenes: electrophilic a:
Reactions of Haloarenes

Haloarenes (Ar–X, X = Cl, Br, I) undergo two major aromatic substitution pathways:

  • Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS): The aromatic ring acts as a nucleophile and attacks an electrophile, displacing the halogen only when it is a good leaving group (e.g., –I in iodonium ion formation). The overall rate follows first‑order kinetics: $\\frac{d[ArX]}{dt} = -k[ArX]$ where $k = A\\,e^{-E_a/RT}$.
  • Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution (SNAr): Requires a strong electron‑withdrawing group (–NO₂, –CN, –COOR) ortho/para to the halogen. The mechanism proceeds via a Meisenheimer complex (σ‑complex). Rate law: $\\frac{d[ArX]}{dt} = -k[ArX][Nu^-]$ (second order).

Key Factors

FactorEASSNAr
Leaving group abilityGood (I > Br > Cl)Good (I > Br > Cl)
Activating groupElectron‑donating (–OMe, –NH₂) ↑ rateElectron‑withdrawing (–NO₂) ↑ rate
SolventPolar protic favours carbocation formationPolar aprotic stabilises $\\text{Nu}^-$

Typical SNAr Example

Reaction: $\\text{p‑Nitrochlorobenzene} + NaOH \rightarrow p\text{-Nitrophenol} + NaCl$

Solution:

  1. Formation of Meisenheimer complex: $\\text{C}_6H_4(NO_2)Cl + OH^- \rightarrow [C_6H_4(NO_2)Cl(OH)]^{\!-}$
  2. Elimination of Cl⁻ to restore aromaticity: $[C_6H_4(NO_2)Cl(OH)]^{\!-} \rightarrow C_6H_4(NO_2)OH + Cl^-$

Overall rate: $k = 1.2\times10^{-3}\,\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ at $298\,\text{K}$ (experimental). The reaction exemplifies the necessity of a –NO₂ group ortho/para to the halogen for a feasible SNAr pathway.

Take‑away: EAS dominates when the ring is electron‑rich; SNAr requires strong –EWG activation and a good leaving halide, proceeding via a σ‑complex with second‑order kinetics.
long_notes.Factors affecting reactivity and selecti:
Factors affecting reactivity & selectivity in haloalkanes

  • Leaving group ability: Better leaving groups stabilize the carbanion formed after bond cleavage. Order: $I^- > Br^- > Cl^- > F^-$ (in polar protic solvents).
  • Nucleophilicity: Depends on charge, basicity and solvent. In polar protic media $Nu^-$ > $NuH$; trend $RS^- > RO^- > H^-$. Rate law for $S_N2$: $rate = k[RX][Nu^-]$ with $k$ in $M^{-1}s^{-1}$.
  • Solvent effect: Polar protic solvents stabilise ions, favour $S_N1$; polar aprotic solvents enhance $S_N2$ by not solvating $Nu^-$. Dielectric constant ($\epsilon$) is the SI unit‑less measure of polarity.
  • Steric hindrance: $S_N2$ rate decreases sharply from primary $< $secondary $< $tertiary. $S_N1$ rate increases with carbocation stability: $3^circ > 2^circ > 1^circ$.
  • Bond dissociation energy (BDE): Lower $C–X$ BDE accelerates both $S_N1$ and $S_N2$. Typical values: $C–Iapprox 240;kJ,mol^{-1}$, $C–Clapprox 340;kJ,mol^{-1}$.

Haloarenes

  • Reactivity governed by aromatic resonance and leaving‑group ability. $S_NAr$ proceeds via Meisenheimer complex; electron‑withdrawing groups (–NO$_2$, –CN) ortho/para accelerate the reaction.
  • Activation energy ($E_a$) relation: $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$ (Arrhenius). $A$ (frequency factor) in $s^{-1}$.
  • Solvent polarity influences $S_NAr$ less than aliphatic $S_N$ because the rate‑determining step is intramolecular.

Solved Example

Calculate the relative rate of $S_N1$ for $tert$‑butyl bromide ($C_4H_9Br$) vs $1$‑bromopropane at $25^circ C$, given $k_{tert}=1.2\times10^{-3}\;s^{-1}$ and $k_{1^circ}=2.5\times10^{-6}\;s^{-1}$.

Solution: $\frac{rate_{tert}}{rate_{1^circ}} = \frac{k_{tert}}{k_{1^circ}} = \frac{1.2\times10^{-3}}{2.5\times10^{-6}} \approx 4.8\times10^{2}$. Hence $tert$‑butyl bromide reacts ~480 times faster than $1$‑bromopropane in $S_N1$, illustrating the dominant role of carbocation stability.
long_notes.Industrial applications and environmenta:
Industrial Applications

  • Manufacture of chloroform and carbon tetrachloride by chlorination of methane: $\text{CH}_4 + 3\,\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CCl}_4 + 4\,\text{HCl}$.
  • Synthesis of vinyl chloride monomer (VCM) from 1,2‑dichloroethane, a key step in PVC production.
  • Preparation of pharmaceutical intermediates such as chloramphenicol and organophosphorus insecticides.
  • Use as solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) and refrigerants (CFC‑12).

Environmental Impact

  • Haloalkanes are persistent, bio‑accumulative and ozone‑depleting; many are listed under the Montreal Protocol.
  • Photolysis in the stratosphere releases chlorine radicals that catalyse $\text{O}_3$ destruction: $\text{Cl} + \text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{ClO} + \text{O}_2$; $\text{ClO} + \text{O} \rightarrow \text{Cl} + \text{O}_2$.
  • Ground‑level release leads to groundwater contamination; toxicity expressed as $\text{LD}_{50}$ (mg kg$^{-1}$).

Key Formulas

ParameterExpressionSI Unit
Reaction rate (first order)$r = k\,C$mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$
Half‑life (first order)$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$s
Yield$\%Y = \frac{\text{actual moles}}{\text{theoretical moles}}\times 100$\%

Solved Example

Calculate the mass of $\text{CCl}_4$ obtained when $5.0\,\text{mol}$ of $\text{CH}_4$ is completely chlorinated (theoretical yield only).

Balanced equation: $\text{CH}_4 + 3\,\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CCl}_4 + 4\,\text{HCl}$. Moles of $\text{CCl}_4$ = moles of $\text{CH}_4$ = $5.0\,\text{mol}$. Molar mass of $\text{CCl}_4$ = $12.01 + 4\times35.45 = 153.81\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. Mass = $5.0\times153.81 = 7.69\times10^2\,\text{g}$.

short_notes.title: Important Formulas
short_notes.html:
ConceptFormula
Rate of SN1$k[\text{R\u2013X}]$
Rate of SN2$k[\text{R\u2013X}][\text{Nu}^-]$
Reactivity order (alkyl halides)$\text{RI} > \text{RBr} > \text{RCl} > \text{RF}$
Reactivity order (aryl halides)$\text{I} > \text{Br} > \text{Cl} > \text{F}$ (in presence of catalyst)

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Haloalkane (alkyl halide): Organic compound containing a halogen atom covalently bonded to an sp3 hybridised carbon.
  • Haloarene (aryl halide): Halogen attached to an sp2 hybridised carbon of an aromatic ring.
  • Nucleophilic substitution (SN): Replacement of a leaving group (X) by a nucleophile (Nu-).
  • SN1 mechanism: Unimolecular; rate depends only on substrate. $\text{Rate}=k[\text{R\u2013X}]$; involves carbocation intermediate.
  • SN2 mechanism: Bimolecular; concerted backside attack. $\text{Rate}=k[\text{R\u2013X}][\text{Nu}^-]$; inversion of configuration.
  • Elimination (E1/E2): Competing reactions where a hydrogen and the leaving group are removed to form an alkene.
  • Markovnikov's rule (for addition to alkenes, relevant for halogenation of alkenes): Hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, halogen to the carbon with fewer.
  • Reactivity trends: Primary > Secondary > Tertiary for SN2; Tertiary > Secondary > Primary for SN1. Aryl halides undergo SNAr only under strong nucleophile + electron‑withdrawing substituent.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
• Always identify the type of substrate (primary, secondary, tertiary, allylic, benzylic, or aryl) before choosing SN1 or SN2.
  • Do not confuse the rate laws: SN1 is first order in substrate only; SN2 is second order (substrate + nucleophile).
  • Remember that aryl halides do NOT undergo SN1/SN2 under normal conditions; they require SNAr mechanism with a strong nucleophile and a –NO2 (or other –EWG) ortho/para to the halogen.
  • In SN2, the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group – leading to Walden inversion. Forgetting inversion leads to wrong stereochemistry.
  • When calculating % yield, use the theoretical yield based on the limiting reagent, not the stoichiometric amount of the halide.
  • Common error: treating F as a good leaving group. In haloalkanes, F is a poor leaving group; reactions are slower compared to Cl, Br, I.
  • For elimination, check the base strength: strong bases favour E2, weak bases favour E1 (often with carbocation formation).
  • Do not overlook solvent effects: polar protic solvents stabilise carbocations (favor SN1/E1), while polar aprotic solvents enhance nucleophilicity (favor SN2/E2).

numericals.question: Calculate the rate of an SN1 reaction for 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane when $[\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C–Br}]=0.020\ \text{M}$ and the rate constant $k=1.5\times10^{3}\ \text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $[\\text{(CH}_3)_3\\text{C–Br}]=0.020\\ \\text{M}$, $k=1.5\\times10^{3}\\ \\text{M}^{-1}\\text{s}^{-1}$.

Formula: Rate $=k[\\text{substrate}]$ for a first‑order SN1 process.

Calculation: Rate $=1.5\\times10^{3}\\times0.020=30\\ \\text{M\\,s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $30\\ \\text{M\\,s}^{-1}$ (i.e., $30\\ \\text{mol\\,L}^{-1}\\text{s}^{-1}$).

numericals.question: 2.5 g of 1‑chloropropane ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$, $M=78.5\ \text{g\,mol}^{-1}$) is hydrolysed with excess NaOH: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}+\text{NaOH}\rightarrow\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}+\text{NaCl}$. Find the mass of NaCl formed.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $m_{\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{Cl}}=2.5\\ \\text{g}$, $M_{\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{Cl}}=78.5\\ \\text{g\\,mol}^{-1}$, $M_{\\text{NaCl}}=58.44\\ \\text{g\\,mol}^{-1}$.

Formula: $n=\\frac{m}{M}$ and stoichiometry $1:\\!1$ for $\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{Cl}$ to NaCl.

Calculation: $n_{\\text{C}_3\\text{H}_7\\text{Cl}}=\\frac{2.5}{78.5}=3.18\\times10^{-2}\\ \\text{mol}$. Hence $m_{\\text{NaCl}}=n\\times M_{\\text{NaCl}}=3.18\\times10^{-2}\\times58.44=1.86\\ \\text{g}$.

Answer: $1.86\\ \\text{g}$ of NaCl are obtained.

numericals.question: A solution is prepared by dissolving $0.50\ \text{mol}$ of bromoethane in $1.0\ \text{kg}$ of water. Given $K_{\text{b}}=0.512\ ^\circ\text{C\,kg\,mol}^{-1}$, calculate the boiling‑point elevation $\Delta T_{\text{b}}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $m=0.50\ \text{mol}$, $\text{kg of solvent}=1.0\ \text{kg}$, $K_{\text{b}}=0.512\ ^\circ\text{C\,kg\,mol}^{-1}$.

Formula: $\Delta T_{\text{b}}=K_{\text{b}}\times m_{\text{solute}}$, where $m_{\text{solute}}=\frac{\text{mol solute}}{\text{kg solvent}}$.

Calculation: $m_{\text{solute}}=\frac{0.50}{1.0}=0.50\ \text{mol\,kg}^{-1}$. $\Delta T_{\text{b}}=0.512\times0.50=0.256\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

Answer: The boiling point is raised by $0.256\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

pyq.question: State the type of nucleophilic substitution (SN1 or SN2) that a primary haloalkane undergoes when treated with aqueous NaOH.
pyq.answer_html: Primary haloalkanes undergo $\text{SN2}$ mechanism with aqueous NaOH. (1 mark for identifying SN2, 1 mark for mentioning primary substrate)

pyq.question: Write the mechanism for the reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with aqueous NaOH and state the rate law.
pyq.answer_html:
Mechanism: $\text{SN1}$ – formation of a tertiary carbocation followed by attack of $\text{OH}^-$.
Rate law: $\text{Rate}=k[\text{R–Br}]$ (first order in substrate). (1 mark each for mechanism, carbocation formation, rate law)

pyq.question: Explain why the boiling points of haloalkanes are higher than those of the corresponding alkanes of the same carbon number. Include the trend with the nature of the halogen.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Halogen atoms are heavier and more polarizable than hydrogen, increasing London dispersion forces. (1 mark)
2. C–X bond dipole introduces dipole‑dipole interactions; polarity increases from $\text{F}<\text{Cl}<\text{Br}<\text{I}$. (1 mark)
3. Larger atomic size of halogen enlarges molecular surface area, further strengthening dispersion forces. (1 mark)
4. Consequently, $\text{BP}_{\text{haloalkane}} > \text{BP}_{\text{alkane}}$ for the same carbon skeleton. (1 mark)
5. Trend: $\text{BP}_{\text{CH}_3\text{I}} > \text{BP}_{\text{CH}_3\text{Br}} > \text{BP}_{\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}} > \text{BP}_{\text{CH}_3\text{F}}$ due to increasing mass and polarizability. (1 mark)

pyq.question: Provide the IUPAC name of the compound shown: a benzene ring with a bromo substituent at position 1 and a chloro substituent at position 2.
pyq.answer_html: 1‑Bromo‑2‑chlorobenzene (or 2‑chloro‑1‑bromobenzene). (1 mark for correct name, 1 mark for correct numbering)

pyq.question: Predict the major product when chlorobenzene is treated with excess NaNH$_2$ in liquid NH$_3$.
pyq.answer_html: Product: Phenylacetylene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$). (1 mark for recognizing nucleophilic aromatic substitution, 1 mark for formation of benzyne intermediate, 1 mark for final product)

pyq.question: Discuss the differences between SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with respect to (i) kinetics, (ii) stereochemistry, and (iii) substrate preference.
pyq.answer_html:
(i) Kinetics: SN1 – rate $=k[\text{substrate}]$ (unimolecular); SN2 – rate $=k[\text{substrate}][\text{nucleophile}]$ (bimolecular). (2 marks)
(ii) Stereochemistry: SN1 proceeds via planar carbocation → racemisation (partial loss of configuration). SN2 involves backside attack → inversion of configuration (Walden inversion). (2 marks)
(iii) Substrate preference: SN1 favours tertiary > secondary > primary (stable carbocation). SN2 favours primary > secondary (less steric hindrance) and is hindered by tertiary substrates. (1 mark)

mcq.q: Which of the following haloalkanes will react fastest in an $S_{N}2$ reaction with $NaOH$ (aq.)?
mcq.explain: In $S_{N}2$, primary halides react faster and the reactivity increases with the size of the leaving group. $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I$ (primary iodide) is the most reactive.

mcq.q: Which statement correctly describes the rate-determining step of an $S_{N}1$ reaction?
options: Bimolecular collision between substrate and nucleophile
Concerted removal of a proton and leaving group
Formation of a cyclic transition state
mcq.explain: The rate‑determining step of $S_{N}1$ is the unimolecular ionisation of the substrate to give a carbocation.

mcq.q: In the solvolysis of $tert$‑butyl bromide in water, the observed rate is higher than in 80% ethanol. This is because:
options: Water is a better nucleophile than ethanol
$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ stabilises the carbocation more effectively than ethanol
Ethanol participates in $E2$ elimination, reducing the $S_{N}1$ rate
Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with the leaving group, slowing the reaction
mcq.explain: Polar protic water stabilises the developing positive charge on the carbocation better than less polar ethanol, increasing the $S_{N}1$ rate.

mcq.q: Arrange the nucleophilicity of the following anions in protic solvent (increasing order): $F^-$, $Cl^-$, $Br^-$, $I^-$.
mcq.explain: In protic solvents, larger, less basic anions are less strongly solvated, so nucleophilicity increases down the group: $F^- < Cl^- < Br^- < I^-$.

mcq.q: Reaction of $C_6H_5Br$ with excess $NaNH_2$ in liquid ammonia gives:
mcq.explain: $NaNH_2$ acts as a nucleophile, displacing bromide via $S_{N}Ar$ to give aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$).

mcq.q: The Finkelstein reaction (halogen exchange) of $CH_3CH_2Cl$ with $NaI$ in acetone proceeds because:
options: $NaCl$ precipitates out, driving the reaction forward
$I^-$ is a better leaving group than $Cl^-$
mcq.explain: In acetone, $NaCl$ is insoluble and precipitates, removing the product and shifting the equilibrium toward $CH_3CH_2I$.

mcq.q: When $2$‑methyl‑2‑butanol is treated with $t$‑BuOK, the major product is:
mcq.explain: $t$‑BuOK$ is a bulky base, favoring the Hofmann elimination that gives the less substituted alkene $2$‑methyl‑1‑butene.

mcq.q: In the reaction $CH_3CH_2Cl + NaI (acetone) \rightarrow$ ?, which statement is correct?
options: The reaction does not occur because $Cl^-$ is a better nucleophile than $I^-$
The reaction proceeds to give $CH_3CH_2I$ and $NaCl$ precipitates
mcq.explain: Finkelstein exchange: $I^-$ replaces $Cl^-$; $NaCl$ precipitates in acetone, driving the formation of $CH_3CH_2I$.

mcq.q:
Assertion (A): In haloarenes, the C–X bond is stronger than in the corresponding haloalkanes.
Reason (R): The C–X bond in haloarenes has partial double‑bond character due to resonance.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Aromatic halides have a C–X bond strengthened by resonance (partial double‑bond), making it stronger than in aliphatic halides; R correctly explains A.

mcq.q: A primary haloalkane $CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl$ reacts with aqueous $NaOH$. The major product is:
mcq.explain: Primary halides undergo $S_{N}2$ with aqueous $NaOH$, giving the corresponding primary alcohol $CH_3CH_2CH_2OH$ as the major product.

long_notes.Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Et:
Definition: Alcohols, phenols and ethers are organic compounds containing –OH or –O– groups attached to saturated carbon atoms.

  • Alcohols: Hydroxyl group ($-OH$) bonded to a saturated carbon.
  • Phenols: Hydroxyl group directly attached to an aromatic ring.
  • Ethers: Two alkyl/aryl groups linked by an oxygen atom ($R-O-R'$).

IUPAC Naming Rules – Alcohols

StepRule
1Identify the longest carbon chain containing the –OH group; this chain is the parent hydrocarbon.
2Number the chain so that the carbon bearing –OH gets the lowest possible locant.
3Replace the –OH suffix with “‑$\\text{ol}$”. If more than one –OH, use “‑$\\text{diol}$”, “‑$\\text{triol}$”, etc., with appropriate locants.
4Insert prefixes for substituents and give their locants.

Phenols

  • Parent name is the aromatic ring (benzene → “phenol”).
  • If substituents are present, use “‑$\\text{ol}$” as a suffix and number the ring to give the –OH the lowest locant.

Ethers

  • Two naming methods: (i) “alkoxy‑alkane” (e.g., $\\text{methoxypropane}$) where the shorter alkyl is the alkoxy part; (ii) “symmetrical ethers” named as “dialkyl ether” (e.g., $\\text{diethyl ether}$).
  • When both sides are different, the alkoxy name is preferred.

Solved Example

Name the compound: $\\text{CH}_3\\text{CH}_2\\text{CH}(\\text{OH})\\text{CH}_2\\text{CH}_3$.

Solution: Longest chain = 5 C → “pentane”. Number from the end nearest the –OH → locant 3. Replace –e with –$\\text{ol}$ → “3‑pentanol”.
Definition: Alcohols are organic compounds containing a hydroxyl group ($-\!OH$) attached to a saturated carbon atom.

Key Methods:

  • Acid‑catalysed hydration of alkenes
  • Reduction of aldehydes and ketones

Acid‑catalysed hydration

General equation: $C_nH_{2n}+H_2O\xrightarrow{H_2SO_4,\,\Delta}C_nH_{2n+1}OH$

Conditions: 60–80 $^\circ$C, 1–2 atm, conc. $H_2SO_4$ (≈98 %).

Reduction of carbonyls

For aldehydes: $RCHO+H_2\xrightarrow{Ni,\,\Delta}RCH_2OH$

For ketones: $RCOR'+H_2\xrightarrow{Ni,\,\Delta}RCH_2R'$

Using metal hydrides: $RCHO+NaBH_4\rightarrow RCH_2OH$ (room temp, $MeOH$).

ReagentProduct
$NaBH_4$Primary alcohol
$LiAlH_4$Secondary/tertiary alcohol

Solved Example

Hydrate 10 g ethene ($C_2H_4$) to ethanol. Molar masses: $M_{C_2H_4}=28.05\,$g·mol$^{-1}$, $M_{C_2H_5OH}=46.07\,$g·mol$^{-1}$. Moles of ethene $n=\frac{10}{28.05}=0.357\,$mol. Assuming 100 % yield, $n_{ethanol}=0.357\,$mol. Mass of ethanol $m=n\times M=0.357\times46.07=16.45\,$g.

Key points: the reaction follows Markovnikov’s rule, the acid catalyst is regenerated, and reduction must be controlled to avoid over‑reduction.
long_notes.Methods of Preparation of Phenols (e.g.,:
Definition: Phenols are aromatic compounds containing a hydroxyl group directly attached to an sp$^2$ hybridised carbon of a benzene ring (Ar–OH). They exhibit acidic behaviour ($pK_a\approx10$) and are important industrial intermediates.

1. Hydrolysis of aryl halides (high‑temperature alkaline hydrolysis)

  • General reaction: $\text{Ar–X} + \text{NaOH}_{(aq)} \xrightarrow{\text{300–350\,°C}} \text{Ar–OH} + \text{NaX}$ where X = Cl, Br, I.
  • Requires a strong base and a sealed tube to achieve temperatures $\ge300\,\text{°C}$ and pressures $\approx10\,\text{atm}$.

2. Cumene (isopropylbenzene) process

  • Step 1 – Oxidation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{70–80\,°C}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{OOH}$ (cumene hydroperoxide).
  • Step 2 – Acidic cleavage: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{OOH} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CO}$ (acetone).

Key conditions

StepTemperature (°C)Pressure (atm)
Alkali hydrolysis300–350~10
Cumene oxidation70–801 (atmospheric)

Solved Example (Cumene process)

Calculate the mass of phenol obtained from $10\,\text{g}$ of cumene ($M_{\text{cumene}}=120.19\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$) assuming 100 % conversion.

\[\text{Moles of cumene}=\frac{10}{120.19}=0.0832\,\text{mol}\]

One mole of cumene yields one mole of phenol ($M_{\text{phenol}}=94.11\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$).

\[\text{Mass of phenol}=0.0832\times94.11=7.83\,\text{g}\]

Thus, $10\,\text{g}$ cumene can theoretically give $7.8\,\text{g}$ phenol.
long_notes.Methods of Preparation of Ethers (e.g.,:
Definition: Ethers are compounds having an alkoxy group ($-OR$) bonded to another carbon atom ($R'-O-R$). General formula: $R-O-R'$ where $R$ and $R'$ may be alkyl or aryl.

1. Williamson Ether Synthesis

  • Reaction: $R-O^-\;(\text{alkoxide}) + R'X \rightarrow R-O-R' + X^-$
  • Alkoxide is prepared by treating alcohol with Na or K metal: $R-OH + 2\,\text{Na} \rightarrow R-O^-Na^+ + NaH$
  • Best for primary alkyl halides; secondary/tertiary give elimination.
  • Typical conditions: anhydrous ether, reflux, inert atmosphere.
ReagentCondition
$R-OH$ + Na/Kdry $\\text{THF}$, $0-25^\circ\text{C}$
$R'X$ (primary)reflux $\\text{ether}$, $50-80^\circ\text{C}$

2. Acid‑catalyzed Dehydration of Alcohols

  • Reaction: $2\,R-OH \xrightarrow[\\text{conc. }H_2SO_4]{\\Delta} R-O-R + H_2O$
  • Effective for symmetrical ethers (e.g., di‑ethyl ether) and phenols.
  • Requires strong acid, temperature $140-180^\circ\text{C}$; higher temperature leads to alkenes.

Solved Example

Prepare ethyl phenyl ether using Williamson method.

  1. Generate phenoxide: $C_6H_5OH + Na \rightarrow C_6H_5O^-Na^+ + \frac{1}{2}H_2$
  2. React with ethyl bromide: $C_6H_5O^-Na^+ + C_2H_5Br \rightarrow C_6H_5-O-C_2H_5 + NaBr$
  3. Yield $\approx 78\%$; product confirmed by $\\text{m.p.}=-$ (liquid) and IR $\\nu_{C-O}\approx 1100\\,\\text{cm}^{-1}$.

Key Points for Exams

  • Use primary halides for Williamson; avoid steric hindrance.
  • Dehydration gives symmetrical ethers; control temperature to prevent side reactions.
  • Write balanced equations with correct stoichiometry and state symbols.
long_notes.Physical and Chemical Properties of Alco:
Definition: Alcohols are organic compounds containing a hydroxyl group (–OH) attached to a saturated carbon atom. General formula $C_nH_{2n+2}O$ (for acyclic, non‑cyclic primary, secondary, tertiary).

Physical properties

  • Boiling point (BP) is higher than corresponding alkanes due to H‑bonding.
  • BP trend: $BP_{primary} > BP_{secondary} > BP_{tertiary}$ because steric hindrance reduces H‑bonding ability.
  • Density: $1.0\text{–}1.1\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ (higher than water for most low‑molecular alcohols).
AlcoholStructureBP (°C)
Methanol$CH_3OH$$64.7$
Ethanol$CH_3CH_2OH$$78.4$
2‑Propanol$CH_3CHOHCH_3$$82.5$
tert‑Butanol$(CH_3)_3COH$$82.2$

Chemical properties (oxidation)

  • Primary alcohols → aldehydes → carboxylic acids (or further to CO2).
  • Secondary alcohols → ketones.
  • Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under mild conditions.

Key oxidation equations

  • Primary: $RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{[O]} RCHO$ (mild) ; $RCHO \xrightarrow{[O]} RCOOH$ (strong).
  • Secondary: $R_2CHOH \xrightarrow{[O]} R_2C=O$.

Example

Oxidation of ethanol with acidic $KMnO_4$:

$$CH_3CH_2OH + 2[O] \rightarrow CH_3COOH + H_2O$$

Steps: ethanol → acetaldehyde (intermediate) → acetic acid. The reaction is carried out at $80\text{–}100^\circ\text{C}$, and the amount of $KMnO_4$ required is calculated using $n_{KMnO_4}=2n_{ethanol}$.
long_notes.Physical and Chemical Properties of Phen:
Phenol (C6H5OH) is a weakly acidic aromatic compound containing a hydroxyl group directly attached to a benzene ring.

Acidity

  • Phenol ionises in water: $C_6H_5OH \rightleftharpoons C_6H_5O^- + H^+$.
  • Acid dissociation constant: $K_a = \frac{[C_6H_5O^-][H^+]}{[C_6H_5OH]}$ (dimensionless).
  • pKa = $-\log_{10}K_a$; for phenol $pK_a \approx 10$.
  • Acidity is enhanced by electron‑withdrawing groups (e.g., –NO2) and reduced by electron‑donating groups (e.g., –CH3).

Physical Properties

PropertyValue
Melting point$-11.5^\circ\text{C}$
Boiling point$182^\circ\text{C}$
Density (20°C)$1.07\,\text{g cm}^{-3}$
Solubility in water$8.3\,\text{g L}^{-1}$

Electrophilic Substitution

  • The –OH group is strongly activating and ortho/para directing due to resonance donation of lone‑pair electrons.
  • Typical reactions: nitration, sulfonation, halogenation give mainly o‑ and p‑substituted products.
  • Example (nitration): $C_6H_5OH + HNO_3 \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} \text{ortho- and para‑nitrophenol} + H_2O$.

Solved Example

Calculate the pH of a $0.01\,\text{M}$ phenol solution. Given $K_a = 1.0\times10^{-10}$.

  1. Assume $x = [H^+] = [C_6H_5O^-]$ and $[C_6H_5OH] \approx 0.01 - x \approx 0.01$.
  2. From $K_a = \frac{x^2}{0.01}$, $x = \sqrt{K_a\times0.01}=\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-12}}=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{M}$.
  3. pH $= -\log_{10}x = -\log_{10}(1.0\times10^{-6}) = 6.0$.

Thus a dilute phenol solution is mildly acidic (pH ≈ 6).
long_notes.Physical and Chemical Properties of Ethe:
Definition: Ethers are a class of organic compounds having an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups, represented as $R-O-R'$.

Physical Properties

PropertyTypical Value/Trend
Boiling pointLower than corresponding alcohols; $< 100^\circ\text{C}$ for most simple ethers
Solubility in waterIncreases with decreasing carbon chain; $R-O-R'$ (C \le 2) miscible
PolarityDipole moment $\mu = q \times d$ (\approx $1.5$–$2.0$ D); non‑hydrogen‑bonding
Dielectric constant~$4.5$–$5.0$ (dimensionless)

Chemical Properties

  • Cleavage by hydrogen halides: $R-O-R' + HX \rightarrow R-X + R'-OH$ (if $R$ is primary, $R'$ tertiary, etc.).
  • Cleavage by hot concentrated $H_2SO_4$: yields alcohols and alkyl sulfates.
  • Reaction with sodium metal: $R-O-R' + 2Na \rightarrow R-Na + R'-ONa$ (formation of alkoxides).
  • Oxidation of allylic/benzylic ethers gives carbonyl compounds.

Key Formula

Dipole moment: $\mu = q \times d$ (SI: C·m; 1 D = $3.33564 \times 10^{-30}$ C·m).

Solved Example

Complete the cleavage of $0.50\ \text{mol}$ diethyl ether ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-O-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) with hydroiodic acid.

Reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-O-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + HI \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2I + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2OH$.

From stoichiometry, $1\ \text{mol}$ ether requires $1\ \text{mol}$ $HI$. Hence moles of $HI$ needed = $0.50\ \text{mol}$. Mass of $HI$ = $0.50 \times 127.9\ \text{g mol}^{-1}=63.95\ \text{g}$.
long_notes.Important Uses of Alcohols, Phenols and:
Alcohols – organic compounds containing a hydroxyl group $-OH$ attached to a saturated carbon atom. General formula $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$.

Phenols – aromatic compounds where $-OH$ is directly bonded to a benzene ring. General formula $C_6H_5OH$.

Ethers – compounds having an oxygen atom linked to two alkyl or aryl groups, general formula $R-O-R'$.

  • Industrial uses
    • Alcohols: solvent (e.g., $CH_3CH_2OH$), antifreeze ($C_2H_5OH$), raw material for ethyl acetate, acetic acid, and polymers.
    • Phenols: production of bis‑phenol A, phenolic resins, disinfectants, and pharmaceuticals.
    • Ethers: diethyl ether as a laboratory solvent and anesthetic; MTBE as gasoline octane enhancer.
  • Daily life
    • Alcohols: beverages, hand sanitizers, cosmetics.
    • Phenols: antiseptic creams, oral care products.
    • Ethers: flavoring agents, propellants in aerosol cans.

Key formula – Combustion of an alcohol:

ReactionBalanced equation
General$C_nH_{2n+1}OH + \\frac{3n+1}{2} O_2 \\rightarrow n CO_2 + (n+1) H_2O$

Solved Example:

Calculate the mass of ethanol required to produce $50\,\text{g}$ of ethyl acetate ($C_4H_8O_2$) via esterification with acetic acid. Reaction: $CH_3CH_2OH + CH_3COOH \\rightarrow CH_3COOCH_2CH_3 + H_2O$.

Steps:

  1. Molar mass of ethyl acetate = $88\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. Moles needed = $\\frac{50}{88}=0.568\,\text{mol}$.
  2. Stoichiometry: 1 mol ethanol gives 1 mol ethyl acetate → need $0.568\,\text{mol}$ ethanol.
  3. Molar mass of ethanol = $46\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. Mass = $0.568 \times 46 = 26.1\,\text{g}$.

Thus $26\,\text{g}$ of ethanol is sufficient (theoretical yield).

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Alcohol: Organic compound containing a hydroxyl group ($-OH$) attached to a saturated carbon atom.
  • Phenol: Aromatic compound where $-OH$ is directly bonded to a benzene ring ($C_{6}H_{5}OH$).
  • Ethers: Compounds having an oxygen atom singly bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups ($R-O-R'$).
  • Primary, Secondary, Tertiary Alcohols: Classification based on the number of carbon atoms attached to the carbon bearing $-OH$.
  • Markovnikov’s Rule: In addition of HX to unsymmetrical alkenes, hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, and X adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens.
  • Anti‑Markovnikov addition (peroxides present): HBr adds opposite to Markovnikov’s rule.
  • IUPAC Nomenclature: Alcohols – suffix “‑ol”; Phenols – suffix “‑phenol” or “‑ol” as a substituent; Ethers – “alkoxy‑alkane” or “alkyl alkyl ether”.
  • Physical trends: Boiling point $\uparrow$ with increase in molecular weight and hydrogen‑bonding ability (alcohol $>$ phenol $>$ ether).

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Quick recap

  • Alcohols: $-OH$ on sp³ carbon; phenols: $-OH$ on aromatic carbon; ethers: $R-O-R'$.
  • Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes then acids; secondary to ketones; tertiary resist oxidation.
  • Phenols are weak acids ($pK_a \approx 10$) due to resonance stabilization of phenoxide ion.
  • Ethers are relatively inert; undergo cleavage with strong acids (e.g., $R-O-R' + HBr \rightarrow RBr + R'OH$).

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Confusing phenol with alcohol – remember phenol’s $-OH$ is attached to a benzene ring, not a saturated carbon.
  • Using Markovnikov’s rule for HBr in presence of peroxides – it becomes anti‑Markovnikov.
  • Incorrect IUPAC naming of ethers – avoid “alkyl ether”; use “alkoxy‑alkane” or list both alkyl groups alphabetically.
  • Assuming all alcohols are soluble in water – solubility drops sharply after $C_4$ due to loss of hydrogen‑bonding dominance.

numericals.question: An unknown alcohol of formula C$_x$H$_y$O gives 0.55 g of H$_2$O on complete combustion of 1.00 g sample. Determine its molecular formula.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Sample mass = 1.00 g, H$_2$O produced = 0.55 g.

Formula: Mass of H = $\\frac{\text{mass of H}_2\text{O}\times2}{18}$; Mass of O = $\\frac{\text{mass of H}_2\text{O}\times16}{18}$.

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Mass of H = $\\frac{0.55\times2}{18}=0.0611\text{ g}$.
  2. Mass of O = $\\frac{0.55\times16}{18}=0.4889\text{ g}$.
  3. Mass of C = 1.00 g – 0.0611 g – 0.4889 g = 0.4500 g.
  4. Moles: $n_{\text{C}}=\\frac{0.4500}{12}=0.0375\text{ mol}$, $n_{\text{H}}=\\frac{0.0611}{1}=0.0611\text{ mol}$, $n_{\text{O}}=\\frac{0.4889}{16}=0.0306\text{ mol}$.
  5. Divide by the smallest mole value (0.0306): C = 1.23 ≈ 1, H = 2.00 ≈ 2, O = 1.

Result: Empirical formula = C$_1$H$_2$O. Molecular weight $M = \frac{12+2+16}{0.0306}=74\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, which corresponds to C$_4$H$_{10}$O (butanol).

numericals.question: Calculate the boiling point elevation ($\Delta T_b$) when 5.0 g of ethylene glycol (C$_2$H$_6$O$_2$) is dissolved in 100 g of water. $K_b$(water) = 0.512 °C kg mol$^{-1}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $m$ = 5.0 g, $M_{\text{ethylene glycol}}$ = 62.07 g mol$^{-1}$, $\text{mass of solvent}$ = 0.100 kg, $K_b$ = 0.512 °C kg mol$^{-1}$.

Formula: $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$ where $m = \frac{\text{moles solute}}{\text{kg solvent}}$ and $i=1$ for nonelectrolyte.

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Moles of ethylene glycol = $\\frac{5.0}{62.07}=0.0805\text{ mol}$.
  2. Molality $m = \frac{0.0805}{0.100}=0.805\text{ mol kg}^{-1}$.
  3. $\Delta T_b = 1\times0.512\times0.805 = 0.412\text{ °C}$.

Final Answer: Boiling point elevation $\Delta T_b = 0.41\text{ °C}$.

pyq.question: Write the IUPAC name of the compound $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Identify the functional group as alcohol.
1 mark: Correct IUPAC name – ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).

pyq.question: State one physical property that distinguishes phenols from aliphatic alcohols.
pyq.answer_html: Phenols have a higher boiling point than comparable aliphatic alcohols due to stronger hydrogen‑bonding caused by the aromatic ring’s electron‑withdrawing effect.

pyq.question: Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Phenol ionises to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$.
1 mark: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance – the negative charge is delocalised over the aromatic ring ($\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}\,$ each ortho and para carbon).
1 mark: The aromatic ring exerts an –I effect, withdrawing electron density and further stabilising the anion, making phenol ($pK_a\approx10$) stronger than ethanol ($pK_a\approx16$).

pyq.question: Write the mechanism of the Williamson ether synthesis and mention the condition required for its success.
pyq.answer_html:
Step 1: $\text{R–X} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{R}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{X}^-$ (formation of alkoxide).
Step 2: $\text{R}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{R'–X} \rightarrow \text{R–O–R'} + \text{NaX}$ (SN2 attack).
Condition: Both alkyl halide and alkoxide must be primary (or methyl) to avoid elimination; a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone) is preferred.

pyq.question: Write the balanced equation for the acid‑catalysed dehydration of 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol to give an ether. Mention the type of reaction and the conditions required.
pyq.answer_html:
Reaction type: Acid‑catalysed intermolecular dehydration (ether formation).
Balanced equation:
$\displaystyle 2\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow[\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{140-150\,°C}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{O}\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
Conditions: Conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, temperature $140-150\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, removal of water to shift equilibrium.

pyq.question: Discuss the industrial preparation of phenol and comment on the significance of the cumene process.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Phenol is produced mainly by the cumene (Hock) process.
2 marks: Steps – (i) Alkylation of benzene with propylene to give cumene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$).
(ii) Oxidation of cumene with $\text{O}_2$ to cumene hydroperoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3)_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3)_2\text{OOH}$).
(iii) Acid‑catalysed cleavage of hydroperoxide to phenol and acetone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3)_2\text{OOH} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CO}$).
2 marks: Significance – Provides phenol and acetone simultaneously; both are high‑value chemicals. The process uses inexpensive raw materials (benzene, propylene, air) and gives high yield (~95%). It is economically and environmentally favourable compared to the older chlorination‑hydrolysis route.

mcq.q: What is the IUPAC name of $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}$?
mcq.explain: The longest chain containing the –OH group has two carbon atoms; the suffix –anol gives ethanol.

mcq.q: Which of the following compounds has the highest boiling point?
mcq.explain: Boiling point increases with molecular weight and hydrogen‑bonding ability; 1‑butanol (four‑carbon primary alcohol) boils higher than the others.

mcq.q: Primary alcohols are oxidised by $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ to give:
mcq.explain: Under acidic conditions $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ oxidises primary alcohols directly to carboxylic acids.

mcq.q: Phenol is more acidic than aliphatic alcohols because:
options: The phenoxide ion is resonance stabilised
Phenol has a larger atomic radius
mcq.explain: Deprotonation of phenol yields phenoxide ion, whose negative charge is delocalised over the aromatic ring, increasing acidity.

mcq.q: When $\mathrm{R-O-R'}$ (asymmetric ether) is treated with $\mathrm{HI}$, the major product is:
mcq.explain: Iodide attacks the less hindered carbon; the C–O bond cleaves to give the primary alkyl iodide and the corresponding alcohol.

mcq.q: In the Williamson ether synthesis, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br}$ reacts with $\mathrm{NaOCH_2CH_3}$ to give:
mcq.explain: The alkoxide $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2O^-}$ attacks the primary bromide, forming $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3}$ via an $S_N2$ mechanism.

mcq.q: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give:
mcq.explain: Bromination of phenol occurs at the ortho and para positions, producing a white precipitate of 2,4‑dibromophenol.

mcq.q: Ethylene oxide is primarily used for the industrial production of:
mcq.explain: Ring‑opening polymerisation of ethylene oxide yields polyethylene glycol (PEG).

mcq.q:
Assertion (A): Phenol is more acidic than aliphatic alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance stabilised.
Reason (R): In phenol, the –OH group is attached directly to an sp$^2$‑hybridised carbon which withdraws electron density.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Both statements are true and the resonance delocalisation of the phenoxide ion explains the increased acidity of phenol.

mcq.q: 1,2‑Ethylene glycol belongs to which class of compounds?
mcq.explain: Both –OH groups are attached to adjacent carbon atoms, each bearing one –OH; thus it is a secondary diol.
