long_notes.Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Et:
Definition: Alcohols, phenols and ethers are organic compounds containing –OH or –O– groups attached to saturated carbon atoms.

Key Points for Nomenclature

  • Parent chain is the longest continuous carbon chain containing the –OH (alcohol) or –O– (ether) group.
  • Numbering starts from the end nearest to the principal functional group; the –OH gets the lowest possible locant.
  • Suffix “‑$\\text{ol}$” for alcohols, “‑$\\text{phenol}$” for phenols; ethers are named using the “alkoxy‑” prefix (e.g., $\\text{methoxy}$‑propane).
  • Multiple –OH groups: “‑$\\text{diol}$”, “‑$\\text{triol}$”, etc., with locants.
  • When –OH is attached to an aromatic ring, the compound is named as a phenol; the aromatic ring is treated as a substituted benzene.
Number of –OHSuffix
1$\\text{ol}$
2$\\text{diol}$
3$\\text{triol}$

General formula: $C_{n}H_{2n+2}O$ for saturated alcohols; molecular weight $M=\sum M_{i}$ (g·mol$^{-1}$).

Example (Solved): Name $CH_{3}CH(CH_{3})CH_{2}OH$.

Step 1: Longest chain containing –OH has 3 carbon atoms → propan‑.

Step 2: –OH receives the lowest locant → 1‑propanol.

Step 3: Methyl substituent on C‑2 → 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol.

Answer: 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol.
long_notes.Methods of Preparation of Alcohols:
Methods of Preparation of Alcohols – Alcohols are mainly obtained by (i) addition of water to unsaturated compounds, (ii) reduction of carbonyl compounds, (iii) Grignard reaction, (iv) fermentation, and (v) hydrolysis of alkyl halides.

  • Acid‑catalysed hydration of alkenes: $R-CH=CH_2 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4, 300^\circ C} R-CH_2-CH_2-OH$.
  • Hydroboration‑oxidation: $R-CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{BH_3, THF} R-CH_2-CH_2-BH_2 \xrightarrow{H_2O_2/NaOH} R-CH_2-CH_2-OH$ (anti‑Markovnikov).
  • Reduction of carbonyl compounds: $R-CHO + H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 150^\circ C} R-CH_2OH$; $R_2C=O + H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni} R_2CHOH$.
  • Grignard reaction: $R-MgX + R'CHO \xrightarrow{Et_2O} R-R'CH(OH)R$ (primary/secondary alcohol).
  • Fermentation: $C_6H_{12}O_6 \xrightarrow{yeast} 2 C_2H_5OH + 2 CO_2$ (ethanol).
MethodRepresentative Reaction
Acidic hydration$C_2H_4 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4, 300^\circ C} C_2H_5OH$
Hydroboration‑oxidation$CH_2=CHCH_3 \xrightarrow{BH_3} CH_3CH_2CH_2BH_2 \xrightarrow{H_2O_2/NaOH} CH_3CH_2CH_2OH$
Reduction of aldehyde$CH_3CHO + H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni} CH_3CH_2OH$

Solved Example: Prepare ethanol by hydration of ethene. 10.0 g ethene ($M=28.05\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) is reacted. Moles of ethene $=\frac{10.0}{28.05}=0.357\,\text{mol}$. Theoretical ethanol $=0.357\times46.07=16.4\,\text{g}$. If 14.0 g ethanol is obtained, % yield $=\frac{14.0}{16.4}\times100=85.4\%$. Key formula: $\%\,\text{yield}=\frac{\text{actual mass}}{\text{theoretical mass}}\times100$ (SI units: mass in g, temperature in $^\circ C$, pressure in $\text{atm}$).
long_notes.Methods of Preparation of Phenols:
Definition: Phenols are aromatic compounds in which a hydroxyl group is directly bonded to a benzene ring, formula $C_6H_5OH$.

Key Methods of Preparation

  • Cumene (Isopropylbenzene) Process: Alkylation of benzene to cumene, oxidation to cumene hydroperoxide, acid‑catalysed cleavage giving phenol and acetone.
    Overall: $C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2 + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{acid}} C_6H_5OH + (CH_3)_2CO$.
  • Hydrolysis of Phenylmagnesium Bromide: $C_6H_5MgBr + H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_5OH + Mg(OH)Br$ (dry ether, $0\!\,^\circ C$).
  • Diazonium Salt Hydrolysis: $C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} C_6H_5OH + N_2 + HCl$ (70–80$\,^{\circ}C$, $\approx 1\,atm$).
  • Fusion of Sodium Phenoxide: $C_6H_5SO_3H + NaOH \xrightarrow{\text{fusion 300$\,^{\circ}C$}} C_6H_5ONa + Na_2SO_3$, then acidification gives phenol.
  • Hydrolysis of Phenyl Acetate: $C_6H_5OCOCH_3 + NaOH \xrightarrow{\text{reflux}} C_6H_5OH + CH_3COONa$.
  • Substitution of Phenyl Halides: $C_6H_5Cl + NaOH \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH, $\approx 200\,^{\circ}C$}} C_6H_5OH + NaCl$ (requires strong nucleophile).

Summary Table

MethodReagentsConditionsRemarks
Cumene ProcessCumene, $O_2$, $H_2SO_4$300–350$\,^{\circ}C$, 1–2 atmIndustrial, high yield
Grignard HydrolysisPhenylMgBr, $H_2O$Dry ether, $0\!\,^\circ C$Laboratory scale
Diazonium HydrolysisPhenyl diazonium chloride, $H_2O$80$\,^{\circ}C$, $1\,atm$Gives $N_2$ gas

Solved Example (Cumene Process)

Calculate mass of phenol obtained from $150\,g$ cumene ($C_9H_{12}$) with $85\%$ yield.

Molar mass $M_{cumene}=120\,g\,mol^{-1}$, $M_{phenol}=94\,g\,mol^{-1}$.
\[n_{cumene}=\frac{150}{120}=1.25\,mol\]
Stoichiometry: 1 mol cumene → 1 mol phenol.
\[m_{theoretical}=1.25\times94=117.5\,g\]
Actual mass $=117.5\times0.85=99.9\,g\approx100\,g$.

SI Units: Mass – $g$, Temperature – $\,^{\circ}C$, Pressure – $atm$, Yield – $\%$.
long_notes.Methods of Preparation of Ethers:
Definition: An ether is a class of organic compounds having the general formula $R\! -\! O\! -\! R'$ where $R$ and $R'$ are alkyl or aryl groups. The oxygen atom is divalent and links two carbon chains.

Major methods of preparation (exam‑oriented):

  • Williamson ether synthesis: Alkoxide ion $RO^-$ reacts with a primary alkyl halide $R'X$ under SN2 conditions.
    $$R O^- + R' X \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\text{Na}} R O R' + X^-$$
    Key points: $R'$ must be primary (or methyl); $R$ may be primary, secondary or phenyl; no elimination side‑reaction.
  • Acid‑catalysed dehydration of alcohols: Two molecules of a primary alcohol condense \in the presence of concentrated $H_2SO_4$ at $140\!\,^\circ\!C$.
    $$2\,R\! -\! OH \xrightarrow[\text{140\,°C}]{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} R\! -\! O\! -\! R + H_2O$$
    Works best for symmetrical ethers (e.g., diethyl ether).
  • Dehydration of vicinal diols: Heating a 1,2‑diol with $H_2SO_4$ at $180\!\,^\circ\!C$ gives a cyclic ether (tetrahydrofuran from 1,4‑butanediol).
    $$HO\! -\! (CH_2)_n \! -\! OH \xrightarrow[\text{180\,°C}]{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} \text{cyclic ether} + H_2O$$

SI units \to remember: Temperature $\text{K}$ (or $\!^\circ\!C$), pressure $\text{Pa}$ (or $\text{atm}$), concentration $\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.

Solved example (1 mark – 2 marks): Prepare diethyl ether from ethanol.

  1. Take $50\,\text{mL}$ of absolute ethanol \in a dry flask.
  2. Add $5\,\text{mL}$ of conc. $H_2SO_4$ dropwise while maintaining the temperature below $140\!\,^\circ\!C$.
  3. Heat the mixture at $140\!\,^\circ\!C$ for $30\,\text{min}$; collect the ether vapour by distillation (boiling point $34.6\!\,^\circ\!C$).
  4. Dry the distillate over anhydrous $CaCl_2$ and measure the yield.

Overall reaction:
$$2\,CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow[\text{140\,°C}]{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3 + H_2O$$

Key take‑away: For unsymmetrical ethers, Williamson synthesis is preferred; for symmetrical ethers, acid‑catalysed dehydration is the quickest laboratory method.
long_notes.Physical and Chemical Properties of Alco:
Alcohols – Definition: Organic compounds containing one or more hydroxyl ($-\\mathrm{OH}$) groups attached to a saturated carbon atom.

Physical Properties

  • Boiling point: higher than corresponding hydrocarbons due to H‑bonding. Approx. $\\Delta T_b = K_b \\cdot m$ where $K_b$ is ebullioscopic constant (unit $\\,^{\\circ}\\mathrm{C\\,kg\\,mol^{-1}}$).
  • Density: $0.79-0.88\\,\\mathrm{g\\,cm^{-3}}$ at $20\\,^{\\circ}\\mathrm{C}$.
  • Refractive index ($n_D$): $1.33-1.48$.
  • Solubility: miscible with water if $\\le 3$ carbon atoms; decreases with chain length.

Chemical Properties

  • Oxidation: primary alcohol $\\xrightarrow{[O]}$ aldehyde $\\rightarrow$ acid; secondary alcohol $\\rightarrow$ ketone; tertiary alcohol resistant.
  • Dehydration (acid catalysed): $\\mathrm{RCH_2CH_2OH \\xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} RCH=CH_2 + H_2O}$.
  • Esterification: $\\mathrm{RCH_2OH + R'COOH \\xrightarrow{H^+} R'COOR + H_2O}$.
  • Substitution (SN1/SN2) with $\\mathrm{HX}$ or $\\mathrm{ROH}$.
PropertyExpression / Value
Boiling‑point elevation$\\Delta T_b = K_b \\cdot m$
Ethanol $K_b$$0.52\\,^{\\circ}\\mathrm{C\\,kg\\,mol^{-1}}$
Density (20°C)$0.789\\,\\mathrm{g\\,cm^{-3}}$ (ethanol)

Solved Example

Calculate the mass of ethanol required to raise the boiling point of $500\\,\\mathrm{g}$ of ethanol by $0.5\\,^{\\circ}\\mathrm{C}$. Use $K_b = 0.52\\,^{\\circ}\\mathrm{C\\,kg\\,mol^{-1}}$ and $M_{ethanol}=46.07\\,\\mathrm{g\\,mol^{-1}}$.

  1. Molality needed: $m = \\frac{\\Delta T_b}{K_b}=\\frac{0.5}{0.52}=0.962\\,\\mathrm{mol\\,kg^{-1}}$.
  2. Mass of solvent (ethanol) = $0.500\\,\\mathrm{kg}$, so moles of solute $= m \\times 0.500 = 0.481\\,\\mathrm{mol}$.
  3. Mass of solute = $0.481\\,\\mathrm{mol}\\times 46.07\\,\\mathrm{g\\,mol^{-1}} = 22.2\\,\\mathrm{g}$.

Thus $22\\,\\mathrm{g}$ of a non‑volatile solute (e.g., glucose) would raise the boiling point by $0.5\\,^{\\circ}\\mathrm{C}$.
long_notes.Physical and Chemical Properties of Phen:
Definition: Phenol (hydroxybenzene) is an aromatic compound with the formula $C_6H_5OH$ where a hydroxyl group is directly attached to a benzene ring.

Physical Properties (typical values):

  • Melting point: $40.5^\circ\text{C}$
  • Boiling point: $182^\circ\text{C}$
  • Density: $1.07\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$
  • Solubility in water: $8.3\ \text{g per 100 mL}$ (at $25^\circ\text{C}$)
  • Acidic character: weak acid, $pK_a \approx 10$

Key Chemical Properties:

  • Acidity: $C_6H_5OH \rightleftharpoons C_6H_5O^- + H^+$; $K_a = 10^{-pK_a} \approx 1.0\\times10^{-10}$.
  • Reaction with NaOH: $C_6H_5OH + NaOH \\rightarrow C_6H_5ONa + H_2O$ (forms phenoxide salt).
  • Electrophilic substitution: ortho-/para-directing; e.g., bromination gives $2,4,6$‑tribromophenol.
  • Oxidation: strong oxidants (e.g., $KMnO_4$) convert phenol to $p$‑benzoquinone.
  • Formation of ethers: phenol + alkyl halide $\\xrightarrow{NaOH}$ alkyl phenyl ether.
Compound$pK_a$Acid Strength
Phenol$10$Weak
Carboxylic acid (e.g., acetic acid)$4.8$Stronger

Solved Example: Calculate the pH of a $0.010\ \text{M}$ phenol solution.

Given $K_a = 1.0\\times10^{-10}$, let $x$ be $[H^+]$ formed.

$K_a = \\frac{x^2}{c-x} \approx \\frac{x^2}{c}$ (since $x \ll c$). Hence $x = \\sqrt{K_a c} = \\sqrt{1.0\\times10^{-10}\\times0.010} = 1.0\\times10^{-6}\ \text{M}$.

pH $= -\\log x = -\\log(1.0\\times10^{-6}) = 6.00$.

Thus a dilute phenol solution is only mildly acidic.
long_notes.Physical and Chemical Properties of Ethe:
Definition: An ether is an organic compound containing an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups, general formula $R\!{-}\!O\!{-}\!R'$.

Physical properties

  • Boiling point ($T_b$) lies between corresponding alcohols and alkanes; increases with molecular weight and polarity.
  • Solubility: Low in water due to weak hydrogen‑bonding; soluble in organic solvents.
  • Polarity: Dipole moment ($\mu$) arises from C–O–C angle (~$110^\circ$). Typical values $\mu = 1.5\text{–}5.0\,\text{D}$ (1 D $=3.33564\times10^{-30}\,\text{C·m}$).
  • Density: $0.70\text{–}0.85\,\text{g·cm}^{-3}$.

Key formulae

  • Dipole moment: $\mu = q\,d$ where $q$ is effective charge separation and $d$ distance.
  • Boiling‑point elevation: $\Delta T_b = K_b\,i\,m$ (SI: $K_b$ in K·kg·mol$^{-1}$, $m$ in mol·kg$^{-1}$).

Chemical properties

  • Cleavage with HX: $R\!{-}\!O\!{-}\!R' + HX \rightarrow R\!{-}\!X + R'\!{-}\!OH$ (e.g., $\text{CH}_3\!{-}\!O\!{-}\!\text{CH}_3 + HBr \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\!{-}\!Br + \text{CH}_3\!{-}\!OH$).
  • Oxidation: Strong oxidizers convert ethers to carbonyl compounds (e.g., $\text{R}_2\!O + \text{[O]} \rightarrow \text{RCHO}$ for methyl ethyl ether).
  • Peroxide formation: $\text{R}_2\!O + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{ROOR}$ – hazardous.

Typical values (SI units)

PropertyTypical rangeUnit
Boiling point30–150°C
Dipole moment1.5–5.0D (1 D = $3.33564\times10^{-30}$ C·m)
Density0.70–0.85g·cm$^{-3}$

Solved example (dipole moment)

Calculate the dipole moment of diethyl ether if the effective charge separation is $q = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$ and the distance $d = 1.2\times10^{-10}\,\text{m}$.

Solution:

  • $\mu = q\,d = (1.6\times10^{-19})(1.2\times10^{-10}) = 1.92\times10^{-29}\,\text{C·m}$
  • Convert to Debye: $\mu_{\text{D}} = \dfrac{1.92\times10^{-29}}{3.33564\times10^{-30}} \approx 5.8\,\text{D}$

Thus, diethyl ether has a dipole moment of approximately $5.8\,\text{D}$, explaining its moderate polarity and solubility behaviour.
long_notes.Uses and Applications:
Definitions

  • Alcohol: organic compound containing a hydroxyl group $-OH$ attached to a saturated carbon; general formula $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$.
  • Phenol: aromatic compound where $-OH$ is directly bonded to a benzene ring; formula $C_6H_5OH$.
  • Ether: compound with an oxygen atom linking two alkyl or aryl groups; general formula $R-O-R'$.

Key Uses & Applications

CompoundMajor Applications
AlcoholsSolvent (e.g., ethanol), antiseptic (e.g., isopropanol), fuel additive (e.g., methanol), raw material for esters, polymers.
PhenolsDisinfectant (e.g., carbolic acid), precursor to plastics (Bakelite), pharmaceuticals (e.g., aspirin), antioxidants.
EthersOrganic solvent (diethyl ether), anesthetic, gasoline additive (MTBE), synthesis of polymers.

Typical Quantitative Relation

For solution preparation: $M = \dfrac{n}{V}$ where $M$ is molarity ($mol\,L^{-1}$), $n$ is amount of solute in moles, $V$ is volume in litres.

Solved Example

Prepare $500\;mL$ of $0.20\;M$ ethanol solution. Find mass of ethanol required (density $=0.789\;g\,mL^{-1}$, molar mass $=46.07\;g\,mol^{-1}$).

  1. Convert volume to litres: $V = 0.500\;L$.
  2. Calculate moles: $n = M \times V = 0.20 \times 0.500 = 0.10\;mol$.
  3. Mass: $m = n \times M_{r} = 0.10 \times 46.07 = 4.607\;g$.
  4. Volume of ethanol: $V_{eth} = \dfrac{m}{\rho} = \dfrac{4.607}{0.789} \approx 5.84\;mL$.

Thus $5.8\;mL$ of ethanol is diluted to $500\;mL$ to obtain the required solution.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Alcohol: Organic compound containing a hydroxyl group ($-OH$) attached to a saturated carbon atom.
  • Phenol: Aromatic compound where $-OH$ is directly bonded to a benzene ring.
  • Ethers: Compounds with an oxygen atom linked to two alkyl/aryl groups ($R-O-R'$).
  • Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols: Classified by the number of carbon atoms attached to the carbon bearing $-OH$ (1, 2 or 3 respectively).
  • Acidity order: Phenol $>$ Alcohol (due to resonance stabilisation of phenoxide ion).
  • Williamson Ether Synthesis (Law): Alkyl halide reacts with alkoxide ion to give ether; works best with primary halides.
  • Acid‑catalysed dehydration: Primary alcohols give alkenes; secondary give more substituted alkenes; tertiary may undergo rearrangement.
  • Oxidation rules: Primary $ ightarrow$ aldehyde $ ightarrow$ acid; secondary $ ightarrow$ ketone; tertiary $ ightarrow$ no reaction.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
• Remember the structural difference: phenol $-OH$ is attached to an aromatic carbon, alcohol $-OH$ to an sp$^3$ carbon.
  • In naming ethers, the smaller alkyl group is given first (e.g., methyl ethyl ether).
  • Do not confuse the dehydration product of a primary alcohol (often a mixture of alkenes) with the oxidation product (aldehyde).
  • Phenols are acidic ($pK_a \approx 10$) – a common error is treating them like neutral alcohols.
  • Williamson synthesis fails with secondary/tertiary halides due to elimination; always use primary halides.
  • When writing reactions, always show the catalyst (e.g., $H_2SO_4$, $Na$) and the stoichiometric by‑product (e.g., $NaX$, $H_2O$).
  • Common mistake in calculations: forgetting to convert mass of sample to the same unit before using % purity formula.

numericals.question: Calculate the number of moles of ethanol ($\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$) present in 46 g of the compound.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Mass of ethanol = $46\,\text{g}$

Formula: $n=\dfrac{m}{M}$ where $m$ is mass and $M$ is molar mass.

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Calculate molar mass of ethanol: $M=2(12)+6(1)+1(16)+1(1)=2\times12+6+16+1=46\,\text{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
  2. Apply the formula: $n=\dfrac{46\,\text{g}}{46\,\text{g\,mol^{-1}}}=1\,\text{mol}$.

Final Answer: $1\,\text{mol}$ of ethanol.

numericals.question: Find the percent composition by mass of carbon in phenol ($\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Molecular formula of phenol = $\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}$

Formula: $\%\,C = \dfrac{\text{mass of C in one mole}}{\text{molar mass of phenol}}\times100$

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Molar mass of phenol: $M=6(12)+6(1)+16+1=72+6+16+1=95\,\text{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
  2. Mass of carbon in one mole = $6\times12=72\,\text{g}$.
  3. $\%\,C = \dfrac{72}{95}\times100=75.79\%$ (rounded to two decimal places).

Final Answer: Phenol contains $\approx75.79\%$ carbon by mass.

numericals.question: A solution is prepared by dissolving 0.5 mol of diethyl ether ($\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2O}$) in 1 kg of water. Calculate the boiling point elevation of the solution. (K_b of water = $0.512\,\text{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$)
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $i=1$ (non‑electrolyte), $K_b=0.512\,\text{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$, $m=\dfrac{0.5\,\text{mol}}{1\,\text{kg}}=0.5\,\text{mol\,kg^{-1}}$

Formula: $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Substitute values: $\Delta T_b = 1\times0.512\times0.5=0.256\,\text{K}$.

Final Answer: The boiling point of the solution is raised by $0.256\,\text{K}$.

numericals.question: Determine the degree of unsaturation (DU) for the ether $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}$ (diethyl ether).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Molecular formula $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}$ (no N, no halogen).

Formula: $\text{DU}=\dfrac{2C+2-H}{2}$

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Insert values: $\text{DU}=\dfrac{2(4)+2-10}{2}=\dfrac{8+2-10}{2}=\dfrac{0}{2}=0$.

Final Answer: Diethyl ether has $0$ degrees of unsaturation (it is a saturated ether).

numericals.question: Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol using their $pK_a$ values (phenol $pK_a\approx10$, ethanol $pK_a\approx16$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $pK_a$(phenol) $\approx10$, $pK_a$(ethanol) $\approx16$.

Concept: Lower $pK_a$ $Rightarrow$ stronger acid. The acidity is related to the stability of the conjugate base.

Proof:

  1. Write the deprotonation reactions:
    Phenol: $\mathrm{C_6H_5OH \rightleftharpoons C_6H_5O^- + H^+}$
    Ethanol: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH \rightleftharpoons CH_3CH_2O^- + H^+}$
  2. The phenoxide ion ($\mathrm{C_6H_5O^-}$) is resonance‑stabilized, spreading the negative charge over the aromatic ring, whereas the ethoxide ion ($\mathrm{CH_3CH_2O^-}$) lacks such delocalisation.
  3. Greater stabilization of the conjugate base lowers the $\Delta G$ of deprotonation, giving a smaller $pK_a$.

Conclusion: Because phenol’s conjugate base is resonance‑stabilized, phenol is a stronger acid ($pK_a\approx10$) than ethanol ($pK_a\approx16$).

numericals.question: Two moles of ethanol are dehydrated in the presence of concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ at $140\,^{\circ}\text{C}$. Calculate the theoretical mass of diethyl ether ($\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2O}$) formed. (Molar mass of ethanol = $46\,\text{g\,mol^{-1}}$, molar mass of diethyl ether = $74\,\text{g\,mol^{-1}}$)
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $n_{\text{ethanol}}=2\,\text{mol}$, reaction: $2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH \rightarrow (C_2H_5)_2O + H_2O}$

Formula: From stoichiometry, $2\,\text{mol ethanol} \rightarrow 1\,\text{mol diethyl ether}$.

Step‑by‑Step Calculation:

  1. Moles of ether formed = $\dfrac{2\,\text{mol}}{2}=1\,\text{mol}$.
  2. Mass of ether = $n\times M = 1\,\text{mol}\times74\,\text{g\,mol^{-1}}=74\,\text{g}$.

Final Answer: The theoretical yield of diethyl ether is $74\,\text{g}$.

pyq.question: Write the general formula of a primary alcohol and name the compound $CH_3CH_2OH$.
pyq.answer_html:
General formula of a primary alcohol: $\text{C}_nH_{2n+1}OH$.

Compound $CH_3CH_2OH$ is ethanol.

pyq.question: State one method of preparation of phenol on an industrial scale.
pyq.answer_html:
Phenol is prepared by the cumene process:

  1. Alkylation of benzene with propylene to give cumene ($C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2$).
  2. Oxidation of cumene to cumene hydroperoxide.
  3. Acid‑catalysed cleavage of the hydroperoxide to give phenol and acetone.

pyq.question: Write the mechanism for the acid‑catalysed dehydration of a secondary alcohol $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3$ to give an alkene. Mention the role of the acid.
pyq.answer_html:
Steps:

  1. Protonation of the –OH group by $H^+$ forming $CH_3CH(OH_2)^+CH_3$ (makes a good leaving group).
  2. Loss of water to generate a secondary carbocation $CH_3CH^+CH_3$.
  3. Removal of a $ beta$‑hydrogen by a base (usually $H_2O$) gives the alkene $CH_3CH=CH_2$ and regenerates the acid.

Acid acts as a catalyst – it protonates the –OH and is regenerated in the last step.

pyq.question: Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol. Give their $pK_a$ values.
pyq.answer_html:
Phenol $pK_a \approx 10$, ethanol $pK_a \approx 16$.

Reasons:

  • The phenoxide ion is resonance‑stabilised over the aromatic ring, delocalising the negative charge.
  • In ethanol, the alkoxide ion has no such delocalisation; the charge remains localized on oxygen.
  • Inductive effect of the aromatic ring withdraws electron density, further stabilising phenoxide.

pyq.question: (a) Write the Williamson ether synthesis for preparing diethyl ether using ethanol and sodium ethoxide. (b) Why does phenol not give diethyl ether under the same conditions?
pyq.answer_html:
(a) Reaction:

$\text{CH}_3CH_2ONa + CH_3CH_2Br \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3 + NaBr$

Steps:

  1. Formation of sodium ethoxide: $CH_3CH_2OH + Na \rightarrow CH_3CH_2ONa + \frac{1}{2}H_2$.
  2. SN2 attack of $CH_3CH_2O^-$ on ethyl bromide gives diethyl ether.

(b) Phenol is a weak acid ($pK_a \approx 10$). In the presence of Na, it forms phenoxide ($C_6H_5O^-$) which is a poorer nucleophile toward primary alkyl halides because of resonance delocalisation; moreover, phenoxide prefers to undergo $S_NAr$ reactions rather than $S_N2$, so diethyl ether is not formed.

pyq.question: (a) Give the IUPAC name of $CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3$. (b) Predict the major product when it is refluxed with aqueous NaOH. Write a brief mechanism.
pyq.answer_html:
(a) IUPAC name: diethyl ether (systematic name: ethoxyethane).

(b) Reaction with aqueous NaOH (hydrolysis) gives ethanol:

$CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3 + NaOH \xrightarrow{\text{reflux}} CH_3CH_2OH + CH_3CH_2ONa$

Mechanism:

  1. OH$^-$ attacks the electrophilic carbon attached to oxygen (SN2).
  2. Cleavage of the C–O bond forms ethanol and ethoxide ion.
  3. Ethoxide ion is protonated by water to give a second molecule of ethanol.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the correct IUPAC name of $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH$?
mcq.explain: The longest chain containing the –OH group has four carbon atoms, giving the parent name butane; the –OH suffix changes it to butanol.

mcq.q: The primary oxidation product of a primary alcohol $R-CH_2OH$ is:
mcq.explain: Primary alcohols are oxidized first to aldehydes ($R-CHO$); further oxidation gives carboxylic acids.

mcq.q: In the Williamson ether synthesis, which combination of reagents is used?
mcq.explain: A primary alkyl halide ($R-X$) reacts with a sodium alkoxide ($R'ONa$) to give an ether $R-O-R'$ via an $S_N2$ mechanism.

mcq.q: The acid-catalyzed dehydration of $2$‑methyl‑1‑propanol yields:
mcq.explain: Dehydration of a secondary alcohol under acid gives the corresponding alkene; $2$‑methyl‑1‑propanol loses water to form isobutene ($CH_2=C(CH_3)_2$).

mcq.q: Which of the following ethers is most susceptible to cleavage by HI?
mcq.explain: Ethers with a tertiary alkyl group undergo rapid $S_N1$ cleavage; $tert$‑butyl methyl ether is cleaved faster than the others by HI.

mcq.q: The pK$_a$ of phenol is approximately:
mcq.explain: Phenol is a weak acid with $pK_a\approx10$, whereas aliphatic alcohols have $pK_a\approx16$.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): Phenol is more acidic than ethanol. Reason (R): The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance delocalization of the negative charge over the aromatic ring.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Phenol ($pK_a\approx10$) is indeed more acidic than ethanol ($pK_a\approx16$). The phenoxide ion’s negative charge is delocalized over the aromatic ring, stabilizing it and accounting for the higher acidity.

mcq.q: In the oxidation of a secondary alcohol $R_2CHOH$, the major product is:
mcq.explain: Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones; further oxidation is difficult under normal conditions.

mcq.q: Which of the following reactions illustrates the formation of an ether by the acid-catalyzed dehydration of two alcohol molecules?
mcq.explain: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of two ethanol molecules yields diethyl ether ($CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3$) and water.

long_notes.General introduction, classification and:
General introduction, classification and importance

  • Aldehydes: Organic compounds containing the carbonyl group attached to at least one hydrogen atom. General formula $RCHO$ where $R$ may be alkyl or aryl.
  • Ketones: Carbonyl group flanked by two carbon atoms. General formula $RCOR'$ ( $R$ and $R'$ can be identical or different).
  • Carboxylic acids: Contain the –$COOH$ (carboxyl) group. General formula $RCOOH$.

All three families are classified on the basis of the nature of $R$:

  • Aliphatic – $R$ is a straight‑chain or branched‑chain alkyl.
  • Aromatic – $R$ contains a phenyl or substituted phenyl ring.
  • Saturated vs. Unsaturated – Presence or absence of C=C or C≡C bonds in $R$.

Key physical trends (SI units): boiling point (K), density (kg·m$^{-3}$), dipole moment (D), p$K_a$ (dimensionless). The carbonyl group is polar ($\delta$ = $\pm$3.5 D) leading to higher boiling points than corresponding alkanes.

FamilyGeneral formulaIUPAC suffix
Aldehyde$RCHO$-al
Ketone$RCOR'$-one
Carboxylic acid$RCOOH$-oic acid

Importance

  • Industrial feed‑stocks: formaldehyde (resins), acetone (solvent), acetic acid (vinegar, ester production).
  • Biological roles: aldehydes in metabolic pathways, ketones as energy substrates, fatty acids as carboxylic acids.
  • Pharmaceutical precursors for drugs, fragrances and polymers.

Solved example (high‑yield)

Calculate the molar mass of acetaldehyde ($CH_3CHO$) and the % mass of carbon in it.

Solution:

$M_{CH_3CHO}=2(12.01)+4(1.008)+16.00=44.05\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Mass of carbon = $2\times12.01=24.02\,\text{g}$

\%C $=\frac{24.02}{44.05}\times100=54.5\%$ (rounded to 1 d.p.).

This type of calculation is frequently asked in NCERT‑based questions.
long_notes.Nomenclature and IUPAC naming rules for:
Definition – Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are oxygen‑containing functional groups. The general formulas are $R-CHO$, $R_1-CO-R_2$ and $R-COOH$ respectively.

  • Parent chain: longest continuous chain containing the functional group.
  • Numbering: give the carbon bearing the principal group the lowest possible locant.
  • Suffixes: –aldehyde → “$-al$”, –ketone → “$-one$”, –carboxylic acid → “$-oic\ acid$”.
Functional groupSuffixExample
Aldehyde$-al$ethanal
Ketone$-one$propan-2-one
Carboxylic acid$-oic\ acid$butanoic acid

Key rules

  • If both aldehyde and ketone are present, aldehyde gets priority; the ketone is named as a substituent using “oxo-”.
  • When a carboxylic acid and another functional group coexist, the acid suffix dominates; the other group is indicated as a prefix (e.g., hydroxy, chloro).
  • Multiple identical groups are indicated by di-, tri-, etc., with locants in ascending order.
  • For branched chains, use “-yl” substituent names (e.g., methyl, ethyl) placed alphabetically before the parent name.

Solved example

Name the compound: $CH_3CH_2CH(Cl)CH_2CHO$.

Solution: The longest chain containing the –CHO group has five carbons → parent “pentanal”. Numbering from the aldehyde carbon gives the chloro substituent at C-4. Hence the IUPAC name is 4-chloro-pentanal.

SI unit for molar mass: $g\cdot mol^{-1}$.
long_notes.Methods of preparation of aldehydes, ket:
Definition: Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are oxygen‑containing functional groups characterised by the carbonyl ($C=O$) moiety. In aldehydes the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen, in ketones to two carbon atoms, and in carboxylic acids to a hydroxyl group.

Key preparation methods (summary)

  • Oxidation of primary alcohols ($RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{[O]} RCHO$) – mild oxidants (PCC, $CrO_3$ in $CH_2Cl_2$) give aldehydes; stronger oxidants (KMnO$_4$, $K_2Cr_2O_7$) afford carboxylic acids.
  • Reduction of acid derivatives – acid chlorides ($RCOCl \xrightarrow{H_2,\ Pd/C}\ RCHO$ – Rosenmund) and esters ($RCOOR' \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4}\ RCH_2OH$) lead to aldehydes/ketones.
  • Hydration of alkynes – Markovnikov addition of water in presence of $HgSO_4$/$H_2SO_4$ yields methyl ketones ($RC\equiv CH \xrightarrow{H_2O,\ HgSO_4}\ RC(=O)CH_3$).
  • From nitriles – $RCN \xrightarrow{[H^+]\,\text{or}\,\text{hydrolysis}} RCOOH$ (carboxylic acids) or $RCN \xrightarrow{[H_2]\,\text{Pd/C}} RCHO$ (aldehydes).

Typical reagents & conditions

TargetStarting materialReagentConditions
AldehydePrimary alcoholPCC or $CrO_3$ in $CH_2Cl_2$0–25 °C, inert atmosphere
KetoneSecondary alcohol$Na_2Cr_2O_7$, $H_2SO_4$Reflux, 60–80 °C
Carboxylic acidPrimary alcoholKMnO$_4$ or $K_2Cr_2O_7$Reflux, aqueous medium

Solved example (oxidation of ethanol to acetaldehyde)

Given 46.1 g of ethanol ($C_2H_5OH$), calculate the theoretical yield of acetaldehyde ($CH_3CHO$) using PCC.

Molar masses: $M_{C_2H_5OH}=46.07\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$, $M_{CH_3CHO}=44.05\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

\[n_{ethanol}=\frac{46.1}{46.07}=1.00\ \text{mol}\]

Stoichiometry (1:1) gives $n_{acetaldehyde}=1.00\ \text{mol}$.

Mass of product: \[m_{acetaldehyde}=1.00\times44.05=44.05\ \text{g}\]

Thus, the maximum amount of acetaldehyde obtainable is $44.05\,\text{g}$ under ideal conditions.

SI units: mass (kg), temperature (K or °C), pressure (Pa or atm), concentration (mol L$^{-1}$).
long_notes.Physical properties and structural aspec:
Definition: Aldehydes (‑CHO), ketones (‑CO‑) and carboxylic acids (‑COOH) contain a carbonyl group ($C\! =\! O$). The carbonyl C is sp$^2$ hybridised, planar and polar, giving characteristic physical properties.

  • Bonding: C=O consists of one sigma ($\sigma$) and one pi ($\pi$) bond. The $\pi$ bond is weaker, making carbonyl compounds susceptible to nucleophilic attack.
  • Dipole moment ($\mu$): $\mu = Q \times d$ (C·m). For carbonyls $\mu$ lies between 2–3 D; higher $\mu$ raises intermolecular dipole–dipole forces.
  • Boiling point trend: $BP \propto$ molecular weight $+$ dipole moment $+$ hydrogen‑bonding ability. Carboxylic acids show the highest $BP$ because of strong $\text{O–H}\cdots\text{O}$ hydrogen bonds.
CompoundFunctional groupTypical $\mu$ (D)Boiling point (°C)
Aldehyde (acetaldehyde)‑CHO2.720.2
Ketone (acetone)‑CO‑2.956.0
Carboxylic acid (acetic acid)‑COOH1.7 (effective $\approx$ 5 D due to H‑bonding)118.1

Key formula: Net dipole for two bond dipoles $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ at angle $\theta$ is $\mu_{net}=\sqrt{\mu_1^{2}+\mu_2^{2}+2\mu_1\mu_2\cos\theta}$.

Example: Estimate the dipole moment of acetaldehyde. Given $\mu_{C=O}=1.6\,\text{D}$, $\mu_{C–H}=0.4\,\text{D}$ and $\theta=120^{\circ}$,

$$\mu_{net}=\sqrt{1.6^{2}+0.4^{2}+2\times1.6\times0.4\cos120^{\circ}}=\sqrt{2.56+0.16-0.64}=\sqrt{2.08}=1.44\,\text{D}$$

The calculated $\mu_{net}$ (~1.4 D) explains why aldehydes have moderate boiling points, higher than alkanes of similar weight but lower than acids that benefit from hydrogen bonding.
long_notes.Characteristic chemical reactions of ald:
Definition: Aldehydes are organic compounds containing the carbonyl group $>C=O$ attached to at least one hydrogen atom ($RCHO$). They readily undergo oxidation, reduction and nucleophilic addition.

1. Oxidation

  • General equation: $RCHO + [O] \rightarrow RCOOH$ (aldehyde $ ightarrow$ carboxylic acid).
  • Typical oxidising agents: $K_2Cr_2O_7/H_2SO_4$, $KMnO_4$, $Na_2Cr_2O_7$.
  • Temperature: $25\,^{\circ}C$ (room temperature) unless otherwise specified.

2. Reduction

  • General equation: $RCHO + H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni,\,\text{cat.}} RCH_2OH$ (aldehyde $ ightarrow$ primary alcohol).
  • Alternative reagents: NaBH$_4$, LiAlH$_4$.

3. Nucleophilic addition

  • General equation: $RCHO + NuH \rightarrow RCH(OH)Nu$ where $Nu$ = $CN^-$, $NH_2^-$, $CH_3O^-$ etc.
  • Mechanism: nucleophile attacks carbonyl carbon forming a tetrahedral alkoxide, which on protonation gives the addition product.

Key reagents & products

ReactionReagentProduct
Oxidation$K_2Cr_2O_7/H_2SO_4$$RCOOH$
Reduction$H_2$, Ni$RCH_2OH$
Nucleophilic addition$CN^-$, $NH_2^-$, $CH_3O^-$$RCH(OH)Nu$

Solved example (oxidation of ethanal)

Oxidise $CH_3CHO$ to acetic acid using acidic $K_2Cr_2O_7$.

  1. Write the balanced redox equation:
    $3CH_3CHO + K_2Cr_2O_7 + 4H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 3CH_3COOH + Cr_2(SO_4)_3 + K_2SO_4 + 4H_2O$.
  2. Identify oxidation numbers: C in $CH_3CHO$ changes from $0$ to $+3$ (loss of $3e^-$ per molecule).
  3. Calculate moles of $K_2Cr_2O_7$ needed for $0.05\,mol$ ethanal:
    $0.05\,mol\,CH_3CHO \times \frac{1\,mol\,K_2Cr_2O_7}{3\,mol\,CH_3CHO}=0.0167\,mol$.
  4. Perform the reaction at $80\,^{\circ}C$ for $15\,min$; the precipitated $Ag$ in Tollen's test disappears confirming complete oxidation.

Thus, aldehydes show characteristic oxidation to acids, reduction to primary alcohols, and nucleophilic addition forming various functional groups.
long_notes.Characteristic chemical reactions of ket:
Ketones – Characteristic Reactions

  • Nucleophilic addition: General reaction $\\ce{RCOR'} + Nu^- \rightarrow RCO(R')Nu$; the carbonyl carbon bears a partial positive charge $\\delta+$ making it electrophilic.
  • Reduction: $\\ce{RCOR'} \xrightarrow[\\text{solvent}]{\\text{NaBH}_4\text{ or }\\text{LiAlH}_4} RCH_2R'$; NaBH$_4$ reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol under mild conditions, while LiAlH$_4$ works in aprotic solvents and gives the same alcohol.
  • Haloform reaction: Methyl ketone $\\ce{RC(=O)CH_3}$ reacts with $\\ce{X_2}$ (X = Cl, Br) in $\\ce{NaOH}$ to afford a carboxylate ion and haloform $\\ce{CHX_3}$:
    $\\ce{RC(=O)CH_3 + 3X_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow RCOONa + CHX_3 + 3NaX + 3H_2O}$.
ReagentProduct
$\\ce{NaBH_4}$$\\ce{RCH(OH)R'}$ (secondary alcohol)
$\\ce{X_2/NaOH}$$\\ce{RCOO^- + CHX_3}$

Solved Example (Reduction of Acetone)

Given 0.10 mol of acetone ($\\ce{(CH_3)_2CO}$) and excess $\\ce{NaBH_4}$, write the balanced equation and calculate the mass of 2‑propanol formed.

Balanced equation:
$\\ce{(CH_3)_2CO + NaBH_4 + 2H_2O \rightarrow (CH_3)_2CHOH + NaBO_2 + 4H_2}$

Moles of acetone = 0.10 mol ⇒ moles of 2‑propanol formed = 0.10 mol (1:1 stoichiometry).
Molar mass of 2‑propanol = $\\mathrm{C_3H_8O}=60.10\,\\text{g mol}^{-1}$.
Mass = $0.10\,\\text{mol}\times60.10\,\\text{g mol}^{-1}=6.01\,\\text{g}$.

Thus, 6.01 g of 2‑propanol is obtained under standard conditions (25 °C, 1 atm).
long_notes.Reactions of carboxylic acids (acid‑base:
Acid‑base reaction

  • General equation: $RCOOH + OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + H_2O$ (neutralisation, $K_{eq}=10^{pK_a-pK_w}$).

Reduction

  • To aldehydes (dry ether, LiAlH$_4$): $RCOOH \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\text{LiAlH}_4} RCHO + H_2O$.
  • To primary alcohols (LiAlH$_4$ or $H_2/\text{Ni}$): $RCOOH \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} RCH_2OH$.

Esterification (Fischer)

  • Equation: $RCOOH + R'OH \xrightleftharpoons[\text{H_2O}]{\text{H}^+} RCOOR' + H_2O$.
  • Equilibrium constant: $K_{eq}=\frac{[RCOOR']}{[RCOOH][R'OH]}$; removal of water shifts equilibrium to the right.

Decarboxylation

  • General: $RCOOH \xrightarrow{\Delta} RH + CO_2$ (requires $\Delta H \approx +30\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).
ReagentProduct
NaOH$RCOONa$
LiAlH$_4$$RCH_2OH$

Solved example (reduction of acetic acid)

Given: $CH_3COOH$ + 4 $[H]$ $\xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4}$ $CH_3CH_2OH$ + $H_2O$.
Step 1: Write the half‑reaction for the acid: $CH_3COOH + 2e^- \rightarrow CH_3CHO + H_2O$.
Step 2: Add two electrons (from LiAlH$_4$) to convert the aldehyde to alcohol: $CH_3CHO + 2e^- + 2H^+ \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH$.
Overall: $CH_3COOH + 4[H] \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH + H_2O$.
Result: one mole of acetic acid yields one mole of ethanol; molar mass of ethanol = $46\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$, so 60 g (1.3 mol) of $CH_3COOH$ gives $1.3\times46=59.8\,\text{g}$ ethanol.
long_notes.Important derivatives (acyl halides, anh:
Important Derivatives of Carboxylic Acids

Acyl halides (RCOX, X = Cl, Br), anhydrides ((RCO)2O), esters (RCOOR'), and amides (RCONH2, RCONHR', RCONR'2) are obtained by replacing the –OH group of the parent acid.

DerivativeTypical PreparationKey Reaction
Acyl halide$\\mathrm{RCOOH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow RCOCl + SO_2 + HCl}$Nucleophilic acyl substitution – acid chloride reacts with $\\mathrm{H_2O}$ to give acid.
Anhydride$\\mathrm{2 RCOOH \xrightarrow{P_2O_5} (RCO)_2O + H_2O}$Reaction with $\\mathrm{R'OH}$ gives mixed anhydride then ester.
EsterFischer esterification: $\\mathrm{RCOOH + R'OH \xrightleftharpoons[\text{conc. H_2SO_4}]{\Delta} RCOOR' + H_2O}$Hydrolysis in $\\mathrm{H_2O/H^+}$ returns acid.
Amide$\\mathrm{RCOCl + 2 NH_3 \rightarrow RCONH_2 + NH_4Cl}$ (or $\\mathrm{RCOOH + NH_3 \xrightarrow{Dehydrating\ agent} RCONH_2}$)Reduction with $\\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ gives amine.

Representative Example (Fischer Esterification)

Acetic acid (60.0 g, $\\mathrm{1.00\,mol}$) is refluxed with ethanol (46.1 g, $\\mathrm{1.00\,mol}$) in $\\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ catalyst. After 2 h, 68.0 g of ethyl acetate is isolated. Theoretical yield = $\\mathrm{1.00\,mol \times 88.1\,g\,mol^{-1}=88.1\,g}$. % yield = $\\frac{68.0}{88.1}\\times100 = 77\%$.

Key points: keep water removal (Dean–Stark) to shift equilibrium; temperature $\\approx 60\\,\degree C$; catalyst conc. $\\approx 5\%$.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the –CHO group attached to at least one hydrogen.
  • Ketone: Organic compound containing the >C=O group attached to two carbon atoms.
  • Carboxylic acid: Compound containing the –COOH (–C(=O)OH) functional group.
  • Acidic hydrogen: The hydrogen of the –COOH group that ionises in water.
  • Markovnikov's rule (addition to unsymmetrical alkenes): In acid‑catalysed addition, the hydrogen adds to the carbon bearing more hydrogens, the electrophile to the more substituted carbon.
  • Oxidation state of carbonyl carbon: $+2$ in aldehydes and ketones, $+3$ in carboxylic acids.
  • Reactivity order towards nucleophiles: Aldehyde $>$ Ketone $>$ Carboxylic acid $>$ Ester $>$ Amide.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
1. Remember that aldehydes are easily oxidised to acids, whereas ketones are resistant to oxidation under mild conditions.
  2. Do not confuse the direction of the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation; it is $pH = pK_a + \log \frac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$, not the reverse.
  3. When writing reduction reactions, always indicate the catalyst (e.g., $\text{H}_2$, Ni) or reducing agent (NaBH$_4$, LiAlH$_4$).
  4. Acid‑catalysed hydrolysis of esters proceeds via a tetrahedral intermediate; the rate law involves $[\text{H}^+]$, not $[\text{H}_2O]$.
  5. Do not treat the carbonyl carbon of a carboxylic acid as equally electrophilic as that of an aldehyde; resonance with the –OH reduces its reactivity.
  6. For pK_a calculations, ensure the correct logarithm base (base 10) and sign convention.

numericals.question: Calculate the number of moles of acetone required to prepare 250 mL of a 0.20 M solution.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Volume $V=250\,\text{mL}=0.250\,\text{L}$, Molarity $M=0.20\,\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.
Formula: $n = M\times V$.
Calculation: $n = 0.20\,\text{mol\,L}^{-1}\times 0.250\,\text{L}=0.050\,\text{mol}$.
Answer: $0.050\,\text{mol}$ of acetone are needed.

numericals.question: A 5.00 g sample of benzyl alcohol (C₆H₅CH₂OH) is oxidised to benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO). If 4.20 g of benzaldehyde is obtained, calculate the percentage yield.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $m_{\text{exp}}=4.20\,\text{g}$, $M_{\text{C₆H₅CH₂OH}}=108.12\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$, $M_{\text{C₆H₅CHO}}=106.12\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$, $m_{\text{sample}}=5.00\,\text{g}$.
Formula: $\text{Yield}\,\% = \dfrac{m_{\text{exp}}}{m_{\text{theo}}}\times100$.
Step‑1 (theoretical moles): $n_{\text{theo}} = \dfrac{5.00}{108.12}=0.0462\,\text{mol}$.
Step‑2 (theoretical mass of benzaldehyde): $m_{\text{theo}} = n_{\text{theo}}\times106.12=4.90\,\text{g}$.
Step‑3 (percentage yield): $\text{Yield}\,\% = \dfrac{4.20}{4.90}\times100 = 85.7\%$.
Answer: $85.7\,\%$ yield.

numericals.question: Calculate the pH of a 0.010 M aqueous solution of acetic acid (CH₃COOH) given $K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $C = 0.010\,\text{M}$, $K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$.
Formula (ICE table): $K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{C-x}\approx\dfrac{x^2}{C}$ for weak acids.
Calculation: $x = \sqrt{K_a\times C}=\sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.010}=\sqrt{1.8\times10^{-7}}=1.34\times10^{-4}\,\text{M}$ (which is $[H^+]$).
pH $= -\log[H^+] = -\log(1.34\times10^{-4}) = 3.87$.
Answer: pH $= 3.87$.

numericals.question: The half‑life of the first‑order decomposition of propionic acid is 2.5 h. Determine the rate constant $k$ (in $\text{h}^{-1}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $t_{1/2}=2.5\,\text{h}$ for a first‑order reaction.
Formula: $k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$.
Calculation: $k = \dfrac{0.693}{2.5}=0.277\,\text{h}^{-1}$.
Answer: $k = 0.277\,\text{h}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: A 5.00 g sample of butyric acid (C₃H₇COOH) is completely combusted. Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced. (Molar mass of C₃H₇COOH = 88.11 g mol⁻¹, CO₂ = 44.01 g mol⁻¹)
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $m_{\text{acid}}=5.00\,\text{g}$, $M_{\text{acid}}=88.11\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$, $M_{\text{CO₂}}=44.01\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$.
Balanced combustion: $\text{C₃H₇COOH}+\frac{5}{2}\,\text{O₂}\rightarrow5\,\text{CO₂}+4\,\text{H₂O}$.
Step‑1 (moles of acid): $n_{\text{acid}} = \dfrac{5.00}{88.11}=0.0567\,\text{mol}$.
Step‑2 (moles of CO₂, 5 mol per mol acid): $n_{\text{CO₂}} =5\times0.0567=0.2835\,\text{mol}$.
Step‑3 (mass of CO₂): $m_{\text{CO₂}} = n_{\text{CO₂}}\times44.01=12.5\,\text{g}$.
Answer: $12.5\,\text{g}$ of CO₂ are evolved.

numericals.question: A 0.10 M solution of sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) is prepared. Using $K_a$(CH₃COOH) = $1.8\times10^{-5}$, calculate the equilibrium concentration of acetate ion $[\text{CH₃COO}^-]$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $C_{\text{salt}}=0.10\,\text{M}$, $K_a=1.8\times10^{-5}$. For the hydrolysis: $\text{CH₃COO}^-+\text{H₂O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH₃COOH}+\text{OH}^-$. $K_b = \dfrac{K_w}{K_a}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-14}}{1.8\times10^{-5}}=5.56\times10^{-10}$.
ICE table (approximation $x\ll C$): $K_b = \dfrac{x^2}{C}$, where $x=[\text{OH}^-]=[\text{CH₃COOH}]$.
Calculation: $x = \sqrt{K_b\times C}=\sqrt{5.56\times10^{-10}\times0.10}=7.46\times10^{-6}\,\text{M}$.
Thus $[\text{CH₃COO}^-]_{\text{eq}} = C - x \approx 0.10 - 7.5\times10^{-6}=0.09999\,\text{M}$.
Answer: $[\text{CH₃COO}^-] \approx 0.100\,\text{M}$ (to three significant figures).

pyq.question: Write the general formula of an aldehyde.
pyq.answer_html: General formula of aldehydes is $RCHO$.

pyq.question: Identify the functional group present in acetone.
pyq.answer_html: Acetone contains the carbonyl functional group $>C=O$ attached to two alkyl groups (ketone).

pyq.question: Explain why aldehydes are more readily oxidised than ketones.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Aldehydes have a hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl carbon, which can be removed easily during oxidation (1 mark).
2. The carbonyl carbon in aldehydes is less sterically hindered than in ketones, allowing easier attack by oxidising agents (1 mark).
3. Formation of a carboxylic acid from an aldehyde is thermodynamically favourable, whereas oxidation of ketones gives less stable products (1 mark).

pyq.question: Write the IUPAC name of the compound $CH_3CH_2CHO$.
pyq.answer_html: The longest chain containing the –CHO group has three carbon atoms; therefore the compound is named propanal (3‑carbon aldehyde). (3 marks)

pyq.question: Discuss the mechanism of nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde leading to a cyanohydrin.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen by $H^+$ increases electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon (1 mark).
2. Nucleophilic attack of cyanide ion $CN^-$ on the carbonyl carbon forms a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate (1 mark).
3. The alkoxide abstracts a proton from the medium (usually water) to give the cyanohydrin $RCH(OH)CN$ (1 mark).
4. Overall, the reaction converts $RCHO$ to $RCH(OH)CN$ with retention of configuration at the carbonyl carbon (1 mark).
5. The cyanohydrin is a useful synthetic intermediate for further transformations (1 mark).

pyq.question: Compare the acidities of carboxylic acids, phenols and alcohols, giving reasons for the observed order.
pyq.answer_html:
Typical $pK_a$ values: carboxylic acids $\approx 4-5$, phenols $\approx 10$, alcohols $\approx 15-16$ (1 mark).
1. Carboxylic acids: the conjugate base $RCOO^-$ is resonance‑stabilised over two oxygen atoms, greatly delocalising the negative charge (1 mark).
2. Phenols: the phenoxide ion $ArO^-$ benefits from resonance with the aromatic ring, but the delocalisation is less extensive than in carboxylates (1 mark).
3. Alcohols: alkoxide $RO^-$ lacks resonance stabilisation; the negative charge resides on a single oxygen, making it the least stable (1 mark).
4. Inductive effects: the electronegative carbonyl carbon in carboxylic acids withdraws electron density, further stabilising $RCOO^-$; phenols have a moderate –I effect, while aliphatic alcohols have the weakest (1 mark).
Thus the acidity order is: carboxylic acids $>$ phenols $>$ alcohols (1 mark).

mcq.q: The acidity of $α$-hydrogen in aldehydes follows the order:
mcq.explain: Formaldehyde has the most electron‑withdrawing effect of the $\mathrm{-CHO}$ group, increasing the acidity of its $\alpha$‑hydrogen compared to higher aldehydes.

mcq.q: Which statement about the oxidation of secondary alcohols to ketones is correct?
options: The reaction requires a strong acid catalyst
The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate
The reaction involves removal of two hydrogen atoms
The reaction forms an aldehyde as intermediate
mcq.explain: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol removes one hydrogen from the hydroxyl group and one from the adjacent carbon, totaling two hydrogens, yielding a ketone.

mcq.q: Which of the following acids has the highest $pK_a$ value?
mcq.explain: Propionic acid ($pK_a \approx 4.87$) is less acidic than acetic ($pK_a \approx 4.76$) and benzoic ($pK_a \approx 4.20$) acids; formic acid is the strongest.

mcq.q: The rate of hydrolysis of an ester under acidic conditions depends on:
options: Both acid concentration and water concentration
mcq.explain: Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis is a bimolecular reaction involving the protonated ester and water; rate = $k[H^+][H_2O]$.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements about carboxylic acids is FALSE?
options: They are stronger acids than alcohols
They undergo nucleophilic substitution at the carbonyl carbon
They are less soluble in water than aldehydes of similar molecular weight
mcq.explain: Carboxylic acids are generally more soluble in water than aldehydes of comparable size due to extensive hydrogen bonding.

mcq.q: The $\alpha$‑halogenation of a ketone using $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ in acidic medium proceeds via which intermediate?
mcq.explain: Acidic conditions favor enol formation; the enol reacts with $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ to give the $\alpha$‑chloro ketone.

mcq.q:
Assertion: $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$ reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids.
Reason: $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$ is a milder reducing agent than $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$ selectively reduces carbonyl groups of aldehydes/ketones; its milder nature prevents reduction of the more stable carboxylic acid functional group.

mcq.q:
Assertion: In the presence of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, acetic anhydride reacts with an alcohol to give an ester.
Reason: $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ acts as a dehydrating agent, facilitating the removal of water.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Sulfuric acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, increasing electrophilicity and also absorbs the water formed, driving esterification forward.

long_notes.Structure & nomenclature of aldehydes an:
Definition: Aldehydes contain a carbonyl group ($>C=O$) bonded to at least one hydrogen atom, represented as –$CHO$. Ketones have a carbonyl group flanked by two carbon atoms, represented as –$CO-$.

General formulas (saturated):

  • Aldehyde: $C_{n}H_{2n+1}CHO$ (or $C_{n}H_{2n+2}O$)
  • Ketone: $C_{n}H_{2n}O$

Key IUPAC naming rules:

  1. Identify the longest carbon chain containing the carbonyl carbon.
  2. Number the chain so that the carbonyl carbon gets the lowest possible locant.
  3. For aldehydes, replace the –$e$ of the parent alkane with –$al$; for ketones, replace –$e$ with –$one$.
  4. If substituents are present, name them in alphabetical order with their locants.
  5. When the carbonyl is at the end of the chain, the aldehyde locant is omitted (e.g., $propanal$).

Summary table:

Functional groupSuffixExample
Aldehyde–$al$CH$_3$CH$_2$CHO → $propanal$
Ketone–$one$CH$_3$COCH$_3$ → $propanone$ (acetone)

Solved example:

Give the IUPAC name of the following structure:
CH$_3$–CH$_2$–CH(CH$_3$)–CHO

Solution:

  1. Longest chain containing –$CHO$ has 4 carbons → base name $butanal$.
  2. Number from the carbonyl end: carbonyl carbon is C‑1.
  3. There is a methyl substituent on C‑3.
  4. Combine: $3$‑$methyl$ $butanal$.

Important SI units: Boiling point, melting point, density etc. are expressed in $^circ C$, $g,cm^{-3}$ respectively.
long_notes.Methods of preparation of aldehydes and:
Definitions

  • Aldehyde: $RCHO$ (carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen).
  • Ketone: $RCOR'$ (carbonyl carbon attached to two alkyl/aryl groups).

Key Methods of Preparation

MethodReagents / ConditionsProduct
Oxidation of primary alcohol$RCH_2OH$ + $[O]$ (e.g., $PCC$, $KMnO_4$ (cold))$RCHO$
Ozonolysis of alkenes$RCH=CH_2$ + $O_3$ → $H_2O_2$ work‑up$RCHO$ + $R'CHO$
Hydration of terminal alkyne$RC\equiv CH$ + $H_2O$ (HgSO$_4$, $H_2SO_4$)$RCHO$
Reduction of acid derivatives$RCOCl$, $RCOOR'$, $RCOOH$, $RCONH_2$ + $LiAlH_4$ (or $NaBH_4$ for acid chloride)$RCHO$ (or $RCOR'$ for ketone)
From nitriles$RCN$ + $H_2$ (Raney Ni) or $LiAlH_4$$RCH_2NH_2$ → $RCHO$ (via hydrolysis)
From carboxylic acids$RCOOH$ + $P_2O_5$ (dry distillation)$RCHO$
Grignard addition to CO$R MgX$ + $CO$ + $H_2O$$RCHO$

Typical conditions: temperature $25-80^\circ C$, pressure $1\ atm$, solvents $CH_2Cl_2$, $EtOH$; yields are reported in %.

Representative Example (Oxidation of Ethanol)

Convert ethanol ($CH_3CH_2OH$) to acetaldehyde ($CH_3CHO$) using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC).

StepReaction
1$CH_3CH_2OH$ + $PCC$ → $CH_3CHO$ + $Cr^{3+}$ + $Cl^-$
2Work‑up with $H_2O$ gives pure $CH_3CHO$ (boiling point $20.2^\circ C$).

Key points: Use a mild oxidising agent to stop at aldehyde; avoid over‑oxidation to acetic acid.
long_notes.Physical & chemical properties of aldehy:
Physical & Chemical Properties of Aldehydes (RCHO)

Aldehydes contain the carbonyl group ($\mathrm{C=O}$) attached to at least one hydrogen atom. They are polar, have characteristic pungent odours and are generally soluble in water up to $\sim$5 % (by mass) due to hydrogen‑bonding.

  • Boiling point: Higher than the corresponding alcohol because of dipole‑dipole interactions, but lower than the analogous ketone (no extra alkyl group).
  • Density: $1.0\text{–}1.2\,\text{g cm}^{-3}$ (close to water).
  • Reactivity: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic; aldehydes undergo nucleophilic addition, oxidation to carboxylic acids and reduction to primary alcohols.
PropertyTrend in Aldehydes
Boiling point (°C)Increases with molecular weight; $\mathrm{CH_2O}$ = -19, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O}$ ≈ 120
Solubility in waterDecreases with chain length; $\mathrm{CH_2O}$ fully miscible, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O}$ ≈ 5 %
Acidity of $α$‑HpK_a ≈ 17 (more acidic than alkanes)

Key Chemical Reactions

  • Oxidation: $\mathrm{RCHO + [O] \rightarrow RCOOH}$ (e.g., $\mathrm{CH_2O + 2[O] \rightarrow HCOOH}$). Rate law often first order: $\text{Rate}=k[\text{aldehyde}]$.
  • Reduction: $\mathrm{RCHO + 2[H] \rightarrow RCH_2OH}$ (e.g., NaBH$_4$).
  • Nucleophilic addition (e.g., formation of hemiacetal with $\mathrm{ROH}$).

SI Units

  • Temperature – kelvin (K) or degree Celsius (°C).
  • Pressure – pascal (Pa).
  • Amount – mole (mol).

Solved Example

Calculate the moles of formaldehyde ($\mathrm{CH_2O}$) formed when $5.0\,\text{g}$ of methanol is oxidised completely.

Step 1: Molar mass of $\mathrm{CH_2O}$ = $12.01 + 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 30.03\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Step 2: $n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{5.0\,\text{g}}{30.03\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 1.66\times10^{-1}\,\text{mol}$.

Thus, $0.166\,\text{mol}$ of formaldehyde is produced.
long_notes.Physical & chemical properties of ketone:
Definition: Ketones are organic compounds containing a carbonyl group ($C=O$) bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups.

Physical properties

  • Polarity: dipole moment $\mu$ \approx $2.9\,\text{D}$ for acetone; higher than alkanes.
  • Boiling points: follow $\text{BP} \uparrow$ with molecular weight; acetone $56\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, 2‑butanone $80\,^{\circ}\text{C}$.
  • Solubility: miscible with water up to $\approx 100\,\%$ for acetone due to H‑bond acceptor ability.

Key formula – Heat of vapourisation

Compound$\Delta H_{vap}^\circ$ (kJ·mol$^{-1}$)
Acetone$31.3$
2‑Butanone$38.0$

Chemical properties

  • Nucleophilic addition is the principal reaction; carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
  • Reaction with $\text{NaBH}_4$ gives secondary alcohols: $\ce{RCOR'} + \text{NaBH4} \rightarrow \ce{RCH(OH)R'}$.
  • Oxidation: secondary ketones are resistant; α‑hydrogen can be removed by $\ce{LDA}$ to form enolates.
  • Halogenation in acidic medium yields α‑halo ketones: $\ce{RCOR' + X2 \xrightarrow{H+} RCHXCO R'}$.

Solved example

Oxidise $\pu{10.0\,g}$ of 2‑propanol ($\text{M}=60.1\,\text{g·mol}^{-1}$) with $\ce{NaOCl}$ to acetone. Theoretical yield of acetone = $\pu{10.0\,g} \times \frac{58.1}{60.1}=\pu{9.66\,g}$. If $\pu{8.50\,g}$ acetone is isolated, % yield = $\frac{8.50}{9.66}\times100 = 88\%$.
long_notes.Important reactions of aldehydes & keton:
Definitions

  • Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the carbonyl group attached to at least one hydrogen atom, general formula $RCHO$.
  • Ketone: Carbonyl group flanked by two carbon atoms, general formula $RCOR'$.

Nucleophilic Addition

  • Mechanism: $C=O$ is electrophilic; nucleophile $Nu^-$ attacks carbon, forming alkoxide intermediate $RCH(O^-)Nu$ which is protonated to give $RCH(OH)Nu$.
  • Typical reagents: $NaBH_4$, $LiAlH_4$, $H_2$, $HCl$ (for addition of $HCl$).

Oxidation

  • Aldehydes $\rightarrow$ carboxylic acids; ketones are generally resistant.
  • Common oxidising agents: $KMnO_4$, $K_2Cr_2O_7$ in $H_2SO_4$, $Na_2Cr_2O_7$.

Reduction

  • Aldehydes/ketones $\rightarrow$ primary/secondary alcohols.
  • Reagents: $NaBH_4$ (mild), $LiAlH_4$ (strong).

Haloform Reaction

  • Applicable to methyl ketones $RC(O)CH_3$ and ethanol.
  • Reagents: $X_2$ (Cl$_2$, Br$_2$) + $NaOH$.
  • Overall: $RC(O)CH_3 + 3X_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow RCOONa + CHX_3 + 3NaX + 3H_2O$.
ReactionReagentProduct
Oxidation of $RCHO$$KMnO_4$ (acidic)$RCOOH$
Reduction of $RCOR'$$NaBH_4$$RCH(OH)R'$

Solved Example

Reduce $CH_3CHO$ (acetaldehyde) to ethanol using $NaBH_4$. 5 mmol of $NaBH_4$ is taken. Write the balanced equation and calculate moles of ethanol formed.

Balanced: $CH_3CHO + NaBH_4 + 3H_2O \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH + NaBO_2 + 3H_2$.

One mole of $NaBH_4$ reduces one mole of aldehyde; thus 5 mmol $NaBH_4$ gives 5 mmol $CH_3CH_2OH$ (0.005 mol, $0.005 \times 46 = 0.23$ g).
long_notes.Structure & nomenclature of carboxylic a:
Definition: A carboxylic acid is an organic compound containing the functional group $\text{-COOH}$ (carboxyl group) attached to a carbon skeleton.

General formula: For a saturated monocarboxylic acid, $C_{n}H_{2n+1}COOH$ or equivalently $C_{n+1}H_{2n+2}O_{2}$ (where $n\ge 1$). The molar mass $M$ is obtained by $M=\sum M_{i}$ (sum of atomic masses in g·mol$^{-1}$).

IUPAC nomenclature rules

  • Identify the longest chain containing the $\text{-COOH}$ group; it must be numbered so that the carbon of $\text{-COOH}$ gets the lowest possible locant (always 1).
  • Replace the alkane suffix “‑e” with “‑oic acid”.
  • Number substituents on the chain and name them as prefixes (e.g., 2‑methyl, 3‑chloro).
  • If the acid has more than one $\text{-COOH}$, use “‑dioic acid”, “‑trioic acid”, etc., with appropriate locants.

Common (trivial) names

IUPAC nameCommon name
methanoic acidformic acid
ethanoic acidacetic acid
propanoic acidpropionic acid

Physical properties

  • Boiling points increase with molecular weight due to extensive hydrogen‑bonding.
  • Acids are strong hydrogen‑bond donors; $\text{-COOH}$ has a dipole moment of about $1.4\,\text{D}$.

Solved example

Calculate the percentage mass of carbon in acetic acid ($CH_{3}COOH$).

Molar mass $M_{CH_{3}COOH}=2(12.01)+4(1.008)+2(16.00)=60.05\,\text{g·mol}^{-1}$.

Mass of carbon $=2\times12.01=24.02\,\text{g}$.

\[\%\,C = \frac{24.02}{60.05}\times100 = 40.0\%\]

Thus, acetic acid contains $40.0\%$ carbon by mass.
long_notes.Methods of preparation & physical proper:
Definition: Carboxylic acids are organic compounds containing the –$COOH$ functional group.

Physical properties (typical trends):

PropertyTrend with chain length
Boiling pointIncreases due to stronger H‑bonding and Van‑der‑Waals forces
Solubility in waterDecreases; short‑chain acids (\le 4 C) are miscible

Acidic nature: $K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}$, $pK_a = -\log K_a$. Typical $pK_a$ values: formic $\approx 3.75$, acetic $\approx 4.76$.

Methods of preparation:

  • Oxidation of primary alcohols/aldehydes (e.g., $CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{[O]} CH_3COOH$).
  • Hydrolysis of nitriles: $RCN + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} RCOOH + NH_3$.
  • Carboxylation of organometallic reagents: $RMgX + CO_2 \xrightarrow{} RCOOMgX \xrightarrow{H^+} RCOOH$.
  • From acid chlorides: $RCOCl + H_2O \rightarrow RCOOH + HCl$.

SI units: Temperature $^\circ C$, pressure $atm$, concentration $mol\,L^{-1}$.

Solved example: Prepare acetic acid by oxidation of ethanol.

Reaction: $CH_3CH_2OH + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow CH_3COOH + H_2O$.

Given 46 g ethanol (0.99 mol) and excess $O_2$, theoretical yield of $CH_3COOH$ = 0.99 mol $\times$ 60.05 g·mol$^{-1}$ = 59.4 g. If 52 g acid is obtained, % yield = $\frac{52}{59.4}\times100 = 87.5\%$.
long_notes.Important reactions of carboxylic acids:
Definitions

  • Esterification: Acid‑catalysed equilibrium between a carboxylic acid ($RCOOH$) and an alcohol ($R'OH$) forming an ester ($RCOOR'$) and water.
  • Reduction: Conversion of a carboxylic acid or its derivative to the corresponding alcohol using strong reducing agents.
  • Decarboxylation: Thermal removal of $CO_2$ from a carboxylic acid, yielding a hydrocarbon.

Key Equations & Conditions

ReactionReagentsConditions
$RCOOH + R'OH \\rightleftharpoons RCOOR' + H_2O$Conc. $H_2SO_4$ (catalyst)$60-80\\,^{\\circ}C$, removal of $H_2O$ (Dean‑Stark)
$RCOOH \\xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} RCH_2OH$LiAlH$_4$, dry ether$0\\,^{\\circ}C$ to $25\\,^{\\circ}C$, inert atmosphere
$RCOOH \\xrightarrow{\\Delta} R-H + CO_2$Heat$>200\\,^{\\circ}C$, often with $CuO$ or $NaOH$ as catalyst

Mechanistic Insight

  • Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen increases electrophilicity, allowing nucleophilic attack by the alcohol.
  • In reduction, LiAlH$_4$ donates hydride to the carbonyl carbon; subsequent work‑up gives the primary alcohol.
  • Decarboxylation proceeds via a six‑membered cyclic transition state when a β‑keto acid is involved.

Solved Example

Esterify acetic acid with ethanol.

StepDetails
1Mix $CH_3COOH$ (0.1 mol) and $C_2H_5OH$ (0.1 mol) with 5 mL conc. $H_2SO_4$.
2Heat at $70\\,^{\\circ}C$ for 2 h; water removed by Dean‑Stark apparatus.
3Cool, neutralise with NaHCO$_3$, extract ester with diethyl ether.
4Yield $CH_3COOC_2H_5$ = 0.085 mol (85 %).

All reactions are reversible; shifting equilibrium by removing water or using excess alcohol drives ester formation.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the carbonyl group attached to at least one hydrogen atom; general structure $\mathrm{R-CHO}$.
  • Ketone: Carbonyl carbon bonded to two alkyl/aryl groups; general structure $\mathrm{R-CO-R\'}$.
  • Carboxylic Acid: Contains the –$\mathrm{COOH}$ group; formula $\mathrm{R-COOH}$.
  • Nucleophilic addition: Dominant reaction of aldehydes and ketones where a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
  • Oxidation: Increase in oxidation state of carbon; aldehydes → acids, primary alcohols → aldehydes → acids.
  • Reduction: Decrease in oxidation state; acids/aldehydes → aldehydes/alcohols.
  • Markovnikov's rule (addition to unsymmetrical alkenes): Hydrogen adds to the carbon bearing more hydrogens; the electrophile adds to the carbon bearing fewer hydrogens.
  • Cannizzaro reaction: Disproportionation of non‑\textit{α}-hydrogen aldehydes in strong base: $\mathrm{2R-CHO \xrightarrow[\text{NaOH}]{\text{}} R-COO^- + R-CH_2OH}$.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Quick Summary

  • Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and a stronger $\mathrm{C=O}$ dipole.
  • Both undergo nucleophilic addition; however, ketones give slower reactions and often need stronger nucleophiles.
  • Oxidation of aldehydes gives carboxylic acids; ketones resist oxidation unless under vigorous conditions.
  • Carboxylic acids are weak acids; $pK_a$ lies between 4–5. Their derivatives (esters, acid chlorides, anhydrides) are formed via nucleophilic acyl substitution.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Confusing the direction of Markovnikov's rule – remember the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more H atoms.
  • Treating all aldehydes as oxidizable to acids; aromatic aldehydes (e.g., benzaldehyde) are less prone to oxidation under mild conditions.
  • Writing the esterification reaction without the catalyst; acid catalyst (H$^+$) is essential for the equilibrium shift.
  • Assuming ketones undergo Cannizzaro reaction – it occurs only with aldehydes lacking \textit{α}-hydrogen.

numericals.question: Calculate the number of moles of acetaldehyde required to prepare 250 mL of 0.20 M solution.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Volume $V = 250\\ \text{mL}=0.250\\ \text{L}$, Molarity $M = 0.20\\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.
Formula: $n = M \times V$.
Step‑by‑Step Calculation: $n = 0.20 \times 0.250 = 0.050\\ \text{mol}$.
Final Answer: $0.050\\ \text{mol}$ of acetaldehyde.

numericals.question: A student obtains 5.2 g of benzaldehyde from the oxidation of benzyl alcohol. The theoretical yield is 6.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Actual mass $m_{act}=5.2\\ \text{g}$, Theoretical mass $m_{th}=6.0\\ \text{g}$.
Formula: $\%\text{Yield}=\dfrac{m_{act}}{m_{th}}\times 100$.
Step‑by‑Step Calculation: $\%\text{Yield}=\dfrac{5.2}{6.0}\times 100=86.7\%$.
Final Answer: $86.7\%$ (rounded to one decimal place).

numericals.question: Determine the pH of a 0.010 M aqueous solution of acetic acid ( $K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$ ).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $C = 0.010\\ \text{M}$, $K_a = 1.8\\times10^{-5}$.
Formula (weak acid): $K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{C-x}\approx \dfrac{x^2}{C}$, $pH = -\log x$.
Step‑by‑Step Calculation: $x = \sqrt{K_a C}=\sqrt{1.8\\times10^{-5}\times0.010}=\sqrt{1.8\\times10^{-7}}=1.34\\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}$. $pH = -\log(1.34\\times10^{-4})=3.87$.
Final Answer: $pH = 3.87$.

numericals.question: The half‑life of the first‑order decomposition of acetone is 2.5 h. Calculate the rate constant $k$ (in $\text{h}^{-1}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $t_{1/2}=2.5\\ \text{h}$.
Formula (first order): $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\;\Rightarrow\;k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$.
Step‑by‑Step Calculation: $k=\dfrac{0.693}{2.5}=0.277\\ \text{h}^{-1}$.
Final Answer: $k = 0.277\\ \text{h}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: Prove that oxidation of a secondary alcohol yields a ketone by showing the change in oxidation state of the carbon bearing the –OH group.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: General secondary alcohol $\text{R}_1\text{-CH(OH)-R_2}$.
Oxidation State (OS) calculation: For carbon attached to –OH, two C–C bonds (each $-1$), one C–H bond ($+1$), and one C–O bond (oxygen is more electronegative, carbon gets $+1$).
OS$_{\text{alcohol}} = (-1)+(-1)+(+1)+(+1)=0$.
After oxidation to ketone $\text{R}_1\text{-C(=O)-R_2}$, the carbon forms a C=O double bond (two C–O bonds, each $+1$) and two C–C bonds ($-1$ each).
OS$_{\text{ketone}} = (-1)+(-1)+(+1)+(+1)=0$ for each C–O bond, but the double bond contributes $+2$, giving OS $=+2$.
Conclusion: The carbon’s oxidation state increases from $0$ to $+2$, confirming oxidation. Hence a secondary alcohol is converted to a ketone.

numericals.question: Calculate the boiling point elevation ($\Delta T_b$) when 1.5 mol kg$^{-1}$ ethanoic acid is dissolved in water. $K_b$(water) = 0.512 °C·kg mol$^{-1}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Molality $m = 1.5\\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$, $K_b = 0.512\\ ^\circ\text{C\,kg mol}^{-1}$.
Formula: $\Delta T_b = K_b \times m$.
Step‑by‑Step Calculation: $\Delta T_b = 0.512 \times 1.5 = 0.768\\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
Final Answer: $\Delta T_b = 0.77\\ ^\circ\text{C}$ (rounded to two decimal places).

pyq.question: Write the general formula for aldehydes and name the functional group attached to carbonyl carbon.
pyq.answer_html:
General formula: $RCHO$
Functional group: $-CHO$ (formyl group)

pyq.question: State one laboratory method for preparing aldehydes from primary alcohols.
pyq.answer_html: Oxidation of a primary alcohol using $PCC$ (pyridinium chlorochromate) or $K_2Cr_2O_7$ in dilute $H_2SO_4$ gives the corresponding aldehyde.

pyq.question: Explain the nucleophilic addition of sodium borohydride ($NaBH_4$) to aldehydes, showing the key steps.
pyq.answer_html:
1. $NaBH_4$ provides a hydride ion $H^{-}$.
2. $H^{-}$ attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of $RCHO$, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate $RCH_2O^{-}$.
3. The alkoxide is protonated by water or an acid work‑up to give the primary alcohol $RCH_2OH$.

pyq.question: Write the IUPAC name of $CH_3CH_2COOH$ and give its common name.
pyq.answer_html:
IUPAC name: Propanoic acid
Common name: Propionic acid

pyq.question: Discuss the methods of preparation of carboxylic acids and mention one industrial example for each method.
pyq.answer_html:
1. Oxidation of primary alcohols/aldehydes (e.g., $CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{K_2Cr_2O_7/H_2SO_4}$ ethanoic acid – industrially used for vinegar).
2. Hydrolysis of nitriles (e.g., $CH_3CN + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+}$ acetic acid).
3. Carbonylation of alkyl halides (e.g., $CH_3Cl + CO + AlCl_3 \rightarrow CH_3COCl$, followed by hydrolysis to acetic acid).
4. Oxidative carbonylation of methanol (industrial route to acetic acid: $CH_3OH + CO \xrightarrow{Rh\,cat.}$ acetic acid).
Each method provides a practical route for large‑scale production of specific carboxylic acids.

pyq.question: Explain the differences in physical properties and reactivity between aldehydes and ketones, referring to boiling point trends and nucleophilic addition reactions.
pyq.answer_html:
Boiling point: Ketones generally have higher boiling points than aldehydes of similar molecular weight because the carbonyl carbon in ketones is attached to two alkyl groups, increasing van der Waals forces.
Polarity: Both contain $C=O$, but aldehydes have a hydrogen attached, making them slightly more polar and often lower boiling.
Reactivity: Aldehydes are more susceptible to nucleophilic addition than ketones because the carbonyl carbon in aldehydes is less sterically hindered and more electrophilic.
Consequences: Aldehydes readily undergo oxidation to carboxylic acids, whereas ketones are resistant to oxidation under mild conditions.

mcq.q: Which of the following reagents is used for the selective oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde without further oxidation to a carboxylic acid?
mcq.explain: Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes and does not over‑oxidise them to acids.

mcq.q: In the Cannizzaro reaction, which statement is correct?
options: It occurs only with aldehydes having no $\alpha$‑hydrogen.
It requires a strong acid catalyst.
It gives a mixture of a primary alcohol and a carboxylic acid from the same aldehyde molecule.
It proceeds via a free‑radical mechanism.
mcq.explain: In the Cannizzaro reaction, a non‑$\alpha$‑hydrogen aldehyde undergoes simultaneous oxidation and reduction to give an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.

mcq.q:
Assertion: $\ce{RCHO}$ (an aldehyde) shows a characteristic $\text{C}=\text{O}$ stretching band near $\pu{1740 cm^{-1}}$ in IR spectrum.
Reason: The carbonyl group in aldehydes is conjugated with a $\pi$‑system, lowering its stretching frequency.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Aldehyde $\text{C}=\text{O}$ stretch appears around $\pu{1725-1740 cm^{-1}}$, but the reason given is incorrect; conjugation actually lowers the frequency, not raises it.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements about $\alpha,\beta$‑unsaturated carbonyl compounds is FALSE?
options: They undergo 1,4‑addition (Michael addition) more readily than 1,2‑addition.
The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond is more reactive towards nucleophiles than the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond.
They show a bathochromic shift in UV due to conjugation.
They are less acidic than saturated carbonyl compounds.
mcq.explain: Conjugation increases acidity of the $\alpha$‑hydrogen; thus $\alpha,\beta$‑unsaturated carbonyls are more acidic, not less.

mcq.q: The rate of nucleophilic addition to $\ce{R2C=O}$ (ketone) compared to $\ce{RCHO}$ (aldehyde) is:
options: Faster for ketone because of greater steric hindrance
Faster for aldehyde because of less steric hindrance
Same for both because carbonyl reactivity is independent of substituents
Faster for ketone because of stronger inductive effect of alkyl groups
mcq.explain: Aldehydes are less hindered and more electrophilic than ketones, so nucleophilic addition is faster with aldehydes.

mcq.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid directly to a primary alcohol?
mcq.explain: Lithium aluminium hydride is a strong reducing agent that reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols.

mcq.q:
Assertion: $\ce{CH3COOH}$ (acetic acid) is a stronger acid than $\ce{CH3CH2COOH}$ (propionic acid).
Reason: The inductive effect of the methyl group in propionic acid decreases the stability of its conjugate base.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: Acetic acid is actually stronger because the extra methylene in propionic acid exerts a weak electron‑donating (+I) effect, slightly decreasing acidity; the reason given is opposite.

mcq.q: In the haloform reaction, which of the following carbonyl compounds can give $\ce{CHX3}$ (X = Cl, Br) upon treatment with $\ce{X2}$ and $\ce{NaOH}$?
mcq.explain: Methyl ketones (including acetone and 2‑butanone) and acetaldehyde (which is a methyl aldehyde) undergo the haloform reaction to give $\ce{CHX3}$.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the acidity order of the following compounds: $\ce{RCOOH}$, $\ce{RCHO}$, $\ce{RCOR'}$?
mcq.explain: Carboxylic acids are the most acidic (pKa ≈ 4–5), aldehydes are weakly acidic (pKa ≈ 17), and ketones are even less acidic (pKa ≈ 20).

mcq.q: Which of the following reagents is most suitable for the preparation of $\alpha$‑bromo aldehydes from aldehydes?
mcq.explain: N‑Bromosuccinimide (NBS) under radical conditions selectively brominates the $\alpha$‑position of aldehydes to give $\alpha$‑bromo aldehydes.
