long_notes.Introduction and classification of amine:
Definition: Amines are nitrogen‑containing organic compounds derived from ammonia by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by alkyl or aryl groups.

General formulae: $RNH_2$, $R_2NH$, $R_3N$ (primary, secondary, tertiary) and quaternary salts $R_4N^+X^-$.

Classification:

  • Primary (1°) amine: $RNH_2$
  • Secondary (2°) amine: $R_2NH$
  • Tertiary (3°) amine: $R_3N$
  • Quaternary ammonium salt: $R_4N^+X^-$

Based on hybridisation of nitrogen:

TypeHybridisationGeometry
Primary$sp^3$Trigonal pyramidal (≈107°)
Secondary$sp^3$Trigonal pyramidal (≈107°)
Tertiary$sp^3$Trigonal pyramidal (≈107°)

Key quantitative relations:

  • Base dissociation constant: $K_b = \frac{[RNH][OH^-]}{[RNH_2]}$
  • $pK_b = -\log K_b$
  • At 25 °C, $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ (water autoprotolysis)

SI units: Concentration – mol·L$^{-1}$; $K_b$ – dimensionless; $pK_b$ – dimensionless.

Solved example: Calculate the pH of 0.010 M methylamine ($CH_3NH_2$) with $K_b = 4.4\times10^{-4}$.

Step 1: Write the equilibrium
$CH_3NH_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons CH_3NH_3^+ + OH^-$
Assume $x$ = [OH⁻] formed.
$K_b = \frac{x^2}{0.010 - x} \approx \frac{x^2}{0.010}$

Step 2: $x = \sqrt{K_b \times 0.010}=\sqrt{4.4\times10^{-4}\times0.010}=2.1\times10^{-3}\,\text{mol·L}^{-1}$

Step 3: $pOH = -\log x = -\log(2.1\times10^{-3}) = 2.68$
$pH = 14 - pOH = 11.32$

Thus a 0.010 M solution of methylamine is strongly basic (pH ≈ 11.3).
long_notes.Nomenclature and isomerism in amines:
Definition: Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia ($NH_3$) by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by alkyl or aryl groups.

General formula: $R_3N$, $R_2NH$, $RNH_2$ where $R$ = alkyl/aryl.

  • Primary amine (1°): $RNH_2$ – one alkyl group attached.
  • Secondary amine (2°): $R_2NH$ – two alkyl groups.
  • Tertiary amine (3°): $R_3N$ – three alkyl groups.

Nomenclature (IUPAC):

TypeParent hydrocarbonSuffixExample
Primaryalkane (remove –$e$)‑$amine$$CH_3CH_2NH_2$ → ethylamine
Secondaryalkane (remove –$e$)‑$amine$ (with “N‑substituted”)$CH_3CH_2NHCH_3$ → N‑methyl‑ethanamine
Tertiaryalkane (remove –$e$)‑$amine$ (with “N,N‑disubstituted”)$(CH_3)_2NCH_2CH_3$ → N,N‑dimethylethanamine

Isomerism: Amines exhibit structural isomerism (chain, position, functional) and stereoisomerism (cis‑trans in cyclic secondary amines, optical in chiral amines).

Key formula – Basicity constant (K_b): $K_b = \frac{[R_3NH^+][OH^-]}{[R_3N]}$ (dimensionless).

Solved Example:

Find the IUPAC name of $CH_3CH_2CH_2NHCH_3$.

  • Identify the longest carbon chain containing the –$NH$– group: 3‑carbon chain → prop‑.
  • Parent hydrocarbon = propane → replace –$e$ with –$amine$ → propan‑amine.
  • The substituent on nitrogen is a methyl group → prefix “N‑methyl”.
  • Final name: N‑methyl‑propan‑1‑amine.
long_notes.Methods of preparation of primary, secon:
Definition: Amines are nitrogen‑containing organic compounds having the general formulas $RNH_2$ (primary), $R_2NH$ (secondary) and $R_3N$ (tertiary), where $R$ denotes alkyl or aryl groups.

Key methods of preparation

  • Alkylation of ammonia (or lower amines): Direct nucleophilic substitution of alkyl halides with ammonia or a lower amine gives the corresponding amine.
    Primary: $R\text{-}X + NH_3 \rightarrow RNH_2 + HX$
    Secondary: $R\text{-}X + R'NH_2 \rightarrow RNR' + HX$
    Tertiary: $R\text{-}X + R'_2NH \rightarrow RNR'_2 + HX$
    Typical conditions: $R\text{-}X$ (alkyl bromide/iodide), excess $NH_3$, $K_2CO_3$ as base, $80\!\!\,^\circ\!C$.
  • Gabriel synthesis (primary amines): $KCN + R\text{-}X \rightarrow RCN$ (nucleophilic substitution). Hydrolysis of the nitrile in acidic medium gives the primary amine:
    $RCN + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} RNH_2 + CO_2$.
  • Reductive amination (secondary & tertiary amines): Carbonyl compound $\xrightarrow{NH_3/\text{primary amine}}$ imine, followed by reduction with $NaBH_4$ or $H_2/Pd$.
    $R_2C=O + NH_3 \rightleftharpoons R_2C=NH + H_2O$
    $R_2C=NH + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd/C} R_2CHNH_2$ (secondary) and further alkylation gives tertiary amine.
  • Hofmann rearrangement (primary amide → primary amine): $RCONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow RNH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O$.

SI units: Temperature $\,^{\circ}\!C$, pressure $\text{atm}$, concentration $\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.

Solved example (Preparation of aniline)

Step 1: Reduction of nitrobenzene with $Fe/HCl$:
$C_6H_5NO_2 + 3Fe + 6HCl \rightarrow C_6H_5NH_2 + 3FeCl_2 + 2H_2O$.
Conditions: $80\!\!\,^\circ\!C$, aqueous medium.
Step 2: Distillation of the crude product gives pure aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$). This method is high‑yielding and frequently asked in CBSE exams.
long_notes.Physical properties and basicity of amin:
Physical properties of amines

  • All amines are soluble in water due to hydrogen‑bond formation (except higher aliphatic amines).
  • Boiling points are higher than corresponding alkanes but lower than alcohols; trend: $RNH_2 > R_2NH > R_3N$.
  • Odour: characteristic fishy/ ammoniacal smell.
  • Density: $<1\text{ g cm}^{-3}$ for most low‑molecular amines.

Basicity

ParameterExpression
Base dissociation constant$K_b = \\frac{[RNH_3^+][OH^-]}{[RNH_2]}$
pK_b$pK_b = -\\log K_b$
Relation with acid constant$K_b = \\frac{K_w}{K_a}$, $pK_b + pK_a = 14$ (at $25^{\\circ}\text{C}$)

Factors affecting basicity:

  • Inductive effect: electron‑donating alkyl groups increase $K_b$.
  • Resonance in aromatic amines decreases $K_b$ (e.g., aniline).
  • Hybridisation: $sp^3 > sp^2 > sp$ for basicity.

Solved example

Given $K_b$ of methylamine $CH_3NH_2$ = $4.4\\times10^{-4}$, calculate $pK_b$ and the corresponding $K_a$ of its conjugate acid.

Solution:

  • $pK_b = -\\log(4.4\\times10^{-4}) = 3.36$ (approx).
  • Using $K_b = \\frac{K_w}{K_a}$ with $K_w = 1.0\\times10^{-14}$, $K_a = \\frac{K_w}{K_b}=\\frac{1.0\\times10^{-14}}{4.4\\times10^{-4}} = 2.27\\times10^{-11}$.
  • Thus $pK_a = -\\log K_a = 10.64$.

Key SI units: concentration – mol L$^{-1}$, temperature – $^{\\circ}$C, pressure – atm or Pa.
long_notes.Reactions of amines with acids, alkyl ha:
Definitions

  • Amines: Organic compounds containing a nitrogen atom bonded to one or more alkyl/aryl groups, general formula $R_3N$, $R_2NH$, $RNH_2$.
  • Basicity constant ($K_b$): $K_b = \\frac{[RNH_3^+][OH^-]}{[RNH_2]}$ (dimensionless).
  • $pK_b$: $pK_b = -\\log K_b$ (unitless).

Reactions with Acids

ReactionEquation
Protonation$RNH_2 + H^+ \\rightleftharpoons RNH_3^+$
Salt formation$R_3N + HCl \rightarrow R_3NH^+ Cl^-$

Reactions with Alkyl Halides

  • Alkylation (primary/secondary amines): $RNH_2 + R'X \rightarrow RNR' + HX$ (mono‑alkylation).
  • Dialkylation (tertiary amine): $R_2NH + 2R'X \rightarrow R_2N(R')_2 + 2HX$.

Reactions with Carbonyl Compounds

  • Formation of imines (Schiff bases): $R_2C=O + R'NH_2 \\rightleftharpoons R_2C=NR' + H_2O$ (acid‑catalysed).
  • Formation of amides: $RCOCl + R'NH_2 \rightarrow RCONHR' + HCl$.

Solved Example

Calculate the pH of a $0.01\\,\\text{M}$ aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$) solution. $K_b$ of aniline = $4.3\\times10^{-10}$.

Using $K_b = \\frac{[C_6H_5NH_3^+][OH^-]}{[C_6H_5NH_2]}$, assume $x = [OH^-]$:

$K_b = \\frac{x^2}{0.01 - x} \approx \\frac{x^2}{0.01}$

$x = \\sqrt{K_b \\times 0.01} = \\sqrt{4.3\\times10^{-10} \\times 0.01}=6.55\\times10^{-6}\\,\\text{M}$

$pOH = -\\log x = 5.18$, $pH = 14 - pOH = 8.82$.
long_notes.Amines in organic synthesis – Gabriel sy:
Definition: Amines are versatile nitrogen‑containing building blocks used to introduce –NH2 or –NHR groups into organic molecules. In synthesis they act as nucleophiles, undergo rearrangements and serve as precursors of amides, nitriles and carbamates.

Gabriel synthesis (primary amine preparation):

  • Step 1: $KPhthalimide$ + $R–X \xrightarrow{\text{DMF}}$ $N$‑alkylphthalimide.
  • Step 2: $N$‑alkylphthalimide + $NaOH$ (or $KOH$, $H_2O$, $\Delta$) $\rightarrow$ $R–NH_2 + KPhthalimide$ (hydrolysis).
ReagentRole
$KPhthalimide$Protected –NH2 source
$R–X$Alkyl halide (primary, $\text{CH}_3$–$\text{CH}_2$–$X$)
$NaOH$Cleaves imide to liberate amine

Hofmann rearrangement (amide → primary amine, one‑carbon loss):

  • Reaction: $R–CO–NH_2 + Br_2 + 4\,\text{NaOH} \xrightarrow{0\,^{\circ}\text{C}} R–NH_2 + CO_2 + 2\,\text{NaBr} + 3\,\text{H_2O}$.
  • Key intermediate: $R–CO–NBr$ (N‑bromoamide) → isocyanate $R–NCO$ → $R–NH_2$ after hydrolysis.

Curtius rearrangement (acyl azide → isocyanate → amine or carbamate):

  • Acyl azide formation: $R–COOH + NaN_3 \xrightarrow{\text{PBr}_3} R–CO–N_3$.
  • Thermolysis: $R–CO–N_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} R–NCO + N_2$.
  • Subsequent capture: $R–NCO + H_2O \rightarrow R–NH_2 + CO_2$ (amine) or $R–NCO + ROH \rightarrow R–NHCOOR$ (carbamate).

Solved example (Gabriel synthesis):

Prepare phenethylamine ($C_6H_5CH_2CH_2NH_2$) from potassium phthalimide and $bromoethane$.

  1. $KPhthalimide + C_6H_5CH_2CH_2Br \xrightarrow{DMF}$ $N$‑ethylphthalimide.
  2. $N$‑ethylphthalimide + $NaOH$ (reflux) $\rightarrow$ $C_6H_5CH_2CH_2NH_2$ + $KPhthalimide$.

Yield is typically $70\!\!\text{–}\!80\%$; the method avoids over‑alkylation and gives a pure primary amine.
long_notes.Important industrial and biological appl:
Definition: Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms with alkyl or aryl groups. They act as bases and nucleophiles, making them valuable in industry and biology.

Industrial applications

  • Polyamide (Nylon) synthesis: Hexamethylenediamine reacts with adipic acid to give Nylon‑6,6. $\text{HOOC-(CH}_2\)_4\text{-COOH + H}_2\text{N-(CH}_2\)_6\text{-NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{[–CO-(CH}_2\)_4\text{-CO-NH-(CH}_2\)_6\text{-NH–]}_n$
  • Corrosion inhibitors: Aromatic amines (e.g., aniline) adsorb on metal surfaces, reducing oxidation rates.
  • Pharmaceuticals: Many drugs contain primary or secondary amine groups (e.g., antihistamines, local anaesthetics).
  • Dyes and pigments: Amines undergo diazotisation and coupling to form azo dyes.

Biological applications

  • Neurotransmitters: Dopamine, serotonin and histamine are biologically active amines that transmit nerve impulses.
  • Vitamin B$_6$ (pyridoxine): A heterocyclic amine essential for amino‑acid metabolism.
  • Enzyme cofactors: Amines such as S‑adenosyl‑methionine donate methyl groups in biosynthetic pathways.

Key formula

The basicity of an amine in water is expressed by $pK_a = -\log K_a$, where $K_a$ is the acid dissociation constant of its conjugate acid. For a typical aliphatic amine $pK_a \approx 10\text{–}11$ (SI unit: dimensionless).

Solved example (neutralisation)

Calculate the mass of aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$, $M = 93.13\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) required to neutralise $25\,\text{mL}$ of $0.10\,\text{M}$ HCl.

Reaction: $C_6H_5NH_2 + HCl \rightarrow C_6H_5NH_3^+Cl^-$

Moles of HCl = $0.10\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\times 0.025\,\text{L}=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{mol}$. Since the stoichiometry is 1:1, moles of aniline needed = $2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{mol}$. Mass = $2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\times93.13\,\text{g mol}^{-1}=0.233\,\text{g}$. Thus, $0.233\,\text{g}$ of aniline will completely neutralise the acid.
long_notes.Environmental impact and safety aspects:
Environmental impact and safety aspects of amines

Amines are basic nitrogen compounds that, when released, can affect air, water and soil. Their toxicity is expressed by LD$_{50}$ (median lethal dose) in $mg\;kg^{-1}$ and by PEL (permissible exposure limit) in $ppm$ (parts per million) or $mg\;m^{-3}$.

  • Air pollution: Volatile amines react with atmospheric $SO_{2}$ and $NO_{x}$ forming secondary amine‑sulfonates and nitrosamines, both carcinogenic.
  • Water pollution: Amines are readily soluble; they raise the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) of water. The BOD increase can be estimated by $BOD = C\times k$, where $C$ is amine concentration ($mg\;L^{-1}$) and $k\approx0.5$.
  • Soil toxicity: High pH caused by amine hydrolysis can disrupt microbial activity. The pH shift $\Delta pH = \log\frac{[OH^-]_{final}}{[OH^-]_{initial}}$.

Safety measures

AspectControl
Personal protectionGloves, goggles, respirator (NIOSH rating $>95\%$ filtration)
EngineeringLocal exhaust ventilation, scrubbers using $H_{2}SO_{4}$
Spill handlingNeutralise with dilute $HCl$ (0.1 M) and absorb on inert material

Solved example

Calculate the PEL (in $ppm$) for a volatile amine with $LD_{50}=200\;mg\;kg^{-1}$ using the empirical relation $PEL = \frac{10^{3}}{LD_{50}}$.

Solution: $PEL = \frac{10^{3}}{200}=5\;ppm$. Thus the workplace concentration must not exceed $5\;ppm$.

Key take‑away: monitor amine emissions, maintain proper ventilation, and use neutralising agents to minimise environmental and health hazards.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Amines: Organic compounds containing nitrogen atom bonded to one or more alkyl/aryl groups; classified as primary ($RNH_2$), secondary ($R_2NH$) and tertiary ($R_3N$).
  • Basicity: Ability to accept a proton; measured by $K_b$ or $pK_b$.
  • Nucleophilicity: Ability to donate a lone pair to an electrophile; order in amines: $RNH_2 > R_2NH > R_3N$.
  • Basicity Order (in water): $R_3N > R_2NH > RNH_2$ (due to solvation effects).
  • Hofmann Elimination: $R_3N \xrightarrow{\text{Ag}_2\text{O},\,\text{heat}}$ alkene + $RNH_2$; gives the least substituted alkene.
  • Gabriel Synthesis: $\text{KPhthalimide} + RBr \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH}}$ $RNH_2$ after hydrazinolysis; avoids multiple alkylation.
  • Williamson Ether Synthesis Analogy: $RNH_2$ can be prepared by $RCl + NaNH_2 \rightarrow RNH_2 + NaCl$ (nucleophilic substitution).
  • Acid–Base Reaction: $RNH_2 + H^+ \rightleftharpoons RNH_3^+$; equilibrium lies to the right for stronger bases.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Amines behave as weak bases and good nucleophiles. Primary amines undergo substitution reactions more readily, while tertiary amines are sterically hindered but more basic in aqueous medium. Remember the dual trend: basicity increases with alkyl substitution, nucleophilicity decreases.

  • Mistake 1: Confusing basicity order with nucleophilicity order. Use $R_3N > R_2NH > RNH_2$ for basicity, but $RNH_2 > R_2NH > R_3N$ for nucleophilicity.
  • Mistake 2: Assuming all amines give the same product in Hofmann elimination. The reaction always yields the least substituted (Hofmann) alkene.
  • Mistake 3: Over‑alkylating in Gabriel synthesis. The phthalimide protects the nitrogen, preventing multiple alkylations.
  • Mistake 4: Ignoring solvation effects when comparing $pK_b$ values; values measured in water differ from gas‑phase trends.

numericals.question: Given $K_b = 4.4 \times 10^{-4}$ for methylamine, calculate its $pK_b$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $K_b = 4.4 \times 10^{-4}$

Formula: $pK_b = -\log K_b$

Calculation:

  • $pK_b = -\log (4.4 \times 10^{-4})$
  • $= -[\log 4.4 + \log 10^{-4}]$
  • $= -[0.6435 - 4]$ (using $\log 4.4 \approx 0.6435$)
  • $= 3.3565$

Final Answer: $pK_b \approx 3.36$ (dimensionless).

numericals.question: Calculate the percentage composition of nitrogen in aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Molecular formula $C_6H_5NH_2$

Molar masses (g mol$^{-1}$): C = 12.01, H = 1.008, N = 14.01

Formula: $\%N = \dfrac{\text{mass of N in one mole}}{\text{molar mass of compound}} \times 100$

Calculation:

  • Mass of N = $14.01$ g
  • Molar mass of aniline = $6(12.01)+7(1.008)+14.01 = 72.06+7.056+14.01 = 93.126$ g
  • $\%N = \dfrac{14.01}{93.126}\times 100 = 15.04\%$

Final Answer: Nitrogen constitutes $15.0\%$ by mass in aniline.

numericals.question: How many moles of $HCl$ are required to neutralise $2.5\,\text{g}$ of ethylamine ($C_2H_5NH_2$)?
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Mass of ethylamine = $2.5\,\text{g}$, reaction: $C_2H_5NH_2 + HCl \rightarrow C_2H_5NH_3^+Cl^-$

Molar mass of ethylamine: $C_2H_5NH_2 = 2(12.01)+7(1.008)+14.01 = 45.08\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Formula: $n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}$

Calculation:

  • $n_{ethylamine}=\dfrac{2.5}{45.08}=0.0554\,\text{mol}$
  • From stoichiometry, $1\,\text{mol}$ ethylamine reacts with $1\,\text{mol}$ $HCl$.
  • $n_{HCl}=0.0554\,\text{mol}$

Final Answer: $0.055\,\text{mol}$ of $HCl$ (≈ $4.99\,\text{g}$, using $M_{HCl}=36.46\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) is required.

numericals.question: Prove that the basicity of a polyamine equals the number of nitrogen atoms present in its molecule.
numericals.solution_html:
Proof:

Consider a polyamine having the general formula $\text{R-(NH}_2)_n\text{-R'}$, where $n$ is the number of –NH$_2$ groups (each containing one nitrogen atom).

Each –NH$_2$ group can accept one proton according to the reaction:

$\text{R-NH}_2 + H^+ \rightarrow \text{R-NH}_3^+$

Since the protonation occurs independently at each nitrogen centre, the total number of protons that can be accepted equals the total number of –NH$_2$ groups, i.e., $n$.

Therefore, basicity = number of nitrogen atoms = $n$.

numericals.question: Find the pH of a $0.025\,\text{M}$ solution of methylamine ($K_b = 4.4 \times 10^{-4}$).
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $C = 0.025\,\text{M}$, $K_b = 4.4 \times 10^{-4}$

Formula (base hydrolysis): $K_b = \dfrac{[CH_3NH_3^+][OH^-]}{[CH_3NH_2]}$ and $[OH^-] = \sqrt{K_b \times C}$

Calculation:

  • $[OH^-] = \sqrt{(4.4 \times 10^{-4})(0.025)} = \sqrt{1.10 \times 10^{-5}} = 3.32 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}$
  • $pOH = -\log(3.32 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.48$
  • $pH = 14 - pOH = 11.52$

Final Answer: $pH \approx 11.5$.

numericals.question: What mass of triethylamine ($C_6H_{15}N$) is needed to prepare $250\,\text{mL}$ of $0.1\,\text{M}$ solution?
numericals.solution_html:
Given: Desired volume $V = 250\,\text{mL}=0.250\,\text{L}$, concentration $C = 0.1\,\text{M}$

Molar mass of triethylamine: $C_6H_{15}N = 6(12.01)+15(1.008)+14.01 = 101.19\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Formula: $\text{mass}= n \times M$, where $n = C \times V$

Calculation:

  • $n = 0.1 \times 0.250 = 0.025\,\text{mol}$
  • Mass $= 0.025 \times 101.19 = 2.53\,\text{g}$

Final Answer: $2.53\,\text{g}$ of triethylamine is required.

pyq.question: Define primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary amines.
pyq.answer_html: 1 Mark each: Primary amine – $\text{R–NH}_2$; Secondary amine – $\text{R}_2\text{NH}$; Tertiary amine – $\text{R}_3\text{N}$; Quaternary ammonium ion – $\text{R}_4\text{N}^+$ (with a counter‑ion).

pyq.question: Write the general formulae for aliphatic and aromatic amines.
pyq.answer_html:
Aliphatic amines: $\text{R–NH}_2$, $\text{R}_2\text{NH}$, $\text{R}_3\text{N}$ (primary, secondary, tertiary).
Aromatic amine: $\text{Ar–NH}_2$ (e.g., aniline).

pyq.question: Explain the order of basicity of aliphatic amines in aqueous solution.
pyq.answer_html:
1 Mark: Basicity increases with the number of alkyl groups attached to N.
2 Marks: $\text{RNH}_2 < \text{R}_2\text{NH} < \text{R}_3\text{N}$ because alkyl groups donate electron density to N, stabilising the $\text{NH}_3^+$ ion formed on protonation.
3 Marks: Steric hindrance in tertiary amines slightly reduces basicity in very concentrated solutions, but in dilute aqueous medium the above order holds.

pyq.question: Write the reaction of a primary amine with nitrous acid and name the product formed.
pyq.answer_html:
Reaction: $\text{RNH}_2 + HNO_2 \rightarrow R\text{–N}\equiv\text{N}^+\text{Cl}^- + H_2O$ (in presence of HCl).
Product: Diazonium salt $\text{R–N}\equiv\text{N}^+$ (aryl diazonium if R is aryl).
Marking: 1 Mark for balanced equation, 1 Mark for correct product name, 1 Mark for condition (cold, acidic).

pyq.question: Discuss the methods of preparation of primary amines and give one example for each method.
pyq.answer_html:
1 Mark each method (5 Marks total).

  • Gabriel synthesis: $\text{KPhthN}\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaNH}_2 \rightarrow \text{PhthNCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$; hydrolysis gives $\text{RNH}_2$ (e.g., $\text{PhNH}_2$).
  • Hofmann degradation: $\text{RCONH}_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2,\,\text{OH}^-} \text{RNH}_2 + CO_2 + Br^-$. Example: $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2 \rightarrow CH_3\text{NH}_2$.
  • Reduction of nitriles: $\text{RCN} \xrightarrow{H_2,\,\text{Ni}} \text{RCH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Example: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} \rightarrow CH_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
  • Alkylation of ammonia: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{R–X} \rightarrow \text{RNH}_2 + HX$ (excess NH$_3$). Example: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow CH_3\text{NH}_2$.
  • Reduction of amides: $\text{RCONH}_2 \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} \text{RNH}_2$. Example: $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} CH_3\text{NH}_2$.

pyq.question: Explain how the structural difference between amines and ammonia influences their physical properties such as boiling point and solubility.
pyq.answer_html:
1 Mark for structural difference: Amine – nitrogen attached to one or more alkyl/aryl groups ($\text{R}_n\text{NH}_{3-n}$); Ammonia – $\text{NH}_3$ with no carbon substituents.
2 Marks for hydrogen‑bonding: Both can H‑bond, but in amines the lone pair is less available due to electron‑donating alkyl groups, reducing H‑bond strength compared to $\text{NH}_3$.
1 Mark for boiling point trend: $\text{NH}_3$ (−33 °C) < primary amine $\text{RNH}_2$ (e.g., $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, −6 °C) < secondary $\text{R}_2\text{NH}$ < tertiary $\text{R}_3\text{N}$ because larger molecular mass and increased van‑der‑Waals forces raise $T_b$.
1 Mark for solubility: Small amines (e.g., $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$) are highly soluble due to H‑bonding; solubility decreases with increasing alkyl chain length as hydrophobic character dominates.
Overall: Presence of carbon groups reduces H‑bonding ability, increases molecular size, and introduces dispersion forces, leading to higher boiling points and lower water solubility compared to ammonia.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the correct IUPAC name of $CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}$?
mcq.explain: The longest carbon chain has two carbon atoms; the –$NH_{2}$ group is treated as a substituent, giving the name ethanamine.

mcq.q: What is the order of basicity of amines in aqueous solution?
mcq.explain: Alkyl groups donate electron density to nitrogen; more alkyl groups increase basicity. Aromatic amines are less basic due to resonance delocalisation.

mcq.q: When a primary aliphatic amine reacts with nitrous acid ($HNO_{2}$) at $0^{\circ}C$, the major product is:
mcq.explain: Primary aliphatic amines form alkyl nitrites ($R\!-$ON=O) on reaction with $HNO_{2}$ at low temperature; diazonium salts are formed only from aromatic amines.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements about the reaction of amines with alkyl halides is correct?
options: Primary amines give only mono‑alkylated products
Secondary amines give only mono‑alkylated products
Tertiary amines undergo nucleophilic substitution to give quaternary ammonium salts
All amines give quaternary ammonium salts directly
mcq.explain: Tertiary amines lack N–H protons and react with alkyl halides to form quaternary ammonium salts via $R_{3}N+R'X\rightarrow R_{3}NR'^{+}X^{-}$.

mcq.q: The boiling point of amines compared to corresponding alkanes of similar molecular weight is:
options: Lower because of weaker van der Waals forces
mcq.explain: Amines can form N–H···$\!$X hydrogen bonds, raising their boiling points relative to non‑hydrogen‑bonding alkanes.

mcq.q: For a series of primary amines $C_{n}H_{2n+1}NH_{2}$, the $pK_{b}$ values:
mcq.explain: Longer alkyl chains donate more electron density, increasing basicity; thus $pK_{b}$ (inverse of basicity) decreases as $n$ increases.

mcq.q: Which reagent converts a primary amine into a primary amide?
mcq.explain: Acid chlorides such as acetyl chloride react with primary amines to give amides via nucleophilic acyl substitution.

mcq.q: Which of the following amines is least soluble in water?
mcq.explain: Aniline is aromatic; its lone pair is delocalised into the ring, reducing its ability to hydrogen‑bond with water, making it the least soluble.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): Aromatic amines are less basic than aliphatic amines because the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring. Reason (R): In aromatic amines, the $\pi$‑electron density of the ring withdraws electron density from nitrogen, reducing its ability to accept a proton.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
mcq.explain: Both statements are correct; resonance delocalisation withdraws electron density, decreasing basicity, and R correctly explains A.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): Oxidation of a primary aliphatic amine with $KMnO_{4}$ yields a carboxylic acid. Reason (R): The carbon attached to the –$NH_{2}$ group is oxidised while the nitrogen is removed as $N_{2}$ gas.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
mcq.explain: Primary aliphatic amines are oxidised to carboxylic acids; the carbon bearing –$NH_{2}$ is oxidised and nitrogen is released as $N_{2}$, so both statements are true and R explains A.

long_notes.Introduction and classification of amine:
Definition: Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_3}$) by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by alkyl or aryl groups.

General formula: $R_n\mathrm{NH_{3-n}}$ where $n = 0-3$.

Classification:

TypeGeneral formulaExample
Primary$\mathrm{RNH_2}$Methylamine ($\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$)
Secondary$\mathrm{R_2NH}$Dimethylamine ($\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}$)
Tertiary$\mathrm{R_3N}$Trimethylamine ($\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}$)
Quaternary$\mathrm{R_4N^+X^-}$Tetramethylammonium chloride ($\mathrm{(CH_3)_4N^+Cl^-}$)

Basicity: In aqueous solution amine $R_3N$ accepts a proton: $R_3N + H_2O \rightleftharpoons R_3NH^+ + OH^-$ . The base dissociation constant is $K_b = \frac{[R_3NH^+][OH^-]}{[R_3N]}$ (unitless). $pK_b = -\log K_b$ and $pK_b = 14 - pK_a$ (at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

Solved example:

Given $K_b$ of aniline = $4.3 \times 10^{-10}$, find $pK_b$ and $pK_a$.

  • $pK_b = -\log(4.3 \times 10^{-10}) \approx 9.37$.
  • $pK_a = 14 - pK_b \approx 4.63$.

Thus aniline is a weak base (higher $pK_b$) and its conjugate acid is a weak acid (lower $pK_a$).
long_notes.Nomenclature and IUPAC naming rules:
Definition: Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia ($NH_3$) by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by alkyl or aryl groups.

General formulas: Primary $RNH_2$, secondary $R_2NH$, tertiary $R_3N$ (where $R$ = alkyl/aryl).

  • Number of carbon atoms in the longest chain containing the –NH– group determines the parent hydrocarbon name.
  • The –NH– group is treated as a substituent named “amino” when it is not the principal characteristic group.
  • If the amine is the highest priority functional group, the suffix “‑amine” is used.
TypeIUPAC nameCommon name
Primary$RNH_2$ → $\text{alkyl}amine$methylamine, ethylamine …
Secondary$R_2NH$ → $\text{dialkyl}amine$dimethylamine …
Tertiary$R_3N$ → $\text{trialkyl}amine$trimethylamine …

IUPAC naming steps:

  1. Identify the longest carbon chain containing the –NH– group; number it to give the –NH– the lowest possible locant.
  2. If the amine is the principal group, replace the –e of the parent hydrocarbon with “‑amine” and add the locant (e.g., 2‑propylamine).
  3. If a higher‑priority group is present, name the amine as “amino‑$R$” substituent(s) with appropriate locants.
  4. For multiple amine groups, use prefixes di‑, tri‑, etc., and suffix “‑diamino”, “‑triamino”, etc.

Solved example:

Name $CH_3CH_2NHCH_3$.

Solution: The longest chain containing –NH– has three carbon atoms → propane. Numbering from the end nearest the –NH– gives the –NH– at C‑2. No higher‑priority group, so suffix “‑amine” is used. The substituent $CH_3$ attached to nitrogen is part of the parent chain, giving 2‑propylamine (common name: isopropylamine).
long_notes.Methods of preparation of primary, secon:
Definitions

  • Primary amine: $RNH_2$
  • Secondary amine: $R_2NH$
  • Tertiary amine: $R_3N$

General methods

Amine typeKey preparation method
PrimaryGabriel synthesis, reduction of nitriles, Hofmann bromamide, alkylation of ammonia
SecondaryAlkylation of primary amine, reductive amination of aldehydes/ketones
TertiaryAlkylation of secondary amine, exhaustive methylation (Hofmann), reaction of amine with alkyl halide in presence of base

Representative reactions

  • Gabriel synthesis: $KPhth + RBr \rightarrow Phthalimido\;R$; $Phthalimido\;R + N_2H_4 \rightarrow RNH_2 + Phthalimide$
  • Reduction of nitrile: $RCN + 2H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni/Pd} RCH_2NH_2$
  • Reductive amination: $RCHO + R'NH_2 \xrightarrow[NaBH_3CN]{pH\;6-8} RCH(NHR')OH \rightarrow RCH_2NHR'$

Solved example

Prepare $C_2H_5NH_2$ (ethylamine) by Gabriel synthesis.

  1. React $KPhth$ with $C_2H_5Br$ at $80^\circ\text{C}$ to give $N$‑ethylphthalimide.
  2. Hydrolyze $N$‑ethylphthalimide with excess $N_2H_4$ at $100^\circ\text{C}$ to liberate $C_2H_5NH_2$ and phthalhydrazide.
  3. Overall: $KPhth + C_2H_5Br \rightarrow N\text{-}C_2H_5Phth + KBr$; $N\text{-}C_2H_5Phth + N_2H_4 \rightarrow C_2H_5NH_2 + Phthalimide$.

Yield is calculated using $\%\text{Yield}= \frac{\text{actual mass}}{\text{theoretical mass}}\times100$.
long_notes.Physical properties and basicity of amin:
Physical properties of amines

  • All amines are basic due to the lone pair on nitrogen.
  • Boiling points increase with molecular weight and are higher than corresponding alkanes but lower than alcohols of similar size because N–H hydrogen bonding is weaker than O–H.
  • Solubility in water decreases down the series: $C_1$–$C_4$ amines are miscible; higher amines are sparingly soluble.
  • In aqueous solution they exist as $R_3N + H_2O \rightleftharpoons R_3NH^+ + OH^-$, giving alkaline pH.

Basicity constants

  • Base dissociation constant: $K_b = \\frac{[BH^+][OH^-]}{[B]}$ (dimensionless).
  • Relation with conjugate acid: $pK_b + pK_a = 14$ (at $25\,^{\circ}C$).
  • $pK_b = -\log_{10}K_b$, $pK_a = -\log_{10}K_a$.

Factors affecting basicity

  • Inductive effect: electron‑donating alkyl groups increase $K_b$ (alkylamines > arylamines).
  • Resonance: lone‑pair delocalisation in aniline reduces basicity.
  • Hybridisation: $sp^2$‑hybridised nitrogen (as in aniline) is less basic than $sp^3$.

Solubility & boiling point trend

CompoundBoiling point (°C)Water solubility
Methylamine$-6.3$Miscible
Ethylamine$16.6$Miscible
Triethylamine$89.5$Partially miscible

Solved example

Given $K_b = 4.4\times10^{-4}$ for aniline, calculate $pK_b$, $pK_a$ of its conjugate acid and $K_a$.

  1. $pK_b = -\log_{10}(4.4\times10^{-4}) \approx 3.36$.
  2. At $25\,^{\circ}C$, $pK_a = 14 - pK_b = 14 - 3.36 = 10.64$.
  3. $K_a = 10^{-pK_a} = 10^{-10.64} \approx 2.3\times10^{-11}$.

Thus aniline is a weak base (higher $pK_b$) and its conjugate acid is a very weak acid (very low $K_a$).
long_notes.Reactions of amines – alkylation, acylat:
Reactions of Amines – Alkylation, Acylation & Hofmann Rearrangement

Alkylation: Primary or secondary amine reacts with an alkyl halide ($R\!X$) in the presence of a base to give a higher substituted amine.

General equation: $R\!X + R'\!NH_2 \xrightarrow{\text{base}} R'\!NR_2 + HX$

  • Typical base: $NaOH$ or $K_2CO_3$.
  • Excess $R\!X$ is avoided to prevent over‑alkylation.

Acylation: Amines react with acid derivatives (acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters) to form amides.

With acid chloride: $R\!COCl + R'\!NH_2 \rightarrow R\!CONHR' + HCl$

With anhydride: $\left(R\!CO\right)_2O + R'\!NH_2 \rightarrow R\!CONHR' + R\!COOH$

Key points: reaction is faster with acid chlorides; a base (e.g., $NaHCO_3$) is used to neutralise $HCl$.

Hofmann Rearrangement (de‑carbonylation of primary amides):

$$\text{R–CONH}_2 + Br_2 + 4\,NaOH \rightarrow \text{R–NH}_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2\,NaBr + 2\,H_2O$$

One carbon atom is lost; the product is a primary amine with one fewer carbon.

ReagentProductConditions
$R\!X$ + $R'\!NH_2$$R'\!NR_2$Base, $0-25\,^{\circ}C$
$R\!COCl$ + $R'\!NH_2$$R\!CONHR'$Base, $0-30\,^{\circ}C$
$R\!CONH_2$ + $Br_2$ + $NaOH$$R\!NH_2$$\text{Ice bath}$, $pH>10$

Solved Example:

0.50 mol of benzamide ($C_6H_5CONH_2$) is subjected \to Hofmann rearrangement. Calculate moles of aniline ($C_6H_5NH_2$) formed.

  1. Stoichiometry from the equation shows 1 mol benzamide → 1 mol aniline.
  2. Therefore, moles of aniline = 0.50 mol.
  3. If the reaction volume is 250 mL, concentration $c = \frac{0.50\,\text{mol}}{0.250\,\text{L}} = 2.0\,\text{mol\,L}^{-1}$.

Thus, 0.50 mol (or 2.0 M in 250 mL) of aniline is obtained.
long_notes.Amines in organic synthesis – Gabriel sy:
Definition: Amines are organic compounds containing nitrogen atom bonded to one or more alkyl/aryl groups ($R\!-$NH$_2$, $R_2\!-$NH, $R_3\!-$N). They behave as bases and nucleophiles.

Key reactions in synthesis

  • Gabriel synthesis – preparation of primary amines from $\text{phthalimide}$.
  • Alkylation of amines – $R\!-$NH$_2$ + $R'X \rightarrow R\!-$NH$-R'$ (excess alkyl halide gives tertiary amine).
  • Acylation – $R\!-$NH$_2$ + $R'COCl \rightarrow R\!-$NHCO$R'$ (amide formation).
  • Hofmann elimination – $R\!-$N(CH$_3$)$_3^+\!$OH$^-$ $\xrightarrow{\Delta}$ alkene + $CH_3NH_2$ (least substituted alkene).
  • Mannich reaction – $\text{aldehyde} + \text{amine} + \text{ketone} \rightarrow \beta\!-$amino carbonyl.

Gabriel synthesis – mechanism

StepReaction
1$\text{Phthalimide} + KOH \rightarrow \text{Potassium phthalimide}$
2$\text{Potassium phthalimide} + R\!-$X \xrightarrow{\text{SN2}} \text{N‑alkylphthalimide}$
3$\text{N‑alkylphthalimide} + \text{hydrazine} \rightarrow R\!-$NH$_2$ + phthalhydrazide$

Solved example

Prepare ethylamine ($CH_3CH_2NH_2$) by Gabriel synthesis using ethyl bromide.

  1. Generate potassium phthalimide: $\text{Phthalimide} + KOH \rightarrow K^+\!$‑phthalimide + H$_2$O.
  2. Alkylate: $K^+\!$‑phthalimide + $CH_3CH_2Br \xrightarrow{\text{SN2}} N$‑ethylphthalimide + KBr.
  3. Hydrolyze: $N$‑ethylphthalimide + $N_2H_4 \xrightarrow{\text{reflux}} CH_3CH_2NH_2 + \text{phthalhydrazide}$.

Yield is high because the $\text{SN2}$ step proceeds without over‑alkylation, a common problem in direct alkylation of ammonia.
long_notes.Biological importance and industrial app:
Biological importance of amines

  • Alkaloids (e.g., morphine, nicotine) are nitrogen–containing bases that act as neurotransmitters or defensive compounds.
  • Polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, spermine) regulate cell growth, DNA stabilization and ion channel function.
  • Histamine, a primary amine, mediates allergic response and gastric acid secretion.
  • Many vitamins (e.g., pyridoxine) contain amine groups essential for enzymatic activity.

Industrial applications

ApplicationRepresentative amineUse
Polyurethane foams$\\text{Methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI)}$ + $\\text{polyol}$Reaction with diamines gives cross–linked polymers.
Corrosion inhibitors$\\text{Triethanolamine}$Forms protective film on metal surfaces.
Dyes & pigments$\\text{Aniline}$Precursor for azo–dyes via diazotisation.
Pharmaceuticals$\\text{Epinephrine}$Beta–adrenergic agonist.

Key relationships

  • For a weak base $B$ : $K_b = \\frac{[BH^+][OH^-]}{[B]}$ ; $pK_b = -\\log K_b$.
  • $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ (at $25\\,^{\\circ}\\text{C}$).

Solved example

Calculate the pH of $0.020\\,\\text{M}$ aniline solution ($K_b = 4.3\\times10^{-10}$).

  1. Set up $K_b = \\frac{x^2}{c - x} \approx \\frac{x^2}{c}$ where $x = [OH^-]$ and $c = 0.020$.
  2. $x = \\sqrt{K_b c} = \\sqrt{4.3\\times10^{-10}\\times0.020}=\\sqrt{8.6\\times10^{-12}}=9.3\\times10^{-6}\\,\\text{M}$.
  3. $pOH = -\\log x = 5.03$ ; $pH = 14 - pOH = 8.97$.

Thus aniline behaves as a weak base, giving a mildly alkaline solution.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Amines: Organic compounds derived from ammonia by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by alkyl or aryl groups. They are classified as primary ($R\text{-}NH_2$), secondary ($R_2\text{-}NH$) and tertiary ($R_3\text{-}N$) amines.
  • Aromatic amines: Amines in which the nitrogen atom is attached directly to an aromatic ring (e.g., aniline).
  • Basicity: Ability of an amine to accept a proton. Measured by $K_b$; higher $K_b$ means stronger base.
  • Order of basicity (aliphatic): $R_3N > R_2NH > RNH_2$ due to electron‑donating alkyl groups.
  • Effect of resonance (aromatic): Aromatic amines are weaker bases because the lone pair delocalises into the ring.
  • Nucleophilicity: Amines act as nucleophiles in substitution reactions; order follows basicity in protic solvents.
  • Hofmann elimination: Tertiary amines on heating with $\text{NaOH}$ give alkenes; the least substituted alkene (Hofmann product) predominates.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Quick recap: Amines are nitrogen analogues of alkanes. Remember the three families (primary, secondary, tertiary) and their general formulas. Basicity increases with alkyl substitution but decreases when the lone pair is delocalised (as in aniline).

Common pitfalls:

  • Confusing amines with amides – amides have a carbonyl attached to nitrogen and are non‑basic.
  • Incorrect naming: For primary amines, the suffix "-amine" is used (e.g., ethylamine). For secondary and tertiary, use "N‑substituted" (e.g., N‑methyl‑ethanamine).
  • Using $K_a$ instead of $K_b$ for basicity calculations; always convert via $K_a\times K_b = K_w$.
  • Neglecting the effect of aromatic resonance on basicity – aniline is far weaker than aliphatic amines.
  • Overlooking the correct stoichiometry in the nitrogen content formula – use the molecular weight of the whole compound, not just the amine part.

Focus on these points while solving numerical problems and naming reactions to avoid loss of marks.

numericals.question: A 0.500 g sample of an unknown primary amine is titrated with 0.100 M HCl. It requires 25.0 mL of acid to reach the equivalence point. Calculate the molecular weight of the amine.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: mass $\\,=0.500\\,\\text{g}$, $M_{\\text{HCl}}=0.100\\,\\text{mol\\,L}^{-1}$, $V_{\\text{HCl}}=25.0\\,\\text{mL}=0.0250\\,\\text{L}$.

Formula: $\\text{M.W.}=\\frac{\\text{mass}}{\\text{moles}}$, moles $=M\\times V$.

Calculation:
moles $=0.100\\times0.0250=2.50\\times10^{-3}\\,\\text{mol}$
M.W. $=\\frac{0.500}{2.50\\times10^{-3}}=200\\,\\text{g\\,mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: Molecular weight = $200\\,\\text{g\\,mol}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: The vapor density (D) of a liquid amine is found to be 45.0 (relative to hydrogen). Determine its molecular weight.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $D=45.0$ (relative to H$_2$).

Formula: $\\text{M.W.}=2\\times D$ (since $D=\frac{M}{2}$ for gases).

Calculation: $\\text{M.W.}=2\\times45.0=90.0\\,\\text{g\\,mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: Molecular weight = $90.0\\,\\text{g\\,mol}^{-1}$.

numericals.question: Calculate the pH of a 0.020 M aqueous solution of aniline (C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$) given $K_b=4.3\\times10^{-10}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given: $C=0.020\\,\\text{M}$, $K_b=4.3\\times10^{-10}$.

Formula: For a weak base, $x=\\sqrt{K_b C}$, $[OH^-]=x$, $pOH=-\\log[OH^-]$, $pH=14-pOH$.

Calculation:
$x=\\sqrt{4.3\\times10^{-10}\\times0.020}=\\sqrt{8.6\\times10^{-12}}=9.27\\times10^{-6}\,\\text{M}$
$pOH=-\\log(9.27\\times10^{-6})=5.03$
$pH=14-5.03=8.97$.

Answer: $pH=8.97$ (approximately).

pyq.question: Write the IUPAC name of the amine $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}$.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Longest carbon chain contains 3 C atoms → propyl.
1 mark: –NH$_2$ group attached to the chain → propylamine.

pyq.question: State the order of basicity of the following amines: $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}$, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}$.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Electron‑donating alkyl groups increase basicity.
1 mark: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N} > \mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH} > \mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$.

pyq.question: Write the reaction of a primary amine with nitrous acid and give the product formed.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: $\mathrm{RNH_2 + HNO_2 \rightarrow RN_2^+ + H_2O}$ (formation of diazonium ion).
1 mark: On warming it decomposes to give an alkene $\mathrm{R–CH=CH_2}$ (or $\mathrm{N_2}$ gas).

pyq.question: Ethylamine reacts with benzoyl chloride. Write the balanced equation and name the product.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Write reactants $\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2 + C_6H_5COCl}$.
1 mark: Show formation of amide $\mathrm{C_6H_5CONHC_2H_5}$ + $\mathrm{HCl}$.
1 mark: Product is N‑ethylbenzamide.

pyq.question: Explain why amines are weaker bases than ammonia.
pyq.answer_html:
1 mark: Lone pair on N is delocalised by +I effect of alkyl groups, reducing its availability.
1 mark: Alkyl groups donate electron density, increasing the N‑H bond polarity and stabilising the conjugate acid less.
1 mark: Hence $K_b$ of amines < $K_b$ of NH$_3$.

pyq.question: Discuss two methods of preparing primary amines and compare the physical properties of primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
pyq.answer_html:
Method 1 (Gabriel synthesis): $\mathrm{KPhthN_2 + R–X \xrightarrow{\text{SN2}} R–PhthN_2 \xrightarrow{\text{hydrolysis}} RNH_2 + PhthOH}$ (1 mark).
Method 2 (Reduction of nitriles): $\mathrm{RC\equiv N \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH_4}} RCH_2NH_2}$ (1 mark).
Physical properties:
• Boiling point: $\mathrm{primary > secondary > tertiary}$ due to H‑bonding ability (1 mark).
• Solubility in water: decreases from primary to tertiary because fewer N–H bonds are available for hydrogen bonding (1 mark).
• Odour: tertiary amines often have a stronger, more unpleasant odour (1 mark).

mcq.q: Amines are defined as organic compounds containing which functional group?
mcq.explain: Amines contain nitrogen atom directly bonded to carbon, represented as $-NH_2$, $-NHR$ or $-NR_2$.

mcq.q: Based on the number of alkyl groups attached to the nitrogen atom, a primary amine is classified as:
options: One alkyl group attached to N
Two alkyl groups attached to N
Three alkyl groups attached to N
Four alkyl groups attached to N
mcq.explain: In a primary amine the nitrogen is bonded to only one alkyl (or aryl) group; the other substituents are hydrogen atoms.

mcq.q: Arrange the basicity of the following amines in decreasing order: $CH_3NH_2$, $(CH_3)_2NH$, $(CH_3)_3N$.
mcq.explain: Basicity decreases with increasing substitution because steric hindrance reduces the availability of the lone pair; thus primary $> $secondary $> $tertiary.

mcq.q: When primary, secondary and tertiary amines react with nitrous acid ($HNO_2$), respectively they give:
mcq.explain: Primary amine → diazonium ion → $N_2$ gas; secondary amine → $N_2O$; tertiary amine does not react with $HNO_2$.

mcq.q: Which statement correctly describes the boiling point trend of aliphatic amines?
mcq.explain: Primary amines can form more N–H···N hydrogen bonds, giving higher boiling points than secondary and tertiary amines.

mcq.q:
Assertion: Aromatic amines are less basic than aliphatic amines.
Reason: The lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the aromatic ring.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcq.explain: In aromatic amines the nitrogen lone pair participates in resonance with the benzene ring, reducing its availability for protonation, hence lower basicity.

mcq.q: The IUPAC name of the compound $CH_3CH_2NHCH_3$ is:
mcq.explain: The longest carbon chain is ethyl; the methyl substituent is attached to nitrogen, giving N‑methylethylamine.

mcq.q: Reaction of ethylamine ($CH_3CH_2NH_2$) with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ yields:
mcq.explain: A primary amine gets protonated by $H_2SO_4$ forming the ethylammonium hydrogen sulfate salt.

mcq.q: In IR spectroscopy, a sharp absorption band near $3300\,cm^{-1}$ in an amine is due to:
mcq.explain: The N–H bond in amines shows a characteristic sharp band around $3300\,cm^{-1}$.

mcq.q: Methylamine ($CH_3NH_2$) is industrially important for the production of:
mcq.explain: Methylamine is a key intermediate in the synthesis of adipic acid, which is used to manufacture nylon.

long_notes.Carbohydrates – classification, general:
Definition: Carbohydrates are organic compounds composed only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the approximate ratio 1:2:1 and serve as a major source of energy and structural material in living organisms.

General formula: The empirical formula of a carbohydrate is $C_{n}(H_{2}O)_{n}$, where $n$ denotes the number of carbon atoms. For polyhydroxy aldehydes (aldoses) the molecular formula is $C_{n}H_{2n}O_{n}$; for polyhydroxy ketones (ketoses) it is $C_{n}H_{2n}O_{n}$ as well.

Classification (based on number of saccharide units):

  • Monosaccharides – single‑unit sugars (e.g., glucose, fructose).
  • Disaccharides – two monosaccharide units linked by a glycosidic bond (e.g., sucrose, lactose).
  • Polysaccharides – long chains of monosaccharide units (e.g., starch, cellulose, glycogen).

Important members

TypeCommon ExampleMolecular FormulaMolar Mass (g·mol$^{-1}$)
MonosaccharideGlucose$C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}$180
DisaccharideSucrose$C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$342
PolysaccharideStarch (amylose)$(C_{6}H_{10}O_{5})_{n}$Variable (depends on $n$)

SI Units: Amount of substance – mol; mass – g; concentration – mol·L$^{-1}$.

Solved Example: Find the number of moles of glucose present in a 90 g sample.
Molar mass of glucose = 180 g·mol$^{-1}$.
$$n = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \frac{90\ \text{g}}{180\ \text{g·mol}^{-1}} = 0.5\ \text{mol}$$
Thus, 90 g of glucose corresponds \to $0.5$ mol, which contains $0.5 \times 6.022\times10^{23} \approx 3.01\times10^{23}$ molecules.
long_notes.Structural features and isomerism of car:
Definition: Carbohydrates are organic compounds composed only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, possessing the empirical formula $C_n(H_2O)_n$ where $n$ is the number of carbon atoms.

Structural features of monosaccharides

  • Contain either an aldehyde (aldose) or a ketone (ketose) group.
  • All other carbon atoms bear a hydroxyl ($-\!OH$) group.
  • Each carbon (except the carbonyl carbon) is a chiral centre, giving rise to optical activity.

Isomerism in carbohydrates

  • Chain isomerism: Different carbon skeletons (e.g., glucose vs. fructose).
  • Positional isomerism: Position of the carbonyl group changes (aldose vs. ketose).
  • Functional‑group isomerism: Same molecular formula but different functional groups (e.g., glucose vs. ribose).
  • Stereoisomerism: Varies in spatial arrangement of $-\!OH$ groups.
    • Enantiomers – non‑superimposable mirror images (D‑ and L‑forms).
    • Dia­stereomers – not mirror images (e.g., $\alpha$‑ and $\beta$‑anomers).

The number of possible stereoisomers for an aldo‑sugar having $n$ chiral centres is $2^{n}$, giving $2^{n-1}$ D‑forms and $2^{n-1}$ L‑forms.

Isomerism typeExample
ChainGlucose (C$_6$) vs. Fructose (C$_6$)
PositionalGlucose (aldose) vs. Fructose (ketose)
Functional‑groupGlucose vs. Ribose (both C$_5$H$_{10}$O$_5$)
StereoisomerismD‑Glucose vs. L‑Glucose

Solved example: Determine the total number of stereoisomers of aldo‑hexose.

Alto‑hexose has $n=6$ carbon atoms. The carbonyl carbon is not chiral; the remaining $n-2=4$ carbons are chiral centres.

Number of stereoisomers $=2^{4}=16$ (8 D‑forms and 8 L‑forms).

Thus, $\text{Total stereoisomers}=16$.

SI units: Optical rotation – degrees ($^{\circ}$); concentration – mol·dm$^{-3}$; path length – dm.
long_notes.Proteins – classification, peptide bond:
Definition: Proteins are large, biologically essential macromolecules composed of amino‑acid residues linked by peptide bonds, exhibiting specific three‑dimensional structures and functions.

Classification:

TypeExamples
Simple proteinsHemoglobin, Albumin
Conjugated proteinsGlycoproteins (e.g., mucin), Phosphoproteins (e.g., casein)
Derived proteinsPepsin (from pepsinogen), Trypsin (from trypsinogen)

Peptide bond formation: Condensation of the $\alpha$‑carboxyl group of one amino acid with the $\alpha$‑amino group of another releases water:
$\text{Amino acid}_1 + \text{Amino acid}_2 \rightarrow \text{Dipeptide} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
The covalent link is represented as $-CO-NH-$.

Levels of protein structure:

  • Primary: Linear sequence of residues.
  • Secondary: Regular patterns – $\alpha$‑helix and $\beta$‑pleated sheet stabilized by hydrogen bonds.
  • Tertiary: Three‑dimensional folding due to side‑chain interactions.
  • Quaternary: Association of two or more polypeptide subunits.

Key formula: Number of peptide bonds in a polypeptide containing $n$ residues is $n-1$.

Example: A protein consists of 150 amino‑acid residues. Calculate (i) the total peptide bonds and (ii) its approximate molecular weight if the average residue mass is $110\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Solution: (i) Peptide bonds $=150-1=149$.
(ii) Molecular weight $M =150\times110=16500\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.
long_notes.Important proteins and their functions:
Important Proteins and Their Functions

Proteins are polymers of α‑amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Their biological role is dictated by the sequence and three‑dimensional conformation.

  • Hemoglobin – transports O$_2$ and CO$_2$ in blood; each subunit contains a heme group that binds one O$_2$ molecule.
  • Myoglobin – stores O$_2$ in muscle cells; single‑chain protein with high affinity for O$_2$.
  • Insulin – regulates glucose metabolism; a peptide hormone of 51 amino‑acid residues.
  • Collagen – provides tensile strength to connective tissue; triple‑helix of Gly‑X‑Y repeats.
  • Enzymes (e.g., Amylase, DNA polymerase) – catalyze biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy.

General formula for molecular weight of a protein

$M = \sum_{i=1}^{n} n_i \; M_i$ where $n_i$ is the number of residues of amino‑acid $i$ and $M_i$ its molar mass (g·mol$^{-1}$).

Amino‑acidResidues ($n_i$)Molar mass ($M_i$, g·mol$^{-1}$)
Glycine1275
Alanine889
Phenylalanine4165

Solved Example

Calculate the approximate molecular weight of a peptide containing 12 Gly, 8 Ala and 4 Phe residues.

Using $M = \sum n_i M_i$:

$M = (12\times75) + (8\times89) + (4\times165) = 900 + 712 + 660 = 2272\,\text{g·mol}^{-1}$.

Thus the peptide’s molar mass ≈ $2.27\times10^{3}$ g·mol$^{-1}$.
long_notes.Nucleic acids – DNA & RNA structure, com:
Definition: Nucleic acids are biopolymers composed of nucleotides that store and transmit genetic information.

Basic unit – Nucleotide

ComponentDetails
Phosphate group$\mathrm{PO_{4}^{3-}}$
SugarDeoxyribose (DNA) / Ribose (RNA)
Nitrogenous basePurines (A, G) or Pyrimidines (C, T/U)

DNA vs RNA

  • DNA: double‑helix, deoxyribose, bases A, T, G, C.
  • RNA: single‑stranded, ribose, bases A, U, G, C.

DNA strands run antiparallel (5'→3' and 3'←5'), forming a sugar‑phosphate backbone that provides structural stability.

Each base pair advances the helix by $0.34\ \text{nm}$; ten base pairs complete one full turn ($3.4\ \text{nm}$ pitch).

Base‑pairing rules

  • DNA: A $\leftrightarrow$ T (2 H‑bonds, ~2\ kcal·mol$^{-1}$), G $\leftrightarrow$ C (3 H‑bonds, ~3\ kcal·mol$^{-1}$).
  • RNA: A $\leftrightarrow$ U (2 H‑bonds), G $\leftrightarrow$ C (3 H‑bonds).

Key formula – Molecular weight of a nucleotide

$M_{\text{nuc}} = M_{\text{base}} + M_{\text{sugar}} + M_{\text{phosphate}} - n_{\text{H_{2}O}} \times 18.015\ \text{g\ mol}^{-1}$

SI unit: g·mol$^{-1}$ for molecular weight.

Functions

  • DNA: genetic storage, replication, transcription.
  • RNA: messenger (mRNA), transfer (tRNA), ribosomal (rRNA), regulatory (siRNA, miRNA) and catalytic ribozymes.

Example

Calculate the molecular weight of deoxyadenosine monophosphate (dAMP).

Given: $M_{\text{A}} = 135.13$, $M_{\text{deoxyribose}} = 134.13$, $M_{\text{PO_{4}}} = 94.97$ (g·mol$^{-1}$). One water molecule is lost on condensation ($n_{\text{H_{2}O}}=1$).

$M_{\text{dAMP}} = 135.13 + 134.13 + 94.97 - 18.015 = 346.215\ \text{g\ mol}^{-1}$.

Thus one mole of dAMP weighs $3.46 \times 10^{2}\ \text{g}$.
long_notes.Lipids – classification, structure of fa:
Lipids – Classification, Structure of Fats, Phospholipids and Steroids

  • Simple lipids: fats & oils (triglycerides) and waxes.
  • Complex lipids: phospholipids, glycolipids, lipoproteins.
  • Derived lipids: steroids, prostaglandins, fat‑soluble vitamins.

Structure of Fats (Triglycerides)

Triglyceride formation is an esterification reaction:

$C_3H_5(OH)_3 + 3\,RCOOH \rightarrow C_3H_5(OOCR)_3 + 3\,H_2O$

where $R$ denotes the hydrocarbon chain of a fatty acid. Melting point is expressed in $^\circ C$ and density in $kg\,m^{-3}$.

Phospholipids

General formula:

$C_3H_5(OOCR_1)(OOCR_2)\! -\! PO_4\! -\! X$

Glycerol is esterified with two fatty acids; the third hydroxyl forms a phosphodiester bond with a polar head group $X$ (e.g., choline). This amphiphilic nature creates bilayers in membranes.

Steroids

Core structure: three six‑membered rings (A, B, C) and one five‑membered ring (D) – the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus. Example: cholesterol $C_{27}H_{46}O$ (molar mass $386.65\,g\,mol^{-1}$). Steroids are largely insoluble in water; their solubility is expressed in $mg\,L^{-1}$.

Solved Example

Calculate the molar mass of a triglyceride formed from glycerol and three molecules of palmitic acid ($C_{16}H_{32}O_2$).

ComponentMolar mass (g·mol$^{-1}$)
Glycerol $C_3H_8O_3$$3\times12.01 + 8\times1.008 + 3\times16.00 = 92.09$
Palmitic acid $C_{16}H_{32}O_2$$16\times12.01 + 32\times1.008 + 2\times16.00 = 256.42$
Water (lost, 3 mol)$3\times18.02 = 54.06$

Molar mass of triglyceride $= 92.09 + 3\times256.42 - 54.06 = 807.5\,g\,mol^{-1}$.
long_notes.Vitamins – classification (fat soluble &:
Vitamins – Definition: Organic micronutrients required in minute quantities for normal metabolic functions, which cannot be synthesized endogenously in adequate amounts.

Classification (based on solubility):

Fat‑solubleWater‑soluble
  • Vitamin $A$ (Retinol)
  • Vitamin $D$ (Calciferol)
  • Vitamin $E$ (Tocopherol)
  • Vitamin $K$ (Phylloquinone)
  • Vitamin $C$ (Ascorbic acid)
  • Vitamin $B_1$ (Thiamine)
  • Vitamin $B_2$ (Riboflavin)
  • Vitamin $B_3$ (Niacin)
  • Vitamin $B_5$ (Pantothenic acid)
  • Vitamin $B_6$ (Pyridoxine)
  • Vitamin $B_7$ (Biotin)
  • Vitamin $B_9$ (Folate)
  • Vitamin $B_{12}$ (Cobalamin)

Significance:

  • Fat‑soluble vitamins are stored in hepatic and adipose tissues; deficiency manifests slowly (e.g., night blindness for $A$, rickets for $D$).
  • Water‑soluble vitamins are not stored appreciably; excess is excreted in urine, so regular intake is essential.
  • All vitamins act as co‑enzymes or precursors, facilitating biochemical pathways such as oxidative phosphorylation, DNA synthesis, and antioxidant defence.
  • SI units: $\text{mg}$ (milligram) for most vitamins; $\mu\text{g}$ (microgram) for $A$, $D$, $E$, $K$ (e.g., $900\,\mu\text{g}$ RAE for $A$).

Solved Example:

Calculate the daily vitamin $C$ requirement for a $60\,\text{kg}$ adult if the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is $90\,\text{mg}$ for a $70\,\text{kg}$ reference adult and requirement scales linearly with body weight.

Formula: $\text{Requirement}=\text{RDA}\times\frac{\text{Body weight}}{70\,\text{kg}}$

Substituting: $\text{Requirement}=90\,\text{mg}\times\frac{60}{70}=77.14\,\text{mg}$

Thus, the individual should consume approximately $77\,\text{mg}$ of vitamin $C$ per day.
long_notes.Role of biomolecules in health, deficien:
Biomolecules & Health

Biomolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and vitamins are essential for growth, repair and metabolic regulation. Their adequate intake maintains physiological homeostasis, whereas deficiency leads to specific disorders.

  • Carbohydrates – primary energy source; deficiency causes hypoglycaemia.
  • Proteins – building blocks for tissues, enzymes, antibodies; deficiency → kwashi‑kwashi, edema.
  • Lipids – provide essential fatty acids & fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); deficiency → dermatitis, impaired coagulation.
  • Vitamins & Minerals – act as co‑enzymes & structural components; specific deficiencies cause scurvy, rickets, anemia, etc.

Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)

BiomoleculeRDA (adult)SI Unit
Carbohydrate$130$$\text{g/day}$
Protein$0.8$–$1.0$$\text{g/kg body wt}$
Fat$20$–$35$$\% \text{ of total calories}$
Vitamin C$75$–$90$$\text{mg/day}$

Sample Calculation

Find the daily protein requirement for a 60 kg adult.

Formula: $\text{Protein}_{\text{RDA}} = 0.8 \times \text{Body wt (kg)}$ (g)

Substituting, $\text{Protein}_{\text{RDA}} = 0.8 \times 60 = 48 \,\text{g/day}$.

Thus the individual should consume at least $48\,$g of protein daily to prevent deficiency.

Ensuring a balanced diet with appropriate portions of each biomolecule safeguards against deficiency diseases and supports optimal health.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Biomolecule: Any organic molecule produced by living organisms (e.g., carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids).
  • Carbohydrate: Organic compounds with the empirical formula $(CH_2O)_n$; primary source of metabolic energy.
  • Monosaccharide: Simplest carbohydrate unit (e.g., glucose, fructose).
  • Disaccharide: Two monosaccharides linked by a glycosidic bond (e.g., sucrose, maltose).
  • Polysaccharide: Long chain of monosaccharide units; may be linear (starch) or branched (glycogen).
  • Protein: Polymer of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; contains C, H, N, O and often S.
  • Amino‑acid: $\text{NH}_2-CHR-COOH$ where $R$ is the side‑chain.
  • Nucleic Acid: Polymer of nucleotides; DNA stores genetic information, RNA is involved in protein synthesis.
  • Nucleotide: $\text{(sugar)}-\text{(phosphate)}-\text{(nitrogenous base)}$.
  • Lipid: Hydrophobic biomolecules (fats, oils, waxes, phospholipids); generally insoluble in water.
  • Enzyme: Biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up biochemical reactions.

Key Law: Miller's hypothesis – suggests that simple organic molecules could have formed under pre‑biotic conditions, providing a basis for the origin of biomolecules.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Summary: Biomolecules are the building blocks of life. Carbohydrates provide energy, proteins perform structural and catalytic roles, nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information, and lipids form membranes and store energy. All biomolecules are formed by condensation reactions (loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and can be broken down by hydrolysis.

Common Mistakes to Avoid:

  • Confusing empirical and molecular formulas – always multiply the empirical formula by the appropriate factor to obtain the molecular formula.
  • Ignoring the loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ during polymerisation; this affects the calculation of $\%$ composition.
  • Mixing up saturated and unsaturated fatty acids – remember that double bonds introduce $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and reduce hydrogen count.
  • Overlooking the presence of sulphur in proteins (e.g., cysteine, methionine) when writing empirical formulas.
  • Assuming all nucleic acids have the same sugar; DNA contains deoxyribose, RNA contains ribose.
  • Neglecting stereochemistry in monosaccharides – $\alpha$ and $\beta$ forms have different physical properties.

numericals.question: Calculate the number of moles of glucose present in a 180 g sample of pure glucose. (Molar mass of glucose = 180 g mol⁻¹)
numericals.solution_html:
Given:

  • Mass of glucose, $m = 180\,\text{g}$
  • Molar mass of glucose, $M = 180\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$

Formula: $n = \frac{m}{M}$

Step‑by‑step:

  1. Substitute the values: $n = \frac{180}{180}$
  2. Calculate: $n = 1$

Answer: $1\,\text{mol}$ of glucose is present.

numericals.question: A carbohydrate contains 40 % C, 6.7 % H and 53.3 % O by mass. Determine its empirical formula.
numericals.solution_html:
Given (per 100 g sample):

  • C = 40 g
  • H = 6.7 g
  • O = 53.3 g

Formula: Convert mass to moles and divide by the smallest mole number.

Step‑by‑step:

  1. Moles of C: $n_{C}=\frac{40}{12}=3.33\,\text{mol}$
  2. Moles of H: $n_{H}=\frac{6.7}{1}=6.70\,\text{mol}$
  3. Moles of O: $n_{O}=\frac{53.3}{16}=3.33\,\text{mol}$
  4. Divide each by the smallest (3.33):
    $\frac{n_{C}}{3.33}=1$, $\frac{n_{H}}{3.33}=2$, $\frac{n_{O}}{3.33}=1$

Answer: Empirical formula = $\mathbf{CH_{2}O}$.

numericals.question: The average molecular weight of a starch polymer is $1.0\times10^{6}\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$. Find its degree of polymerisation (DP) given that the monomer unit (glucose) has $M=180\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$.
numericals.solution_html:
Given:

  • Polymer molar mass, $M_{p}=1.0\times10^{6}\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$
  • Monomer molar mass, $M_{m}=180\,\text{g\,mol}^{-1}$

Formula: $\text{DP}=\frac{M_{p}}{M_{m}}$

Step‑by‑step:

  1. Substitute: $\text{DP}=\frac{1.0\times10^{6}}{180}$
  2. Calculate: $\text{DP}\approx5.56\times10^{3}$

Answer: Degree of polymerisation $\approx 5.6\times10^{3}$ glucose units.

numericals.question: If the standard free energy change for ATP hydrolysis is $\Delta G^{\circ'} = -30.5\,\text{kJ\,mol}^{-1}$, how much energy is released when 2 mol of ATP are hydrolysed under standard conditions?
numericals.solution_html:
Given:

  • $\Delta G^{\circ'} = -30.5\,\text{kJ\,mol}^{-1}$
  • Number of moles, $n = 2\,\text{mol}$

Formula: $\Delta G_{\text{total}} = n\times\Delta G^{\circ'}$

Step‑by‑step:

  1. $\Delta G_{\text{total}} = 2\times(-30.5)$
  2. $\Delta G_{\text{total}} = -61\,\text{kJ}$

Answer: $61\,\text{kJ}$ of energy is released (exergonic).

numericals.question: How many grams of protein are required to supply 150 kcal, knowing that 1 g of protein provides 4 kcal?
numericals.solution_html:
Given:

  • Energy required, $E = 150\,\text{kcal}$
  • Energy per gram of protein, $e = 4\,\text{kcal\,g}^{-1}$

Formula: $m = \frac{E}{e}$

Step‑by‑step:

  1. $m = \frac{150}{4}$
  2. $m = 37.5\,\text{g}$

Answer: $37.5\,\text{g}$ of protein.

pyq.question: Write the general formula for a monosaccharide and name the simplest monosaccharide.
pyq.answer_html:
General formula: $C_nH_{2n}O_n$ (or $C_n(H_2O)_n$).
Simplest monosaccharide: Glyceraldehyde ($C_3H_6O_3$).

pyq.question: State two differences between DNA and RNA.
pyq.answer_html:
• DNA contains deoxyribose sugar; RNA contains ribose sugar.
  • DNA uses thymine as a base; RNA uses uracil instead of thymine.

mcq.q: Which of the following is not a component of nucleic acids?
mcq.explain: Nucleic acids are composed of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) and a nitrogenous base. Amino groups are not part of nucleic acid structure.

mcq.q: The primary structure of a protein is determined by
mcq.explain: The primary structure refers to the linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

mcq.q: Assertion: DNA replication is semi-conservative. Reason: Each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental and one newly synthesized strand.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

mcq.q: Which of the following monosaccharides is a ketose?
mcq.explain: Fructose contains a ketone functional group at C-2, making it a ketose, whereas the others are aldoses.

mcq.q: In the structure of a typical phospholipid, the hydrophilic head contains
mcq.explain: The polar head of a phospholipid consists of glycerol linked to a phosphate group (often with additional polar groups).

mcq.q: The enzyme that catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds during protein synthesis is
mcq.explain: Ribosomes facilitate the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids during translation.

mcq.q: Assertion: Unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points than saturated fatty acids. Reason: Presence of cis double bonds introduces kinks, preventing tight packing.
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false

mcq.explain: Cis double bonds create bends in the hydrocarbon chain, reducing van der Waals interactions and lowering the melting point; the reason explains the assertion.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a storage polysaccharide in plants?
mcq.explain: Starch serves as the major storage carbohydrate in plants, whereas cellulose is structural, glycogen is animal storage, and chitin is fungal/exoskeletal.

mcq.q: The functional group present in all amino acids is
mcq.explain: Every amino acid contains both a carboxyl ($-\mathrm{COOH}$) and an amino ($-\mathrm{NH_2}$) group attached to the same carbon atom.

mcq.q: Which vitamin is essential for the synthesis of collagen?
mcq.explain: Vitamin C acts as a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, enzymes required for collagen maturation.

long_notes.Carbohydrates – classification, structur:
Definition: Carbohydrates are organic compounds with the general formula $C_n(H_2O)_n$ (or $C_nH_{2n}O_n$) containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed 1:2:1 ratio. They serve as primary energy sources and structural components in living organisms.

Classification:

  • Monosaccharides – simplest units (e.g., glucose, fructose). Formula $C_6H_{12}O_6$.
  • Disaccharides – two monosaccharide units linked by a glycosidic bond (e.g., sucrose, maltose).
  • Polysaccharides – long chains of monosaccharide residues (e.g., starch, cellulose, glycogen).

Structural Forms:

  • Open‑chain (acyclic) – linear aldehyde (aldose) or ketone (ketose) form.
  • Cyclic – hemiacetal/hemiacetal formation gives furanose (5‑membered) or pyranose (6‑membered) rings.

Isomerism:

  • Structural isomerism – chain, positional and functional‑group isomers.
  • Stereoisomerism –
    • Enantiomers: non‑superimposable mirror images (D‑ and L‑forms). Determined by configuration at the highest numbered chiral carbon.
    • Di­astereomers: stereoisomers not related as mirror images.
    • Anomers: cyclic forms differing at the anomeric carbon ($\alpha$ or $\beta$).

Key Formulae:

  • Molar mass of a carbohydrate = $12n + 2n + 16n = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$ for $C_6H_{12}O_6$.
  • Mass‑% of carbon = $\frac{12n}{180}\times100\% = 40\%$ (for glucose).

SI Units: Molecular weight – g·mol$^{-1}$; concentration – mol·L$^{-1}$.

Solved Example: Calculate moles of glucose in $180\,\text{g}$ sample.

Given molar mass $M_{\text{glucose}} = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$,\[ n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{180\,\text{g}}{180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 1\,\text{mol} \]Thus $180\,\text{g}$ of glucose corresponds to $1\,\text{mol}$ (or $6.02\times10^{23}$ molecules).
long_notes.Monosaccharides – important examples and:
Monosaccharides – simplest carbohydrates containing a single carbonyl group and $C_nH_{2n}O_n$ ( $n = 3$ to $7$ ). They are classified as aldoses (aldehyde group) or ketoses (ketone group).

Important examples

Common NameFormulaType
Glyceraldehyde$C_3H_6O_3$Aldose
Dihydroxyacetone$C_3H_6O_3$Ketose
Glucose (D‑glucose)$C_6H_{12}O_6$Aldose
Fructose$C_6H_{12}O_6$Ketose
Ribose$C_5H_{10}O_5$Aldose

Key reactions

  • Oxidation (to aldonic/uronic acids): $R-CHO + [O] \rightarrow R-COOH$ (aldose) or $R-CO-CH_2OH + [O] \rightarrow R-COOH$ (ketose).
  • Reduction (to alditols): $R-CHO + 2[H] \rightarrow R-CH_2OH$ giving e.g., glucose \rightarrow sorbitol.
  • Formation of glycosidic bond: $R-OH + HO-R' \rightarrow R-O-R' + H_2O$ (condensation).
  • Isomerisation (Lobry de Bruyn–Alberda van Ekenstein): Aldose \leftrightarrow Ketose via enediol intermediate.

Solved example

Calculate moles of glucose in $180\ \text{g}$ sample. Molar mass of glucose $M = 180\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

$$n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{180\ \text{g}}{180\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 1\ \text{mol}$$

Thus $1\ \text{mol}$ of glucose contains $6.02\times10^{23}$ molecules.
long_notes.Disaccharides and polysaccharides – stru:
Disaccharides – A disaccharide is a carbohydrate formed by a glycosidic linkage between two monosaccharide units. The linkage is denoted as $\alpha$ or $\beta$ depending on the anomeric carbon configuration and the carbon numbers involved (e.g., $\alpha$‑1,4, $\beta$‑1,2). Common examples are sucrose, lactose and maltose.

  • Sucrose: $\alpha$‑D‑glucose $\leftrightarrow$ $\beta$‑D‑fructose via $\alpha$‑1,2 bond; non‑reducing.
  • Lactose: $\beta$‑D‑galactose $\leftrightarrow$ $\alpha$‑D‑glucose via $\beta$‑1,4 bond; reducing.
  • Maltose: $\alpha$‑D‑glucose $\leftrightarrow$ $\alpha$‑D‑glucose via $\alpha$‑1,4 bond; reducing.

Polysaccharides – Long chains of monosaccharide units linked by glycosidic bonds. They are classified as homopolysaccharides (e.g., starch, glycogen, cellulose) or heteropolysaccharides (e.g., chitin). Key parameters:

  • Degree of Polymerisation (DP): $\text{DP}=\frac{M_n}{M_0}$, where $M_n$ is the number‑average molar mass (g·mol$^{-1}$) and $M_0$ is the monomer molar mass (g·mol$^{-1}$).
  • Average Molar Mass: $M_n=\frac{\sum n_i M_i}{\sum n_i}$.
PolysaccharideMonomerLinkageFunction
Starch (amylose)\alpha$‑D‑glucose$\alpha$‑1,4Energy reserve \in plants
Glycogen\alpha$‑D‑glucose$\alpha$‑1,4 \text{(branches $\alpha$‑1,6)}Energy reserve in animals
Cellulose\beta$‑D‑glucose$\beta$‑1,4Structural support \in plants

Solved Example

Calculate the degree of polymerisation of amylose if its number‑average molar mass $M_n = 1.2\times10^5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$ and the monomer molar mass $M_0 = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Solution:

  1. Write the DP formula: $\text{DP}=\frac{M_n}{M_0}$.
  2. Substitute the values: $\text{DP}=\frac{1.2\times10^5}{180}$.
  3. Perform the division: $\text{DP}=\frac{1.2\times10^5}{1.8\times10^2}=\frac{1.2}{1.8}\times10^{3}=0.667\times10^{3}\approx 667$.

Thus, the amylose chain contains roughly $667$ glucose units. The result is dimensionless, as DP is a count of monomer units.
long_notes.Proteins – amino acids, peptide bond and:
Proteins – Amino Acids, Peptide Bond & Levels of Organization

  • Amino acid: An organic molecule containing $\\alpha$‑carbon bonded to $\\text{–COOH}$, $\\text{–NH}_2$, a hydrogen and a variable $R$‑group.
  • General formula: $\\text{NH}_2\\text{–CH}(R)\\text{–COOH}$ (molar mass in $\\text{g\cdot mol}^{-1}$).
  • Peptide bond: Covalent $\\text{C–N}$ bond formed by condensation (dehydration) between $\\text{–COOH}$ of one amino acid and $\\text{–NH}_2$ of another, releasing $\\text{H}_2\\text{O}$.
ReactionProducts
$\\text{Amino acid}_1 + \\text{Amino acid}_2$$\\text{Dipeptide} + \\text{H}_2\\text{O}$

Levels of protein organization

  1. Primary – sequence of amino acids.
  2. Secondary – $\\alpha$‑helix, $\\beta$‑sheet (hydrogen bonding).
  3. Tertiary – 3‑D folding (disulphide bridges, hydrophobic interactions).
  4. Quaternary – association of multiple polypeptide chains.

Example: A protein has a molar mass of $5.0\\times10^3\\,\\text{g\cdot mol}^{-1}$ and is composed solely of glycine ($M_{\\text{Gly}} = 75\\,\\text{g\cdot mol}^{-1}$). Find the number of peptide bonds.

Solution:

  1. Number of residues $n = \\frac{M_{\\text{protein}}}{M_{\\text{Gly}}}=\\frac{5.0\\times10^3}{75}=66.7\\approx 67$.
  2. Peptide bonds $= n-1 = 66$.

Thus the protein contains $66$ peptide bonds.
long_notes.Nucleic acids – DNA and RNA structure, n:
Definition: Nucleic acids are high‑molecular‑weight polymers of nucleotides that store and transmit genetic information.

Basic unit – Nucleotide

  • Three components: a nitrogenous base (purine = A,G; pyrimidine = C,T,U), a five‑carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), and one or more phosphate groups.
  • General formula: $\text{Base–Sugar–(PO}_4\text{)}_n$.

DNA vs RNA

  • DNA: double‑helix, antiparallel strands, deoxyribose, bases A,T,G,C.
  • RNA: single‑stranded, ribose, bases A,U,G,C.

Base‑pairing rules (Chargaff’s rule)

  • $[A]=[T]$, $[G]=[C]$ in DNA.
  • In RNA, $[A]=[U]$, $[G]=[C]$.

Average molar mass of a nucleotide

  • DNA: $330\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$
  • RNA: $340\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$

Genetic information flow (Central Dogma)

  • DNA $\xrightarrow{\text{transcription}}$ RNA $\xrightarrow{\text{translation}}$ Protein.

Example: A DNA fragment weighs $10\ \mu\text{g}$ and contains 30 % A, 30 % T, 20 % G, 20 % C. Find the number of nucleotides.

BasePercentMolar mass (g mol$^{-1}$)
A30331
T30331
G20347
C20347

Average molar mass $M_{avg}=0.30\times331+0.30\times331+0.20\times347+0.20\times347=337.4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Moles $n=\frac{10\times10^{-6}\ \text{g}}{337.4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}}=2.96\times10^{-8}\ \text{mol}$.

Number of nucleotides $N=n\times N_A=2.96\times10^{-8}\times6.022\times10^{23}\approx1.78\times10^{16}$.
long_notes.Vitamins – classification, functions and:
Vitamins – Definition: Organic compounds required in minute amounts for normal metabolism, cannot be synthesized in adequate quantity by the human body.

Classification (by solubility):

Fat‑solubleWater‑soluble
Vitamin $A$ ($C_{40}H_{56}O$), Vitamin $D$ ($C_{27}H_{44}O$), Vitamin $E$ ($C_{29}H_{50}O_{2}$), Vitamin $K$ ($C_{31}H_{46}O_{2}$)Vitamin $C$ ($C_6H_8O_6$), B‑complex (B$_1$, B$_2$, B$_3$, B$_5$, B$_6$, B$_7$, B$_9$, B$_12$)

Absorption & Storage: Fat‑soluble vitamins are incorporated into micelles, absorbed with dietary lipids and transported as chylomicrons; they are stored in liver and adipose tissue. Water‑soluble vitamins are absorbed by active transport in the proximal small intestine and excess is eliminated in urine.

Key Functions:

  • Vitamin $A$: Vision, epithelial integrity, immune modulation.
  • Vitamin $D$: Calcium‑phosphate homeostasis, bone mineralisation.
  • Vitamin $E$: Antioxidant, protects membrane lipids.
  • Vitamin $K$: $\gamma$‑carboxylation of clotting factors.
  • Vitamin $C$: Co‑factor for hydroxylases, enhances iron absorption, antioxidant.
  • B‑complex: Co‑enzymes in carbohydrate, protein and lipid metabolism.

Deficiency Disorders (selected):

  • Vitamin $A$ – Night blindness, xerophthalmia.
  • Vitamin $D$ – Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults).
  • Vitamin $C$ – Scurvy: gum bleeding, impaired collagen synthesis.
  • Vitamin $B_1$ – Beriberi: peripheral neuropathy, cardiac failure.
  • Vitamin $B_9$ – Megaloblastic anaemia, neural‑tube defects.

Toxicity: Because fat‑soluble vitamins accumulate, excess intake may cause hypervitaminosis (e.g., $A$, $D$). Water‑soluble vitamins are generally excreted, so toxicity is rare, though very high doses of vitamin $C$ may cause gastrointestinal upset.

Solved Example:

Daily Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) of Vitamin $C$ = $60\ \text{mg}$. One orange provides $50\ \text{mg}$. How many oranges are needed to meet RDA?

Solution: Required number $= \dfrac{60\ \text{mg}}{50\ \text{mg/orange}} = 1.2$ oranges. Hence, at least $2$ oranges are required to satisfy the RDA.
long_notes.Lipids – classification, structure and b:
Definition: Lipids are a diverse group of hydrophobic biomolecules composed mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, which are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.

Classification

TypeExamples
Simple lipidsFats & oils (triacylglycerols), waxes
Compound lipidsPhospholipids, glycolipids, sphingolipids
Derived lipidsSteroids, terpenes, fat‑soluble vitamins

General structure of a triglyceride

Glycerol ($C_3H_8O_3$) esterified with three fatty acids gives the formula $C_{3}H_{5}(OCOR)_{3}$, where $R$ denotes the hydrocarbon chain (e.g., $C_{15}H_{31}$ for palmitic acid).

Biological importance

  • Long‑term energy reserve: $1\;g$ of fat yields $\approx9\;kcal$, about twice that of carbohydrates.
  • Major component of cell membranes – phospholipids form bilayers.
  • Precursors of hormones (steroids) and signaling molecules (eicosanoids).
  • Thermal insulation and mechanical protection.

Solved example

Calculate the molar mass of a triglyceride formed from glycerol and three molecules of palmitic acid ($C_{16}H_{32}O_{2}$).

  1. Write molecular formula: $C_{3}H_{5}(OCOC_{15}H_{31})_{3}$ → overall $C_{55}H_{98}O_{6}$.
  2. Molar mass = $55\times12.01 + 98\times1.008 + 6\times16.00$ g\,mol$^{-1}$ = $660.55 + 98.78 + 96.00 = 855.33\;g\;mol^{-1}$.

Thus the triglyceride has a molar mass of $8.55\times10^{2}\;g\;mol^{-1}$.

short_notes.title: Key Definitions & Laws
short_notes.html:
• Biomolecule: Any organic molecule that is a constituent of living matter (carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids).
  • Carbohydrate: Organic compound with general formula $\text{C}_{n}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{n}$; primary source of energy.
  • Monosaccharide: Simplest carbohydrate; empirical formula $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$.
  • Disaccharide: Two monosaccharide units linked by a glycosidic bond (e.g., sucrose $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$).
  • Polysaccharide: Long chain of monosaccharide units; formula $\text{(C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{5})_{n}$.
  • Protein: Polymer of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; essential for structure, enzymes, transport.
  • Amino Acid: $\text{NH}_{2}\text{-CHR-COOH}$ where $R$ is a side chain.
  • Peptide Bond: Covalent bond $\text{-CO-NH-}$ formed by condensation of $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ groups.
  • Nucleic Acid: Polymer of nucleotides; DNA and RNA store genetic information.
  • Nucleotide: $\text{(Sugar)+(Base)+(Phosphate)}$; basic unit of nucleic acids.
  • Lipid: Hydrophobic biomolecule; includes fats, oils, phospholipids, steroids.
  • Triglyceride: Ester of glycerol with three fatty acids; formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{5}(\text{OCOR})_{3}$.

short_notes.title: Summary & Common Mistakes
short_notes.html:
Summary: Biomolecules are classified into four major groups – carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids. Each group has a characteristic general formula and functional groups. Understanding the linkages (glycosidic, peptide, phosphodiester) is crucial for solving reaction‑type questions.

Common Mistakes:

  • Confusing empirical formula $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$ with molecular formula of a specific monosaccharide (e.g., glucose $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$).
  • Writing the peptide bond as $\text{-CO-CO-}$ instead of $\text{-CO-NH-}$.
  • For nucleic acids, forgetting the phosphate group in the backbone; the correct repeating unit is $\text{-(Sugar)-(Base)-(Phosphate)-}$.
  • Assuming all lipids are triglycerides; phospholipids and steroids have different structures.
  • Mixing up $\text{(C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{5})_{n}$ (polysaccharide) with $\text{C}_{n}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{n}$ (general carbohydrate) in calculations.
